#3220. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

#3217. Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” …

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.

#3215. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3214. GEN Restaurant (GENK) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Divestiture talks could reshape GEN into a retail consumer goods business.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

GEN Restaurant Group, Inc. (GENK +6.34%) reported a strategic transition toward a consumer-packaged goods business model following the announcement of a non-binding letter of intent to divest a significant portion of its restaurant operations. Management stated that the potential transaction would shift the company's focus to its retail brand and product development. The company indicated that the restructuring is intended to simplify its cost structure and significantly reduce corporate overhead as it exits the capital-intensive restaurant segment. According to the company, the remaining operations will center on the GEN brand identity and a manufacturing-light consumer goods model.

Operator: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to the GEN Restaurant Group, Inc. Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] This call is being recorded on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. I would now like to turn the conference over to Lucas Zimmerman, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Lucas Zimmerman: Thank you. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to GEN's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Joining us on today's call are GEN's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, David Kim; as well as Chief Financial Officer, Luke Hewko. Before we begin, I'd like to remind everyone that some of the statements management makes on this call are forward-looking statements that reflect management's current expectations about future operating and financial results. These statements include the proposed transaction with Chubby Group, the negotiation and potential execution of a definitive asset purchase agreement, the satisfaction of closing conditions, any phased restaurant transition as well as the amount and timing of any payments to the company.

They also include statements regarding the potential effects of the transaction on the company's balance sheet, cost structure and liquidity as well as expectations for our consumer packaged goods business, retail placements, revenue run rate, growth, profitability and potential uses of capital, including any return of capital to shareholders. A definitive asset purchase agreement has not yet been executed, and there can be no assurance that an agreement will be signed or that the proposed transaction will be completed on the terms discussed today. Although management believes these expectations and assumptions are reasonable, they remain subject to significant risks and uncertainties, and actual results could differ materially from what is stated or implied today.

For more information, please refer to the forward-looking statements section in today's press release and the risk factors described in the company's annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, and subsequent filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The forward-looking statements made on this call speak only as of today, and the company undertakes no obligation to update them as required by law, except as required by law. Please also note that today's call will include a discussion of adjusted EBITDA and restaurant-level adjusted EBITDA, which are non-GAAP financial measures. Important information, including reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures, is detailed in today's press release.

With that, it is my pleasure to turn the call over to GEN's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, David Kim. David, the floor is yours.

Wook Kim: Thank you, Lucas, and good afternoon, everyone. Today, I want to tell you where GEN is headed. Our goal is for GEN to become the household K-Food brand in America with our products in the everyday American home kitchen. That means a greater focus on our consumer packaged goods business, a business we believe can be very profitable while we continue to operate our restaurants and pursue the proposed transaction with Chubby Group. I will cover 3 things in order: the proposed restaurant transaction, a simpler operating model and cost structure and the work ahead of us in CPG. Luke will then review and -- the third quarter results, which reflects the restaurant portfolio we continue to own and operate.

Both the performance of our current business and the execution of our growth plans matter to our shareholders. As previously announced, we entered into a letter of intent with Chubby Group regarding a potential transaction of 47 of our U.S. restaurants for consideration of up to $100 million payable over time. We have not yet signed a definitive asset purchase agreement. The final terms, payment protections and closing arrangements remain subject to that agreement and the applicable closing conditions. We're focused on reaching terms that support the transition and protect GEN's interest, and we will update shareholders as there are material developments. As we have told everyone, we're looking forward to closing with Chubby.

At the same time, as CEO, I always have backup plans. Korean brands are in demand in today's market, and we are comfortable that GEN has meaningful optionality. The proposed approach is a phased transition. Until a restaurant is transferred under the applicable arrangements, GEN would continue to operate it and bear its operating responsibilities. The timing of any handover would depend on the final agreement and the conditions applicable to each location. Our priority is a workable transition for our guests, employees and business partners. Under the proposed structure, GEN would remain and retain the GEN brand, our CPG business and our restaurant in Cerritos, California.

Those 3 are the foundation of the company we are building. we see Cerritos continuing to support the brand and serving a place for training and CPG product development. Here is why we believe this makes strategic sense. The rest of our portfolio and the CPG business have different operating and capital needs, and we want to devote more of GEN's resources to developing our retail business. Our restaurants built this company over 15 years, and we gave -- and they gave us the recipes and the name our customers know. That recognition gives us a brand to build on.

The business we're building expands through manufacturing and distribution partners with capital focused more on inventory, customer support and working capital and less on facilities, leases and staffing. It still requires a disciplined execution and our objective is to build a business that can grow profitably over time. That brings me to our cost structure. GEN today carries the corporate structure of a company that was opening 10 restaurants a year. The company we are becoming needs a fraction of that. Our plan cuts corporate overhead by about 75% by the end of the transition, with further reduction targeted from there. The functions that exist only to support the restaurants go with the restaurants.

We began restructuring the corporate office in the third quarter when G&A was down 15% from a year ago, and the corporate workforce reduction begins in the fourth quarter. What remains is built around CPG and office space, systems and contracts underneath it is being renegotiated or terminated. Every role in the new GEN must earn its place by growing CPG or keeping us compliant. Now to CPG. This is the part of the call that is most important. For us, the opportunity starts with the food. Our restaurants introduce guests to the flavors of Korean barbecue and the CPG gives us a way to bring those same recipes into meals prepared at home.

We want the products to be approachable for a first-time buyer and consistent enough to become a repeat purchase. That means making the experience simple, a product consumers understand, clear preparation instructions and the flavor they expect from GEN. Our ready-to-cook format lets consumers prepare Korean barbecue at home without starting with a recipe and a long list of ingredients. In the third quarter, we added all 14 Bristol Farms stores. We added 55 Vallarta Supermarket locations and Olé City Markets. And we started to enter 2 channels we had never been in, University dining with UCLA being the first and live entertainment with the likes of SoFi Stadium.

When BTS played 4 sold-out nights at SoFi in September, GEN products were in the building. If you want a picture of how Main Street Korean food has become in America, that is it. Here is where we sit today. In grocery, we are across the Albertsons family of banners, including the likes of Safeway, Albertsons, Vons and Pavilion, The Stater Bros., Save Marts, Smart&Final, Times Supermarkets, Vallarta, Bristol Farms and Berkeley Bowl. In specialty retail, the BevMo! In club, Costco in several regions on rotation, including the Midwest, Texas, San Diego and Northern California, with discussions underway on a national program.

We have met companies, the likes of Walmart, and we anticipate going into those programs the second quarter of next year. Our distribution runs through Sysco, UNFI and C&S Wholesale Grocers, which puts GEN within reach of any retailer. And here is the part that matters most for 2027. We have locked in a significant number of additional placements that are not on the shelves yet. They began reaching stores in the second quarter. None of them is in our third quarter CPG revenue. Next year's wave is what drives the next step up in CPG revenues. And to be clear, we're seeking not just revenue, but profitable revenue.

CPG sales carry a much more attractive margin profile than restaurants, which combined with our increasing lean corporate overhead, positions us with the potential to be profitable. The backdrop keeps getting stronger. Korea's Agri-Food Trade Agency reported in September that K-Food exports are running at a record pace, 19 days ahead of 2025. And the United States was the largest market, up nearly 13%. Korean Food is not a trend in this country anymore. It is a category. In-store demonstrations and road shows are how we turn that interest into sales. They let people taste the food and see how easily it can be prepared.

We want to connect that trial to repeat demand with promotions and store support that makes economic sense for each account. Let me remind everyone how this business is built. Our core is frozen, ready-to-cook, marinated meats led by our 4 SKU, BBQ Beef Bulgogi, BBQ Short Ribs, Spicy Pork Bulgogi and BBQ Chicken Bulgogi, same marinades, same recipes, we serve in our restaurants, ready in minutes on a grill, in a pan or in an air fryer. We do not own a single plant. We produce through co-manufacturing partners in several U.S. states and in South Korea to our own specification. And we add capacity with purchase orders, not construction.

Our capital grows into inventory and shelf space, not build-outs and 20-year leases. That is a big part of why we believe and know this business can be very profitable at scale. In 2027, we'll roll out GEN ready-to-eat, fully cooked, not frozen Korean BBQ meats and complete meals, sold refrigerated in the deli and prepared food sections, heat and eat in minutes. No grill, no pan, no prep. This puts GEN squarely in what the industry calls the home meal replacement, or often called HMR. Competing with brands likes of the (sic) [ the likes of ] Kevin's Natural Foods and the other refrigerated entree lines that have built large businesses.

Deli prepared food are a category of more than $31 billion a year at U.S. retail according to Circana, and it is growing fast. We think we win there for 3 reasons. First, the deli case is where grocery is growing. Shoppers have moved from cooking to assembling. Second, our food is the product, 15 years of marinades, recipe and a brand millions of guests already trust in a category where most entrants are starting from 0 on taste and awareness. Third, our co-manufacturing model means we launch with purchase orders, not plants. The products are developed. The Cerritos kitchen is our test bed and our retail partners already carry our frozen line.

So we're expanding within existing relationships, not opening new doors. Frozen marinated meats built this business and will keep growing. But the ready-to-eat is a larger category with a broader shopper, and we anticipate that over time, it will be bigger for the GEN than the frozen raw marinated meats. This is a huge driver of the growth we see ahead, and it is why we are confident in the long-term trajectory of this business. And we are not stopping at meat. The GEN name already stretches across the whole Korean table. GENJU, our Gen-branded soju, comes in 8 flavors. Our beef chips come in Korean BBQ, Spicy Korean Barbecue and Teriyaki.

We have Korean BBQ Beef Jerky, spicy rice cakes, kimchi and our own sauces, including our Korean BBQ dipping sauce and our green tea salt. And we have GEN Jelly and GEN Vera, our Korean drinks. We have been testing these products and they are starting to grow. They also carry higher margins than our core meat products. We also want to be disciplined about how we expand. Each retailer and channel has different pack sizes, promotional requirements and the selling cost. Our objective is to build sales that remain attractive after those costs while giving our retail partners a product that earns its place on the shelf. Most CPG brands have to buy awareness.

We earned our one table at a time. Millions of guests have cooked at a GEN grill. When one of them sees our package in the freezer case, they are being recognized, not introduced. That is why buyers take our call and it is why our products move once they are on the shelf. We measure ourselves on velocity, not just door counts. A door that does not reorder is not a win, neither in revenue that does not earn a profit. Based on the doors we have secured on the stores in the pipeline, we expect CPG revenue to keep growing through 2027. We're building the team to match.

In August, Mark Cutrona joined us as a Senior Vice President of Sales and Operations in the East Coast with more than 30 years at Kimberly-Clark, TreeHouse Foods and Hormel Foods. He leads our national and regional accounts, broker network, category, management and trade marketing. Our own trained people run our in-store demos. And as the transition progresses, every member of our senior team will be focused on one business. Put those 3 categories together, a proposed transaction for up to $100 million over time, a plan to cut corporate overhead by about 75% or more and a CPG business we are targeting at a $40 million annualized revenue run rate by the end of 2027.

We anticipate there could be more growth, but as the growth comes in, we will, on a quarterly basis, update those projections. That is GEN we are building, and we intend to deliver it. With that, I'll pass the call back to CFO, Luke Hewko. Luke, over to you.

Luke Hewko: Thank you, David, and good afternoon, everyone. Before I walk through the numbers, a word on the transaction status. As David noted, the definitive asset purchase agreement with Chubby has not been signed. The results we are reporting today reflect our full restaurant portfolio for the quarter. I will review those results and then discuss the financial priorities for CPG and a potential restaurant transition. Revenue for the third quarter of 2026 totaled $48.7 million compared to $50.4 million the same year ago, a decrease of 3.3%. Loss from operations was $6 million or 12.4% of revenue in the third quarter of 2026 as compared to $3.7 million or 7.4% of revenue in the same year ago quarter.

General and administrative expenses totaled $5.5 million or 11.2% of revenue as compared to $6.5 million or 12.8% of revenue in the same year ago quarter. The 15.3% decrease reflects reductions in corporate costs and lower stock-based compensation, which more than offset continued investment in the company's CPG go-to-market efforts. Net loss for the third quarter of 2026 was $5.5 million compared to a net loss of $3.6 million the same year ago quarter. Net loss per basic and diluted share of Class A common stock was $0.16 compared to $0.11 in the same year ago quarter.

Adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, reflected a $600,000 loss for the third quarter of 2026 compared to approximately $200,000 loss in the same quarter a year ago. Turning to the balance sheet. Cash and cash equivalents as of September 30, 2026, totaled $2.9 million compared to $2.8 million as of December 31, 2025. Total debt outstanding was $26.8 million as compared to $14.6 million as of December 31, 2025. Reducing debt remains a priority. The amount and timing of any reduction will depend on cash available from operations, any transaction proceeds received and the working capital and other obligations of the business. If the proposed transition is completed, we would expect the ongoing business to have 3 principal components.

First, our CPG business. We continue to target a $40 million annualized run rate by the end of 2027. Achieving that objective depends on new placements, sales within our existing accounts, repeat orders and our ability to supply those customers. Our financial focus is on the profitability of that growth after product cost, promotions, distribution and the overhead needed to support it. Second, our remaining restaurant exposure, which under the proposed transaction would include our GEN in Cerritos and our existing 49% ownership interest in 5 Chubby Group branded restaurants. Third, a corporate cost structure appropriate for the business we retain. General and administrative expenses were $19.5 million for the first 9 months of this year.

We began taking out -- we began taking costs down in the third quarter. In connection with the proposed transaction, we are targeting annual general and administrative expense of approximately $6 million to $8 million with further reductions where appropriate. The timing and extent of these savings will depend on the pace of restaurant transfers and our ability to reduce cost while supporting CPG growth. Our objective is an ongoing business that could support its operating costs and generate cash. Reaching that point will depend on CPG sales and margins, the results of restaurant interest we retain and the overhead working capital required to support them.

Payments received on the restaurant purchase price would be separate from the operating performance of that ongoing business. Once the debt is retired, those payments, together with the earnings we expect from CPG will give us real flexibility in how we allocate capital, including returning capital to shareholders, be that a future buyback or dividend. The revenue run rate objectives described the annualized sales pace we are targeting at the end of 2027. It is not a forecast of revenue for the full year. The timing of placements, customer demand, promotional spending and inventory requirements will affect the path toward that objective. Any restaurant transaction restructuring would also affect consolidated results during the transition. That completes my financial review.

I will turn the call back to David for some closing remarks before we open the line for questions. David?

Wook Kim: Thank you, Luke. Our priorities are very clear, and there are 3 of them. First, work toward a definitive agreement with Chubby and prepare for an orderly transition, if the transaction requirement at each location and taking care of our guests, team members and business partners throughout the process. Second, grow CPG profitably, support the placement that began reaching stores in the second quarter, build repeat demand in existing accounts and deepen our retail relationships. Our distribution partners and broker network can help us reach more customers, while demonstrations and dependable store support can help turn that reach into repeat orders. We'll keep our core products at the center of that work as we bring ready-to-eat to market in 2027.

Third, run GEN with financial disciplines, align overhead with the business we operate, protect liquidity, reduce debt as cash permits and direct investments towards opportunities that can produce sustainable returns. Execute on those 3, and we expect to have choices between the proceeds of the proposed Chubby transaction and what we expect to be a very profitable CPG business. Those choices include returning capital to our shareholders, as we said, when we announced the letter of intent. That would be a dividend. It could be a buyback if we feel our stock price does not reflect the value of this business. We have made no decisions and retiring our debt comes first.

But those are good choices to have and ones we intend to take very seriously as we position ourselves to accumulate an increasingly large cash balance. 15 years ago, GEN was founded in L.A. with a simple idea that Korean barbecue belonged at the center of the American table. We built one of the leading Korean barbecue brands in the country, one grill at a time. The next chapter is to put that same food in millions of American kitchens. I want to make it clear to my fellow shareholders that we did not stumble into this opportunity. We built the brand that made it possible.

And I believe the most valuable chapter of GEN's story is the one we are writing now. With that, operator, let's open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from George Kelly with ROTH Capital Partners.

George Kelly: So a couple to start just on your CPG business. I was hoping you could share more about your $40 million run rate at year-end '27. I guess more specifically, what new distribution has been secured? You talked about some new placements in, I think, May of '27. How big do you think ready-to-eat will be out of the gate? And then, David, you also mentioned that there could be upside you're not factoring in everything that's kind of in the pipeline for '27. So what are those biggest opportunities that are baked into that $40 million number?

Wook Kim: Okay. So first of all, the opportunity right now, a lot of the buyers and their shelf sets, they call it, they're not taking new orders during the holiday season, the Thanksgiving and Christmas. So once that season is over, there's going to be a lot of new orders coming in because everybody is on a standby mode during the holiday season. Once that's over, then we start going in heavily because the -- we have already talks with promotions and other paused agreements and contract will start unpausing and start going in on the first quarter. What's interesting about the other question has to do with prepared food, the HMR.

The HMR business, it's double or triple the sales of the frozen industry. Frozen industry has not had much excitement. And I don't know how to say this in a positive way, but we actually, at GEN, created that because it's a very dormant industry. But the real strong of all the grocery chains are telling us by their data and they have shared data with us is that the prepared meal fully cooked line is a much, much bigger category for everybody.

So we have been asked by the buyers to make those products, and we are very close of getting all the products made so that hopefully, once we get all the packaging done, we have already met a lot of the buyers with our samples, and we can roll those out in the latter part of the second or the beginning of the -- I'm sorry, the latter part of the first quarter and the beginning of the second quarter rollout. So not only are we going to continue with the frozen and the question may come up, are you going to keep the frozen and the HMR? And the answer is yes.

Some might say no, but there is -- there are other competitors in the space that carry the frozen and the HMR, but it's different products, but the same brand. So that's where we will be focusing a lot of our efforts going in next year. And what was the other question that I missed, George?

George Kelly: You mentioned in your prepared remarks that you're not factoring in all the opportunity for next year. I don't know if you're still contemplating going bigger in club? Or I'm not sure what's being sort of excluded, but it seemed like there could be upside to that $40 million if...

Wook Kim: Absolutely. It could be much bigger than $40 million because I cannot tell you what the orders of the likes of Walmart will be. We met Walmart. Walmart asked us to come in and they normally don't do that until you go into their schedule of cycles, but they called us in way ahead of their cycle because companies like Walmart, they look at brands and see where their brands are placed and because we're placed in major supermarkets, they got attracted to our brand.

So as a public company, I don't want to mention all the names that we are -- have talked, have negotiated, but we are in their planograms or they're telling us, we will do first, second, third quarter. We have to be in their planogram. When we started this in October of last year, none of our products went into any planogram. So one has -- a lot of people have asked us, "How did you go into so many stores so fast without a 1-year lead time of planogram?" It's because the buyers of these grocery stores and the clubs, they knew and they know our brand.

And Korean barbecue is such a hot category, nobody is doing it the way we're doing it. So they bypassed all those regular scheduling and brought us in, in emergencies and quickly. They pushed people out. They did a lot of things they're not used to doing. So we had that momentum. Now we're just going to continuously build on that. So this call that we're on today does not contemplate all the other ones that we are so close of getting done. And as they come through and which we have, we will be putting out press releases on who we are bringing on board.

And for example, I won't tell you the company name, but we're almost done with the cruise line company. And that's a very, very big category because they're very consistent. So there's lots of categories that we are in talks or already met and showed them the samples, and they have had interest. They just told us to just wait so that they can get through the Christmas season. And most buyers in this category, they all function that way.

#3213. Ring’s wheeled and flying robots will patrol your home

Some people use a whole bunch of fixed cameras to monitor their homes, but Amazon has just announced a more flexible solution through wheeled and flying robots.

Both the $250 Drone Cam and $1,000 Rover Cam can respond to alarms or door and window sensor alerts in order to go check out what’s happening and send live video …

Amazon says they are the first two Ring Robotics products, with more likely to follow. Both are autonomous.

Ring Drone and Ring Rover are both powered by AI Pilot, a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.

AI Pilot simplifies the customer experience, starting with setup. Simply carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan. It intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points: spots worth extra attention. This could be a side door, windows, a register, or a long corridor, helping eliminate guesswork while also allowing you to add additional points customized to your space and security preferences.

When a patrol or flight is initiated, AI Pilot plans the most efficient route to get to a preset point based on the map it’s created. From there, it reacts in real time—autonomously navigating around furniture, shelving, and any obstacle it encounters.

You can set either device to patrol on a fixed schedule, as well as activate them manually, but they will also automatically respond to sensor alerts and alarms.

When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, [either device] automatically [moves] to previously set patrol points to investigate […] Continuous person motion detection means Ring Rover can alert you and start recording the moment it detects motion in its view—even when docked.

The Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping on December 16 for $999.99, but you can preorder it today. The Drone Cam starts shipping in late January for $249.99, but there’s no preorder yet.

#3211. Adobe unveils new AI tools for Photoshop, Premiere, and more, with MCP support coming in 2027

Adobe today announced a sweeping set of updates at its annual Adobe MAX conference, focused on giving users more ways to automate complex workflows, edit content, and work across its creative apps. Here are the details.

At the Adobe MAX event today, the company unveiled a series of features, many of them AI-powered or AI-assisted, that will begin rolling out across its suite of creative platforms as early as today.

In Photoshop, the new Relight tool offers a way to non-destructively and dynamically add, reposition, and resize light sources in the composition, while Generative Restylelets users** prompt the platform to generate variations of an image’s style and fine-tune the results using adjustable sliders.

Photoshop is also adding a Quick Compare slider to make it easier to track before-and-after results, and is getting several features in the beta app, including, per Adobe:

Following its acquisition of Topaz Labs, Adobe is also introducing two new AI image enhancement models: Wonder 4, which combines upscaling, denoising, deblurring, and sharpening into a single operation, and Image HDR, which converts standard images into HDR with improved brightness and detail.

Adobe Premiere is also getting generative tools that make it easier to prepare raw files for a project, including Enhance Audio, Separate Crosstalk, and Separate Sound Source. Adobe is also adding a Generative Remove tool to Premiere in beta, “bringing you the power to remove unwanted objects, like boom mics and logos or background distractions, directly on your timeline,” says the company.

Premiere is also getting Color Mode, a new color-grading tool starting today, which “supports everything from quick corrections to more advanced grades while keeping your video as the focus.”

Another interesting tool making its way into Premiere is Generative Media Tool. Here’s Adobe:

The Generative Media Tool brings Generate Video, Generate Sound Effects, Generate Soundscape and Generate Music directly into your timeline in Premiere. You can generate missing b-roll, background music or sound for a scene using context from your edit, then keep refining the result in your timeline. You can also choose from Adobe Firefly and models from partners including Google, Kling, Runway and Luma based on the creative needs of your project.

As for iPhone users who rely on Premiere Mobile, Adobe announced that its newly established partnerships with UMG and WMG will bring hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks to the app (for non-commercial use) starting today, with users able to explore trending songs, discover featured artists, and create videos using artist-inspired templates.

Premiere mobile is also getting agentic tools soon, including Quick Cuts, which generates a first cut based on the user’s prompt and the materials they add, and an AI Assistant, which helps users find the right editing tools and execute tasks based on natural language instructions.

In Lightroom, the company is adding multiple new tools that make it easier to edit or more quickly fix small imperfections. That includes Glow, which “adds soft, cinematic light to your photos,” Blemish Removal for quick skin fine-tuning, Open Eyes in beta, and an improved and expanded Camera Tethering on Desktop and the iPad, with support for more cameras and advanced shooting controls, plus the ability to connect cameras directly to an iPad for live previews and photo editing.

Adobe is adding new brushes, gradients, patterns, and graphic styles to Illustrator, alongside new Blend controls, which “make it easier to develop and refine designs with a persistent control panel and live preview,” per the company.

As for InDesign, a new Co-editing feature, available in beta, streamlines collaborative work, while the new Flex Layout tool dynamically adjusts content based on the canvas size and artwork. InDesign is also getting Check Document and Rewrite that more quickly “help identify common editorial and accessibility issues while you’re still working.”

While it will not launch until 2027, this feature will enable users to connect Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects to the AI tools and agents they already use.

In practice, this will mean connecting Photoshop to ChatGPT and having them work in tandem to adapt an entire campaign based on new artwork you develop and attach to your prompt.

This integration will also account for other connected tools, so the user can ask ChatGPT to make edits, add new files to a Google Drive folder, update the team on Slack, and so on.

Here’s Adobe on the upcoming MCP integration:

Because it runs locally on your computer, your agent works directly in your native project files, and your layers, vectors, bins and sequences stay editable.

The company notes that MCP integrations will enter private beta in early 2027, and users can sign up here to learn more.

According to Adobe, Firefly is getting even better at helping users organize and edit their raw material for tasks such as turning travel clips into a vlog, creating social media campaigns, or assembling videos from storyboards.

The new Firefly Video lets users organize scenes, assemble clips, add captions, and generate transitions and B-roll, while Firefly Design brings illustration, image editing, animation, and 3D tools into a single canvas.

Adobe is also adding Quick Actions for common editing tasks, Firefly Graph for creating reusable workflows, and Firefly Builder (in private beta) for prototyping websites and apps using natural language.

Firefly’s AI Assistant is also getting new capabilities, including Plan Mode, which lets users review and approve an agent’s proposed actions, and Model Selector, which lets them choose which AI model to use.

Adobe is also previewing Always-on agents, which can handle recurring tasks such as organizing assets, checking quality, and preparing content for different platforms in the background, even when users step away.

Adobe is also expanding its Creative Agent across Creative Cloud, with AI Assistants now available in beta in Illustrator, Premiere, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io, as well as the Photoshop beta app.

These assistants allow users to execute complex, multi-step tasks using natural language prompts. In Premiere, for example, users can ask the assistant to apply effects to an entire sequence, track subjects across frames, or adjust color and exposure across multiple clips.

To learn more about these and other features announced at Adobe MAX today, stay tuned to the company’s blog.

#3210. Graphon Labs raises $35m to give AI agents a memory that lasts

Graphon Labs says its graph-based memory tops rival systems on three benchmarks. The 20-person company counts HP and the San Francisco 49ers among its users.

Graphon Labs co-founders, from left: Deepak Mishra, chief operating officer; Arbaaz Khan, chief executive; and Clark Zhang, chief technology officer.

Graphon Labs, a San Francisco startup that builds memory for AI agents, has raised $35m. RRE Ventures led the Series A. HP, Energy Impact Partners, Hitachi Ventures and Gaia VC also invested, Graphon said on Tuesday. The round brings its total funding to $43.3m, less than six months after it left stealth with an $8.3m seed round.

The 20-person company will spend the money mainly on engineers and researchers, plus some sales staff. Chief executive Arbaaz Khan gave those details to Shubhangi Goel of Business Insider, which reported the round first.

Khan compares common AI search to tearing the pages out of a book and digging through the scraps for an answer.

“You’ve basically lost all that information because each piece is living on its own,” he told Business Insider.

AI agents can write code and carry out tasks. But they can lose track of past conversations and changing company data. Graphon says common methods can lose context, relationships and timing as data grows. One example is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which feeds a model snippets of stored text.

Graphon’s system is built on graphons, a mathematical framework for very large graphs. Khan and co-founder Clark Zhang built graph-based memory for robots during their PhDs, Khan wrote in a blog post. The software maps the links between a company’s documents, videos and images, including where information came from and when it changed.

“You can basically point your Claude or GPT or whatever to Graphon,” Khan told Business Insider.

Graphon says it scored 93.9% on LoCoMo, a test of memory over long conversations. It used 58% fewer tokens than loading the whole conversation into the model. On ATM-Bench, a University of Cambridge benchmark across video, audio, images and text, it scored 81.7%. That is 5 points ahead of the next system on the public leaderboard.

Graphon says the San Francisco 49ers, Hitachi and other large companies use its software. HP also uses it, Business Insider reported. Costa Kladianos, the 49ers’ executive vice president of technology, said the team is exploring how to use it. One example is finding new sponsorship deals. Hitachi Rail said its evaluation “shows promise” in its industrial setting.

The company has three products: Graphon Enterprise, a developer platform, and on-device memory for phones, laptops, cameras and wearables. Khan told Business Insider that Graphon will stay focused on enterprise customers before moving further into devices and consumer products.

The biggest AI companies are also adding memory to their assistants. In August, Anthropic merged Claude’s memory across chat and Cowork. In October, Apple’s iOS 27.2 gave Siri memory.

#3209. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.
