#3191. Nvidia says it cut off Megaspeed in 2025, but Bloomberg found later imports

Bloomberg also found that Nvidia’s count of Megaspeed chips sold through partners ran 50,000 short. Nvidia’s lawyer had called a top Commerce official about Alice Huang’s detention in Singapore.

Nvidia says it banned all sales and shipments to Megaspeed in June 2025, and that the ban is still in place, a company spokesman told The Wall Street Journal. Since then, Commerce has allowed Nvidia to send it parts and replacement components, the spokesman said.

Malaysian trade records show that Megaspeed imported at least 17,544 of Nvidia’s GB300 chips, worth about $787m, in November 2025, Mackenzie Hawkins reported for Bloomberg. Nvidia gave US officials a count of chips sold to Megaspeed through hardware partners. It was 50,000 units short, Bloomberg found. Megaspeed is still an official Nvidia Cloud Partner. TNW has not independently verified the reports.

Megaspeed is the Singapore company at the centre of the Jensen Huang affair. Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation after Huang admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive. US officials believe she is a Chinese intelligence asset. China has denied the espionage claims.

In mid-November 2025, Nvidia told Bloomberg that its inventory checks found everything where it should be. It also said it had asked the US government whether it needed to cut off Megaspeed, and was told no.

In December 2025, Nvidia told Bloomberg it had checked more warehouses that held the missing hardware. It did not say how many chips it found. Two of the eight data centre operators Nvidia told Washington it had visited said they had no Megaspeed hardware. Nvidia declined to comment on that to Bloomberg. Megaspeed’s largest landlord has since dropped it as a tenant.

About three months ago, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter told a White House official that Alice Huang was “not as important” in Megaspeed as she made out, according to a person familiar with the call. He said that, because of the bad publicity around her, Nvidia had stopped doing business with Megaspeed.

In late summer 2025, Teter called Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce under secretary in charge of chip export curbs. He asked whether Kessler’s Bureau of Industry and Security had a role in Singapore’s detention of Alice Huang. It did not, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. An Nvidia spokesperson said Teter did not know about the affair at the time.

It is unclear whether Teter made any specific requests of Kessler, according to Bloomberg. In the following weeks, bureau staff were told to route all requests of Nvidia through Kessler or get his approval. The people called that highly unusual, and unique to Nvidia. Staff were also told not to name Megaspeed or Speedmatrix, its Malaysian subsidiary, in external communications.

In late 2025, the Justice Department, which was working on the Megaspeed smuggling case with the bureau, asked it to pause. The bureau has made no progress since, despite having enough evidence to move forward, Bloomberg reported.

“BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book,” a bureau spokesman said.

“We work to resolve any allegations of ‘diversion’ promptly, to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers while serving the critical market of lawful customers that help America win worldwide,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Bloomberg.

In December 2023, Jensen Huang and a small group of colleagues met Alice Huang at an Italian restaurant in Singapore, according to The New York Times. She had just restructured Megaspeed. Four days after its ownership change, Nvidia named it a cloud partner, the Times reported on Tuesday.

Megaspeed went on to secure more than $4bn of Nvidia chips. In late 2024, the Commerce Department sent an official to inspect one of its data centres, where some Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes. That year, Taiwan began monitoring Alice Huang’s trips to the island at the suggestion of the US government, a person familiar with the matter told the Times.

In 2025, Singapore barred her from leaving and questioned her in a probe into false import declarations. The investigations against her were closed for lack of evidence, the person said, but Singapore is still investigating Megaspeed. She later flew to Shanghai.

Megaspeed has categorically denied the chip diversion allegations. It told Bloomberg that Singapore’s probe ended this year with no adverse action against it. Its outreach to the US government went unanswered, it said. Nvidia and Megaspeed declined to comment to the Times. Alice Huang did not respond to the Times, and Bloomberg has been unable to reach her.

Senators Jim Banks, a Republican, and Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, urged Commerce to suspend or reconsider Nvidia’s China export licences, Bloomberg reported. Their bill would temporarily bar Nvidia from selling Chinese customers any chip more advanced than the H200. Lawmakers are negotiating to add it to the annual defence bill, which typically passes in December.

“I think we’re going to work hard to make sure that those provisions make it into the final version of the National Defense Authorization Act,” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said.

Senator Richard Blumenthal wants a Senate investigation, Semafor reported. In the House, three committee chairs have asked Huang to attend a closed briefing on 18 November.

What it's about: Kenna (Maika Monroe) returns to her hometown seven years after a tragic accident sent her to prison. Hoping to reconnect with the young daughter she has never known, she faces resistance from the child's grandparents. However, Kenna finds unexpected support in Ledger (Tyriq Withers), a local bar owner with connections to her past, and the two develop a secret romance.

Why you should watch it: "Reminders of Him" brings Colleen Hoover's bestselling novel to the screen, with Maika Monroe and Tyriq Withers at the heart of its emotional story. Their performances give the complicated relationship plenty of weight, while the film explores the challenges of rebuilding a life and finding a way forward after difficult experiences. It's not exactly light viewing, but if you enjoy heartfelt romances with plenty of emotional moments, this one is worth making time for.

What it's about: Teenage Rosaleen (Sarah Patterson) dreams of a mysterious village surrounded by dark woods. Her grandmother (Angela Lansbury) tells her unsettling stories about werewolves and warns her against trusting certain men. When Rosaleen encounters a handsome huntsman during a journey through the forest, she discovers that the dangers in her grandmother's tales may be closer than she imagined.

Why you should watch it: "The Company of Wolves" is a fascinating alternative to more conventional werewolf movies, taking inspiration from the dark side of classic fairytales. Neil Jordan creates an unsettling fantasy world, with elaborate production design and practical effects that give the film a distinctive look. Angela Lansbury and Sarah Patterson are among the standout performers, while its unusual reimagining of Little Red Riding Hood makes for a memorable viewing experience.

Watch "The Company of Wolves" on Shudder now

What it's about: Special Forces veteran James Belmont (Brad Pitt) and his combat dog, Odin, become stranded in the Alaskan wilderness after a devastating plane crash. With rescue seemingly out of reach, the pair must navigate freezing conditions, dangerous wildlife and treacherous terrain while searching for safety. Directed by David Ayer, the adventure thriller also stars J.K. Simmons and Anna Lambe.

Why you should watch it: "Heart of the Beast" is a strong choice if you enjoy survival stories set in the wilderness. Brad Pitt leads the film with a compelling performance, but much of its appeal comes from his relationship with canine co-star Uber. Their bond gives the adventure an emotional centre, while director David Ayer delivers some tense encounters that keep the journey gripping. It’s an entertaining watch for fans of survival thrillers with a bit of heart.

#3188. Web Summit cancels Day 2 in Lisbon as Storm Charles hits Portugal

Portugal’s government advised Web Summit that Wednesday should not go ahead, citing flooding, transport disruption and high winds. The organisers aim to reopen on Thursday for the final day.

Web Summit’s main stage in Lisbon in November 2025

Web Summit has called off Wednesday’s programme in Lisbon because of Storm Charles. Portugal’s government advised the organisers that Day 2 should not take place. Web Summit told attendees by email on Tuesday evening that it aims to hold Day 3, on Thursday 12 November, as planned.

The government cited the risk of tidal flooding and severe disruption to public transport. It also pointed to the effect of high winds on outdoor structures, Web Summit said. The advice followed talks with the civil protection authority, ANEPC, and the Public Security Police (PSP).

“The safety and security of our attendees, staff and contractors is always our absolute priority,” the Web Summit team wrote.

Web Summit said it will keep working with the authorities and emergency services. It will contact those affected directly.

Earlier on Tuesday, Lisbon mayor Carlos Moedas said “everything indicates” the event could not run on Wednesday. Stephen Conneely reported his comments for The Irish Times. Moedas said more than 60,000 people were at the venue in Parque das Nações.

The government has declared a state of alert across mainland Portugal for Wednesday, The Portugal News reported. Schools and non-essential public services will close. Lisbon is shutting its tunnels, parks, gardens and cultural venues from midnight. The weather service IPMA forecast gusts of up to 120km/h.

Web Summit runs from 9 to 12 November. Last month, it released its tech industry survey. In it, 60% of people in tech said AI had increased their workload.

#3187. Endeavour Silver (EXK) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Silver output rose as Terronera's LNG switch cut costs per tonne.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Endeavour Silver Corp. (EXK -3.24%) reported growth in mine operating cash flow and metal production for the third quarter of 2026, supported by higher realized precious metal prices. Management adjusted its annual production and cost guidance to account for temporary operational suspensions at Terronera and capacity reductions at Guanacev. The company reported an improvement in its consolidated cost profile as the Terronera mine transitioned toward steady-state operations following the completion of its liquefied natural gas power plant. Financial flexibility was increased through the conversion of a project loan into a secured revolving credit facility as the company nears the completion of a feasibility study for the Pitarrilla project.

Operator: Thank you for standing by. This is the conference operator. Welcome to the Endeavour Silver Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] The conference is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] I would like to turn the conference over to Allison Pettit, Vice President, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Allison Pettit: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Before we get started, I ask that you view our MD&A for cautionary language regarding forward-looking statements and the risk factors pertaining to these statements. Our MD&A and financial statements are available on our website at edrsilver.com. On today's call, we have Dan Dickson, Endeavour Silver's CEO; and Elizabeth Senez, Endeavour Silver's CFO. Following Dan's formal remarks, we will open the call for questions. And now over to Dan.

Dan Dickson: Thank you, Allison, and good morning, everyone. Our third quarter delivered higher metal production and with stronger metal prices delivered substantial growth in mine operating cash flow. Quarterly cash costs and all-in sustaining cost per silver ounce improved compared to Q3 2025 and our previous 2026 quarters. Most importantly, these metrics reflect the steady operational improvements we anticipated at Terronera throughout 2026. At Terronera, grades have progressively increased over the course of the year, recoveries are now achieving feasibility study targets and our cost profile has continued to improve quarter-over-quarter.

While we see further opportunities to optimize the operation and expect incremental improvements over the next several quarters, Terronera is increasingly demonstrating the consistency and predictability we expect from a steady-state operation. This is an important milestone as the mine continues to perform in line with our expectations. Our quarterly production results were achieved despite 2 operational disruptions during the third quarter. At Terronera, operations were temporarily suspended for 12 days in August while we worked with the local community to address their concerns. We believe our relationship with the community remains positive, and it was important to us that all concerns were heard, understood and appropriately addressed.

We believe these discussions have strengthened our mutual understanding and established a solid foundation to avoid similar disruptions in the future. I want to thank -- I want to take this opportunity to recognize and thank our leadership team in Mexico for the professionalism and commitment they demonstrated throughout these discussions and the way they represented our company. At Guanaceví, a crack identified in the trunnion reduced our capacity for the final 9 days of the quarter. Of course, this is not ideal. However, we met our planned time line for replacement and hope to recover this production in the fourth quarter.

On a consolidated basis, we now expect annual production to be between 7.8 million and 8.1 million silver ounces and 42,000 to 43,500 ounces of gold, representing silver equivalent production of 13.7 million to 14.3 million ounces in 2026. This revised outlook reflects our results to date and the expectations for the fourth quarter. While the temporary operational disruptions combined to the revised guidance, they're only part of the story. At Guanaceví, silver grades have been below plan throughout the year. This is partly due to the natural variability in the ore body, but also reflects the opportunities presented by the higher metal price environment that we've experienced in 2026.

With the stronger metal prices, we've been able to economically mine lower grade material that may not have been attractive in the lower price environment. We've taken a similar approach across our operations where it makes operational and economic sense. While these decisions can impact near-term production grades, the longer-term benefit is the opportunity to recover more ounces from our existing mineral resources and potentially extending mine lives. We have also revised direct operating cost guidance at Terronera to a range of $170 to $180 per tonne. And on a consolidated basis, direct operating cost guidance is now $155 to $165 per tonne. Again, we expect the trend to continue downwards.

However, the higher cost per tonne in the first 6 months of the year was just too much to overcome. Grades, recoveries and operating efficiencies have been improving at Terronera while cost per tonne continuing to come down. Our focus remains on carrying that progress into the coming quarters and with further opportunities to improve operating performance and strengthen cash flow. With that updated outlook in mind, let's take a closer look at our third quarter production and financial results. The company produced 2 million ounces of silver and 10,000 ounces of gold in Q3, bringing total production, including base metals, to nearly 4 million ounces of silver equivalent.

Silver production was up 19% from a year ago, and gold production is up 39%. Total revenue was $185 million, up 29% from Q3 last year, with realized average prices of $62 per ounce of silver and $4,209 per ounce of gold. Mine operating earnings reached $69 million compared with the $16 million a year ago, and mine operating cash flow before taxes was $95 million, an increase of 139%. Cash costs were $16.55 per payable ounce of silver, net of byproducts, a decrease of 9% compared to Q3 last year. All-in sustaining costs were $29.54, down 3% from a year ago as well.

The company reported $54 million of operating earnings compared to $2 million a year ago, and earnings before taxes were $40 million compared with a loss of $38 million in Q3 of last year. Looking at direct operating cost per tonne, we've made progress throughout the year. Consolidated costs declined from $187 in Q1 to $162 in Q2 and now stood at $152 in Q3. That was still 5% above Q3 last year, reflecting the different operating mix, with Terronera now included and while Bolañitos is no longer part of our operations.

At Kolpa, grades and recoveries remain consistent while higher throughput helped bring direct operating costs down to $138 in Q3 compared to $153 in the first half of 2026. The economies of scale are offsetting any pressures we have from a labor standpoint. At Terronera, as I mentioned earlier, direct operating costs continued to decline, reaching $156 here in Q3, down from $169 in Q2 and $195 in Q1. Contractor demobilization and workflow improvements helped bring costs down earlier in the year. And in Q3, we completed the LNG plant, allowing us to switch our power generation from diesel to LNG.

Beyond costs, we're encouraged by the steady improvements in Terronera's grades, recoveries and operating efficiencies over the past 3 quarters. We expect further improvements in the coming quarters with the opportunities to strengthen both operating performance and obviously, cash flow. With the higher metal prices, we are mining material at Terronera that's not included in our resources, with the aim of extending mine life. Further drill results are expected in the fourth quarter, and we look forward to sharing those in the coming weeks. At Guanaceví, direct operating costs were $188 per tonne, reflecting lower throughput and the appreciation of the Mexican peso. Similarly, we'll continue to drill at Guanaceví, and we'll be sharing those results in the coming weeks.

Moving over to our balance sheet. We ended September with $288 million in cash and $247 million in working capital, giving us a strong foundation to support our operations and advance our growth initiatives. We also converted our project loan into a $25 million secured revolving credit facility. It includes an accordion feature for up to an additional $75 million, bringing the maximum potential facility to $100 million. This adds flexibility to fund working capital, operations, permitted acquisitions and investments and the advancement of Pitarrilla. Pitarrilla is a major growth story for Endeavour Silver. Our management team visited the project last week, and the feasibility study is nearing completion. We expect to issue a news release imminently.

Together with the financial flexibility I just outlined, Pitarrilla is central to our long-term growth. We look forward to sharing that next update. To close, I think the third quarter really demonstrated the progress we've made as a company throughout 2026. While we certainly had some challenges along the way, we're seeing the benefits of the work we put into our operations. Terronera continues to improve. Our cost profile has moved in the right direction, and we're generating significantly stronger cash flow. With Pitarrilla's feasibility study nearing completion, we're approaching another milestone for Endeavour. We believe Pitarrilla has the potential to be a transformational asset for the company, and we're excited about what lies ahead.

I want to thank our employees and operating teams for their continued hard work and commitment and our shareholders for their ongoing support. We'll now open up for questions. Operator, please open up the Q&A session.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question is from Heiko Ihle with H.C. Wainwright.

Heiko Ihle: Thank you guys for taking my questions. I appreciate it. Greetings from Zurich. You talked in the release and also earlier on this call about the cost per tonne at Terronera. Obviously, we went from close to $200 to effectively just over $150 in Q3. You raised the direct operating cost guidance at site to $170 to $180. Just looking in the longer term a little bit, how much more cost savings can we see at site? What's the next steps? And what is those cost savings? What are they based on?

And I mean, I guess we can sort of peg the results for Q4 by just backing out Q1 through 3 and then taking the direct operating cost guidance for 2026 as a whole. But aiming a bit higher, do you want to maybe just give a bit of color on what you think we might see next year and what factors might swing pricing into one direction or the other, please? I know that's all.

Dan Dickson: Yes. No, for sure. Thanks for the question, Heiko. Hopefully, you’re enjoying Zurich. We have some of our team there right now. For us at Terronera, obviously, the revised guidance is more a reflection of what happened in the first 6 months and just elongated time period where we thought we could be on the LNG power generation a little bit sooner. And that pushed up our costs on an annualized basis. Obviously, as I said, you saw $153 operating costs for Q3. The expectation is it to continue to come down. Now we're not going to see the same step downs that we saw from Q1 to Q2 and from Q2 to Q3. But there's still opportunity there.

One of the things that mainly comes to mind is the LNG plant came on in July for the upper -- lower and upper platforms and then ultimately for the mine late in the quarter. So we'll have in Q4 for the entire 91 days ultimately be on the LNG diesel plant. We're also developing our mine -- our waste development, we call it waste dump 2, which is just outside Portal 4. Currently, and throughout all of Q3, we trucked it to the other side of the plant, which is ultimately near our tailings facility. We'll be able to cut that 2 kilometers off here in Q4, hopefully sooner rather than later, and start dumping waste here in Q4.

That should save us some operating costs. Obviously, what's most important going forward will also be where the peso sits. We've seen a recent depreciation of the peso. Hopefully, that continues or at least settles here in the mid-18s. Ultimately, our full guidance for 2027 will come out in January of next year. I don't want to get too ahead of that because we are going through management's review of 2027 plans and costs. But there still remains opportunity to reduce costs at Terronera, which is great.

Heiko Ihle: You sort of preempted my follow-up. I was actually going to ask you what exchange rate. I think we're at 18.6, 18.7 right now. I was actually going to ask what exchange rate you guys are using for your Q4 numbers?

Dan Dickson: Yes. We haven't changed any of our assumptions that we used at the beginning of the year when we came out with it. And I want to be -- I believe it's at 17 that we used in our estimates.

Operator: The next question is from Wayne Lam with TD Securities.

Wayne Lam: Maybe just on the updated production guidance. It kind of looks like the implication at the midpoint is a slight decline in Q4. And I would assume it implies flat production quarter-over-quarter at Terronera and Kolpa, along with the lower output at Guanaceví, just given the downtime. So I was just wondering, is that conservative since I would have assumed a bigger step change at Terronera as you enter into the higher grades? Or should we be expecting the grades to hold relatively flat around the 150-ish level and more of a step change in '27 when you get into the La Luz vein?

Dan Dickson: Yes. That's a very fair question. Obviously, we put out what our range is. We feel like with any range, you always want to end up coming at the top end of that range and beat effectively what people are expecting. Terronera, though, it is fair to think of grades being relatively flat to Q3. We hope that they come up a little bit when that comes through. Ultimately, there's 2 things that will happen in 2027.

We'll be more into the high-grade shoot and get more tonnes out of that high-grade shoot and then ultimately bring in La Luz probably midyear to the end of the year, still trying to determine when that will come in because we're drilling in La Luz and trying to figure out what that depth that we want to develop to. But ultimately, expect 2027 to be still higher grades from where we are at Q3.

Wayne Lam: Okay. Great. And then maybe just on the costs. I'm not sure if I missed it, but what was the updated cash cost and AISC guidance on a consolidated basis and then specifically at Terronera. I wasn't sure if that was excluded purposely.

Dan Dickson: We excluded that purposely, just with the number of where we're sitting and where we put our original assumptions in January. We haven't gone out and rechanged and updated all the assumptions from January, just the production expectations for the year.

Wayne Lam: Okay. Because looking at the operating cost per ton, the main driver is a 30% increase at Terronera. So I guess if you could just help us understand maybe how much of that is attributed to the LNG plant versus other factors? And then how much should we add to the cost just based on the $36 silver price used in the guidance versus spot price?

Dan Dickson: Can you clarify -- sorry, Wayne, I'm just kind of misunderstood. Are you asking for the consolidated cost per ton and trying to understand the changes there?

Wayne Lam: No, specifically at Terronera, if you look at the increase in the operating cost per ton, how much of that is attributed to the LNG plant and that we can kind of start to take out of our costs now that's in place.

Dan Dickson: Yes. Yes. So really the decrease, how much the LNG and going from diesel gensets to LNG and how much of the proportion of the drop from the $165 to $153 is part of the -- attributed to the LNG plant. It's anywhere between $8 to $10, depending on how much LNG and how much diesel we are using per ton.

Wayne Lam: Okay. So $8 to $10 on the LNG plant? And then what would be the offset on your labor and consumables pressures that you're seeing?

Dan Dickson: There's a small portion at Terronera. We haven't seen as much labor pressure on our costs. So we lock in our union rates in January, January/February, and we do that on an annualized basis. This year was an increase of 5%, 6%. That was included in it. Where we've seen impacts potentially is we've actually had reduced staff at Terronera. So our labor costs at Terronera have actually come down. Where we are getting pressure on reagents or steel costs, it's been minimal at Terronera. It's significantly been offset by our efficiencies and are using less steel per meter, so to speak, in our development.

Wayne Lam: Okay. Great. And maybe just last one. I guess what's the updated timing on the Pitarrilla study? And do you anticipate a construction decision shortly after? And I know we've kind of walked through the math before, and the balance sheet looks solid with nearly $400 million in liquidity. But just given the CapEx inflation encountered with the Terronera build, is there any appetite to kind of derisk the balance sheet a bit further and build up a bit more flexibility before you dive head first into the next project?

Dan Dickson: We like to dive headfirst. Now a lot there with Pitarrilla. We're very close to completing the feasibility study and then getting all the necessary sign-offs and ultimately putting out a news release and hopefully filing that feasibility study shortly thereafter and not having the full 45 days where it's sitting there. So really just going through final reviews and then getting QP sign-offs, we should have a news release out hopefully in the next 10 days, if not less. As far as our balance sheet is concerned with regards to Pitarrilla, correct. Like I said, we have close to $300 million of cash. We have the ability with that revolver credit facility to what we feel fund Pitarrilla.

The main construction decision point isn't going to be the feasibility study, Wayne. It's ultimately the tailings dam permit. So as you're probably aware, the underground mine is permitted, the plant site is permitted. What we need permitted is the tailings dam permit. We've submitted and we expect permits, which is going through the state of Durango. It's a dry stack facility. So not a lot of environmental concerns compared to conventional tailings. So if we can have that for Q1/Q2 of 2027, that's the gating item to a construction decision.

At that point, we'll be able to determine where we sit from a cash flow, really from the cash flow that we generate, we should be able to fund Pitarrilla. Again, that's dependent on the price environment we're in. So if we're sitting at $50 silver, we should be pretty strong. We'd always look at other mechanisms to ensure that we can fund Pitarrilla all the way through to operations, of course, and make that assessment. So again, we feel like we're in very strong shape from a balance sheet standpoint and the cash flow that we generate. We expect that Pitarrilla news release to be out within 10 days and then the construction decision sometime midyear next year.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The next question is from Alex Terentiew with National Bank.

Alexander Terentiew: Good to see costs coming down. Much of my questions have already been asked. So let me just kind of look through my last remaining ones. One -- maybe one question is on Terronera. There's been a lot of changes here, some exploration. You've got LNG plant. You talked about changing gold metal prices and cutoff grades and some drilling is happening. Is there going to be -- or do you have a plan for a new resource update and mine plan to kind of help us get a sense of what we should expect, not just really in 2027, but over the next few years?

Because yes, I understand I know the old study is probably, I don't know, whatever it is, 4 or 5 years old now and a lot has changed. So any clarity there?

Dan Dickson: Yes. No, that's a very good question. We actually have new resource estimates that will come out. We've locked those down. They'll come out early in the new year for Terronera, Guanaceví and Kolpa actually.

Alexander Terentiew: Okay. So this would be for Kolpa, this would be the official inaugural Endeavour-stamped, 43-101 resource, correct?

Alexander Terentiew: Okay. Okay. And then on the costs, like I said, great to see Terronera's costs coming down. I think that's something we've all been kind of waiting for. But on Guanaceví, I think costs came down there as well. But I'm just curious, is that a function of how much ore is being purchased versus your own ore being milled this quarter? Just kind of trying to gauge what the outlook could be for the rest of this year and into next year on cost?

Dan Dickson: Yes. You'll see in the MD&A and our reconciliation, and we always want to make very clear about this, that we always talk to direct operating costs, and then we also have a direct cost. So direct operating cost per tonne includes mining, processing and G&A. Our direct costs include the royalties, which is our royalties we pay to Frisco, 16% special mining duty that we pay to the governments included in that. And then purchased ore is also included in that direct cost per tonne. So we do a good job separating that and the direct operating cost is what we always speak to. So we did see a decrease in direct operating costs at Guanaceví this quarter.

Can we sustain that? I hope so. We're working towards that. Because ultimately, we start talking about purchased ore, royalties, special mining duty, the price is what really drives that, the silver price and gold price is what really drives that, and that's kind of out of our control. So again, if we can keep our costs here lower at Guanaceví, that would be beneficial. We feel like we've got good control of the water. We've got great ventilation. We are very deep in Guanaceví. So it's always going to be a high-cost operation kind of going forward. But again, we have drill results coming out in the coming weeks. Those drill results will be included in our resource.

And it's a mine that's never had more than a 2-year reserve life, and we've been there for 20 years, and we hopefully continue to have a 2-year reserve life when those resources come out.

Alexander Terentiew: Okay. Great. Just one more question then on Pitarrilla, just following up on Wayne's question there. I mean, this year, you guys noted that spending has been well below what you originally targeted. And I know you're going to have a feasibility study out like you said within the next 10 days, hopefully. So I'm sure there'll be more details there. But are you -- I mean, how are you kind of positioning your planning here? -- Has the delays kind of impacted your plans for 2027? I'm just trying to gauge kind of the schedule here and ramp up and you guys putting orders in to kind of get project in the construction ready or moving into construction mid-2027.

Just trying to get [Audio Gap] other things other than the tailings permit that we need to see.

Dan Dickson: Yes. No, it's -- I mean, as you know us, Alex, we're probably a little bit more aggressive on it. Now we're in a completely different position as a company compared to when we built Terronera. Ultimately from our feasibility study, which is a 43-101 feasibility study and not probably what historically 10, 15, 20 years ago when people talk about bankable feasibility study. So from this feasibility study, we've already engaged a firm to push forward with finalizing basic engineering and going into detailed engineering. There's other aspects of the project that we deem to be early work.

So road improvements, power lines, work that we've started this year that's gone slower than maybe expected, partially because we're waiting for some of the design criteria to be completed that was in the feasibility study. But we need to continue to push on that to make a time line of, say, production by 2030, Q1 2030. So we have a really good feel of what our spend will be in 2027. So we have a very good feel of the first 6 months and doing some of the early work stuff.

I think about wells and water, making sure we can get water to site from wells, again, road improvements and continue to push with power lines with CFE. So it's very clear what we need to do. And so we'll have a pretty definitive budget for 2027 when that comes out in January.

Dan Dickson: I would also add, you see a lot of the engineering firms because of the price environment that we're in, are being pulled in every direction and whether they have a sufficient staff. So things have just taken a little bit longer more from an engineering standpoint than anything else.

Dan Dickson: Thank you, operator, and thanks for everyone for joining our Q3 financial earnings call. Again, we're very excited about how Terronera has been shaping up this year. We've seen grades continue to improve as management's expectation, and we hope to see a little bit more improvement going forward. And ultimately, we've seen our costs come down quarter-over-quarter-over-quarter. So thank you for everybody attending and hopefully here for you in January. Bye.

#3186. New Apple TV 4K remote’s best feature requires a newer iPhone model

A new Apple TV 4K releases this Friday (pre-order here), with an upgraded Siri Remote. But the new remote’s best feature might not work on your iPhone.

If you’re interested in the new Apple TV 4K launching this week, or perhaps you just want to buy the upgraded Siri Remote separately (available here), there’s a key limitation you should know.

Precision Finding on the new Siri Remote requires an iPhone 17 or newer.

The most common problem with the current Siri Remote is that it’s easy to lose. And once you lose it, Apple doesn’t offer many options for finding it. But that’s changing with the 4th gen Siri Remote.

You can use the new Siri Remote with any previous Apple TV 4K or Apple TV HD model. And if you do, you’ll benefit from the remote’s new built-in speaker that can be triggered from the Find My app.

Joining the new speaker, the other main change with this latest Siri Remote is Precision Finding. If you’ve ever used the Find My app to track down a lost AirTag, you’ll probably be familiar with the feature.

Precision Finding lets you get step-by-step, guided directions that take you directly to the lost Siri Remote. It’s a huge upgrade from the old tool for finding the remote—which mostly just told you that it’s in your house somewhere.

But Precision Finding relies on the Bluetooth 6 support found in iPhone 17 and 17 Pro models (not iPhone 17e), iPhone Air, iPhone Duo, and iPhone 18 Pro models.

So if you don’t have one of those iPhones, you’ll still benefit from the built-in speaker that lets you play a sound to find the lost remote, but Precision Finding won’t be available.

You can buy the new Siri Remote for $59 on Amazon.

Will this limitation impact your Siri Remote purchase decision? Let us know in the comments.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

Apple is proud to support the next generation of developers, creators, and entrepreneurs with the Swift Student Challenge. The Challenge gives students from around the world the opportunity to showcase their creativity and app development skills.

#3183. Mercedes’ US fast-charging network hits 100 sites in three years

Its 400 kW network hit 100 sites in North America, while its European hubs went to Electra.

Electric Mercedes-Benz cars at one of the carmaker’s high-power charging hubs in the US.

Mercedes-Benz’s US fast-charging network has reached 100 sites and nearly 1,000 ports in three years, with more than 550,000 sessions. The milestone comes a week after Mercedes sold its 47 European charging hubs to France’s Electra.

Mercedes-Benz’s fast-charging network in North America has reached 100 sites three years after opening its first station, InsideEVs reported. The milestone comes a week after the carmaker sold its European network.

The network now has nearly 1,000 charging points across 28 US states and British Columbia, all able to deliver up to 400 kW. Mercedes says they have handled more than 550,000 sessions for over 245,000 drivers since November 2023. Almost every site has both the older CCS plug and Tesla’s NACS plug, now standard on most new EVs.

Mercedes says its chargers are almost never down. It now focuses on how often a session starts at the first try, which rose from about 84% in 2023 to more than 90%.

Charging costs $0.35 to $0.60 per kWh, depending on the site, which are often near upmarket shopping centres. The largest, in Orlando, Florida, has 20 stalls.

Europe has gone the other way. Last week, Mercedes handed its 47 European charging hubs to French operator Electra, calling the business outside its core, Electrive reported. The US network stays “for the time being.”

Mercedes is also one of eight carmakers behind IONNA, a separate US charging network that has passed 180 sites. The US now has more than 80,000 fast-charging ports in total. US EV sales, meanwhile, remain about 40% below last year’s levels.

If you've tried breathable bed sheets, oscillating fans and frozen pillows but you still wake up sweaty, I've found the solution. The Orion Sleep System, now with $600 off in Orion's Black Friday sale, is a smart cooling system that helps defeat night sweats by actively adjusting the temperature as you sleep.

One of the best smart beds you can buy online, this clever mattress cover is fitted with a series of (imperceptible) water tubes that cool or heat throughout the night. That means a sudden flush of cold if night sweats are coming on, or a gentle warming if things get too chilly.

This is just a cover, so you might need to buy a new bed to go with it — I recommend our best mattress guide for our top rated suggestions. But with $600 off in the Black Friday mattress sales, there has never been a better time to shop the Orion.

I've never seen a bigger price drop from Orion, as this massive $600 off sale takes a queen down to just $1,795 (was $2,395). That's an impressive price for a smart mattress cover with active temperature regulation, particularly as there are no hidden costs (a sleep tracking subscription is optional at $250/year). The extras are average for this type of sleep tech, with a 30-night trial and 2-year warranty.

When we review any mattress, temperature regulation is a key concern. It refers to how well a mattress can kick out excess heat so you don't wake up at 3 a.m. feeling uncomfortably sweaty.

Most of the best mattresses in a box achieve this through cooling materials. That is, copper-infused foams or phase change material (PCM).

The Orion takes a different approach. This smart mattress cover is fitted with a series of water tubes, which connect back to a control hub. During the night, the water flowing through those pipes either cools down or warms up, so you stay at just the right temperature.

And this sci-fi-esque sleep system is impressively effective. I purposely warmed myself up to see if the cooling kicked in (the only time you'll ever catch me doing nighttime jumping jacks) and was greeted by a flush of coolness. For hot flashes and night sweats, this is a dream.

Most of the time, however, the Orion delivers the kind of comfort you hardly notice. It's climbing into a bed that feels just right, sleeping through the night, and waking up feeling snug all the way down to your toes.

While the temperature regulation impressed me, I was less enthused by the Orion's sleep tracking. At $250 extra for a year's subscription, I think you can get better results for less with the Fitbit Air or Withings Sleep Analyzer. Or, for cooling and tracking, there's another solution...

I'm currently testing the Eight Sleep Pod 6, which uses water to cool and heat your mattress to just the right temperature. It's more expensive than the Orion — although you can save up to $200 in the pre-Black Friday sale and get a queen for $2,699 (was $2,899) — but the integrated sleep tracking is accurate and intuitive, delivering detailed insight into your rest. A subscription is required and starts from $17/month.

#3181. Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy

Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs.

The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more.

It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server.

Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details:

Apple is working on a new app called HarborHarbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf

As the post notes, here’s what the app does:

Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone.

Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead.

Are you interested in using Harbor on your Mac? Let us know in the comments.
