This gives us a clear message for customers about our continued commitment to innovation, service, and support. I'm encouraged by the recovery we're seeing in our pipeline. Publications, preprints, and reviews describing research conducted using the Proteograph now total 116, up from 95 at our last quarterly update. I want to highlight the discoveries researchers are advancing, what this growth evidence means for the use of the Proteograph, and how it supports the commercial opportunity we're pursuing.

Turning to slide 3, let me turn to the scientific evidence from the PRECISE-SG100K cohort presented at the 2026 Human Proteome Organization World Congress, or HUPO. PRECISE-SG100K is Singapore's population health study of approximately 100,000 residents of Chinese, Malay, and Indian ancestry designed to understand how genetics, biology, lifestyle, and environment influence health and disease. Within this program, investigators selected our Proteograph workflow combined with Thermo Fisher's Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometry to deeply characterize the plasma proteome of 10,000 participants, complementing affinity-based measurements within the broader study. Professor John Chambers, Chief Scientific Officer of PRECISE and Lead Investigator of PRECISE-SG100K, presented preliminary findings.

Across 9,658 plasma samples, the Proteograph Astral workflow quantified approximately 8,800 protein groups across this study and approximately 88,000 peptides per sample. Performance was consistent across 126 processing batches with no reported sample failure. Population studies require both depth and reliable execution across thousands of samples, and these results demonstrate the ability of our workflow to deliver both. As subsequently reported by Thermo Fisher Scientific, the PRECISE investigators identified more than 4,200 proteins with significant cis-pQTL associations, which link nearby genetic variations with measured protein abundance. They also reported 2,762 genetic protein associations that had not been reported across the 12 reference studies used for comparison and connected proteins to 71 health-related traits.

When combined with disease genetics and other evidence, these relationships can help researchers investigate disease mechanism and prioritize potential therapeutic targets. The PRECISE-SG100K illustrates a central aspect of Seer's value proposition. Proteograph fundamentally expands the biology researchers can see with mass spectrometry. Published studies and customer presentations using matched plasma samples have repeatedly demonstrated that conventional mass spectrometry workflows without the Proteograph achieve approximately 10% to 15% of the protein coverage achieved when Proteograph is paired with a mass spectrometry. Used alongside advanced mass spectrometers, Proteograph substantially expands the biological information available for discovery.

Just as 10x Genomics enabled researchers to use DNA sequencing to resolve biology at the level of individual cells, Seer enables researchers to use mass spectrometry to explore a much deeper landscape of circulating proteins. By bringing thousands of additional proteins within reach of measurement, Proteograph opens new opportunities to uncover genetic protein relationships, investigate disease mechanisms, and identify potential therapeutic targets. This is the discovery capability Seer brings to population-scale research. The PRECISE team is now beginning to analyze the peptide-level data, creating opportunities to investigate protein variants and isoforms beyond the protein-level findings reported to date. For Seer, studies of this scale demonstrate both scientific value and the ability to support substantial sample processing programs.

Turning to slide 4, an independent study published in Clinical Proteomics provides another example of our differentiation. Researchers at CHA University in South Korea compared 7 plasma preparation approaches using accessible mass spectrometry instrumentation. Proteograph XT, together with the Orbitrap Exploris 480, delivered the greatest proteome coverage, identifying an average of approximately 6,060 proteins per sample and the lowest rate of missing protein measurements at 1.9%. These findings demonstrate that Proteograph enables deep proteomic coverage even in laboratories using earlier generations of mass spectrometers. Alongside this performance evidence, we have made important progress in protecting the technology behind it. Our intellectual property portfolio now includes more than 250 patent and patent applications, including 88 issued patents.

On November 5, we announced a significant development in our ITC action with Brigham Women's Hospital (sic) [ Brigham and Women's Hostpital ] against Nanomics. The Commission's final determinations remains pending and is expected by year-end. This is meaningful progress in defending our foundational intellectual property. Our customers commit precious samples, time, and resources to scientific discovery, and we will vigorously protect the innovation they rely on. The downstream impact of the Proteograph-enabled discoveries is also illustrated by PrognomiQ's ProVue Lung, the blood-based lung cancer detection test developed from biomarkers discovered using our technology.

PrognomiQ commercially launched ProVue Lung in November 2025 as a laboratory-developed test, or an LDT, and has reported early results from its ongoing real-world clinical evaluation. In a recent conference presentation, PrognomiQ's Chief Technology Officer Bruce Wilcox described how the protein biomarkers from the original discovery study were independently replicated using both targeted mass spectrometry and immunoassays in a separate patient cohort. The findings supported translation into a multiplex immunoassay for the launch of ProVue Lung. We also reported that the program progressed from initial Proteograph-based discovery to a validated laboratory-developed test in 31 months with clinical deployment to Allegheny Health Network and Penn Highlands Healthcare.

This is a concrete example of how broader biological information at the discovery stage can support the development of a clinical assay. Turning to slide 5, AI is shaping biology, and the capabilities of a model depend on the data it learns from. Proteograph-enabled mass spectrometry produces information at the spectral, peptide, and protein levels. Researchers can use this data to investigate protein abundance, peptide-level differences, and signals that conventional identification-based analysis have yet to fully characterize. Professors Sang-Won Lee and Jaewoo Kang of Korea University presented preliminary findings for more than 5,500 plasma samples at the ASMS and HUPO conference this year.

Their work combines deep Proteograph-enabled plasma measurements with an ID-free AI proteomics approach that uses features from both identified and unidentified spectral signals. Preliminary results showed improved overall cancer classification performance compared with models using only identified peptide features. We believe AI can become an important driver of demand for deep unbiased proteomics. When researchers are searching for new biological relationships, the information available to a model shapes what it can discover. Proteograph allows them to explore thousands of proteins beyond predefined panels while retaining peptide-level information and identifying spectral signals that can be revisited as analytical methods advance. The Korea University work provides an early example of that opportunity.

As more organizations use AI to investigate biology, we see an opportunity to help them generate the deep proteomic datasets those efforts require. That scientific interest is now translating into commercial activity. Our priority is to translate that scientific value into sustained commercial growth. Under Tony Bazarko's leadership as our Chief Commercial Officer, we're concentrating customer engagement and resources on accounts with the potential to generate meaningful repeat revenue. Tony and I are also making AI-driven research an explicit commercial priority, focusing on organizations that need deep proteomic data and have funded programs that can translate into sample volume. Within existing accounts, we're working to expand successful studies into additional funded programs and introduce Proteograph to other research teams.

In new accounts, we're focusing on opportunities with a clear scientific use case, funding, and a defined path to sample processing. We're also in active discussion with public and private population-scale cohorts about how Proteograph can support their next studies. We're also focused on biopharma, where we have signed several new large pharmaceutical customers this year that purchased instruments and consumables for their studies. I know you mentioned a number of times that they're elongated, but, I guess, how should we think about what, sort of, the average timeline is for the sales cycle at this point? And then on that, I think you also talked about going after some bigger customer opportunities, maybe accounts that will spend a little bit more. I guess, can you talk about your sales funnel in terms of maybe academic and government customers versus biopharma customers?

Omid Farokhzad: Yes, Kyle, thanks a lot. So the sales cycle continues to be long, but I think, Kyle, that has reduced in length. I would say today it's about 6 months. Before, I would say it was high single-digit number of months. The shortening of that from the high single-digit number to maybe 6 is a reflection of the fact that we're doing very small number of these proof-of-principle studies. I mean, I think customers are going from initial interaction to an acquisition or a STAC project. That's the first point. Second is, I'm super happy about the addition of Tony Bazarko to our executive team.

Tony is our Chief Commercial Officer, joined about 7 months ago, and then he brought Ryan Gossett as VP of Sales, someone who he had worked with in the past. And Ryan has been with us for about maybe 4 months or so. The 2 have been fantastic. They've been out seeing customers. The 2 of them in the last 7 months that Tony's been on the job, 4 that Ryan has been on the job, together, they have seen 50 distinct customers in person on their site globally.

And by the way, if a particular customer, like a large pharma, has multiple offices at different sites, different cities, I count that as 1, meaning these guys have actually seen more than 50 distinct customers over the last few months. The message that they're bringing to the headquarters is that there's a tremendous amount of appreciation for the kinds of studies that they're getting, and they're targeting progressively more and more biopharma customers. That is a priority for us. These are the customers with recurrent revenue, quarter-after-quarter revenue growth.

And then additionally, also looking at where the samples are, meaning we rather have -- we rather focus our commercial effort on large customers with recurring revenue quarter-after-quarter, and then customers that have the budget, customers that have the samples. We're now in multiple discussions of pharma and other types of customers that the initial discussions are at 10,000-plus samples. I expect to announce 1 of those over the course of the next few weeks that's going to be a 10,000-plus sample customer that -- with an initial order on a couple of thousand sample size. These are the kind of customers that Tony is targeting.

And I think it's a combination of the validation of the platform that is becoming more and more seen in the eyes of the customer that translates into these kinds of activities.

Kyle Boucher: Maybe just one more on pull-through. So I guess, can you just talk about what you're seeing from a pull-through perspective? I think in the past, you noted that it could take somewhere around 6 to 9 months for customers to reorder consumables after purchasing an instrument. Omid Farokhzad: Kyle, let me introduce you to Charles, and Charles is going to take that. I might add at the end of it, but Charles?

Charles Endweiss: Yes, Kyle. So the pull-through was relatively flat, sequentially quarter over quarter. Our established customers continued to purchase consumables, including accounts with purchases across multiple consecutive quarters. The purchasing remains project driven, so individual customers may order for a study and then there's a gap between when they reorder. We're also seeing the pipeline development with Tony and his team amongst our existing customers, where we're getting longer visibility into their project pipeline. Our priority is to build a broader base of repeat usage and higher utilization, and we're working to expand the number of active programs within each of these accounts.

#3153. Claude’s new Personal Finance tool aims to help analyze your spending – read-only, of course

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Anthropic has released what appears to be its answer to ChatGPT Finances.

You can now share your financial information with Claude and ask the chatbot for insights on your spending.

Also: Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info

Personal Finance in Claude, which Anthropic announced Thursday, reviews your connected accounts through read-only access via Plaid. That security measure follows OpenAI’s equivalent feature, ChatGPT Finances, which launched in May. Here’s what to know.

Functionally, this feature appears similar to ChatGPT Finances: It lets you link as many bank and credit card accounts as you’d like to Claude via Plaid with read-only access. You can then ask Claude where you spent your money this month or whether you can afford to take a vacation in six months, for example.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

According to Anthropic, the feature is a response to existing use patterns: the company’s April usage report found that financial advice was one of the main topics users ask Claude for help with.

“For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank’s name, each account’s name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train our models.”

The idea behind the feature is that you can ask follow-up questions and request more insights about spending habits, trends over time, and future goals based on what Claude finds, similar to any other Claude conversation. The tool will also generate tables and charts to visualize your financial information.

“You can ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what’s due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds it as an artifact you can keep adjusting and coming back to,” an Anthropic representative told ZDNET via email.

Also: I connected ChatGPT to my bank, and it’s my go-to finance app now

You can also expect an ad-free experience in the feature.

“Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer,” the company said in the announcement.

The company added that because Claude is using actual transaction data and not memory, the feature shouldn’t hallucinate.

“It can list the exact transactions behind any number so you can check its math,” Anthropic said via email. “Like any AI, it can make mistakes, so for anything important, we recommend confirming with your bank.”

Still, the difference — and for many, the appeal — here is the natural language interface. Other finance apps don’t necessarily have an easy, accessible chat function where users can shoot off quick questions like they would to a human financial planner. These assistants also present historical budget analysis in plain English, rather than requiring users to interpret dashboards themselves, which users may see as a perk.

Also: 5 ways to use AI when your budget is tight

On Reddit, many users find ChatGPT Finances to be accurate and reliable. One Reddit user said ChatGPT Finance seemed to have Mint or Monarch potential, but noted it was still “weaker” than those apps in some areas, such as historical syncing, high-quality dashboards, and generating full statement PDFs.

“ChatGPT has genuinely helped me make better financial decisions,” she wrote.

Anthropic noted that users shouldn’t look to Personal Finance for Claude as a total authority. “Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust,” the company said in the announcement.

“We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it” — indicating a more integrated financial planning system within Claude may be on the way.

#3152. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#3151. NASA Just Made a Bunch of Moon Base Announcements: Here’s What They Are

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The agency just unveiled new lunar missions, a nuclear-powered rover and $10 billion in contracts to build a moon base for astronauts.

NASA just wrapped up its Max Power event, the agency’s first-ever aerospace technology expo that took place Wednesday through Sunday at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Featuring discussions, panels, announcements and technology demonstrations, the biggest part of the event was NASA’s update on the Ignition initiative, which promises to put a base on the moon by 2032.

The Moon Base Program is an expensive endeavor that requires the help of various space companies to complete on time. Max Power discussed the various technologies and projects to make a base work, including the new CLPS 2 contract, a nuclear-powered moon rover and other lunar architecture.

NASA will rely heavily on commercial aerospace companies for many of these components: Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, SpaceX, Voyager Technologies and ispace-US. Most of those companies have also been supplying tech for the Artemis program, which is slated to launch its third mission in 2027 and send people back to the moon in 2028. While the Artemis missions are important in their own right, NASA is also using them as a precursor to the Moon Base. That’s one of many reasons why it was a huge deal when Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket exploded in May.

“We are building the moon base mission by mission,” NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said during Max Power. “When our astronauts return to the moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the moon base already waiting for them on the surface.”

The CLPS 2 contract is part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative, which plays a pivotal role in the moon base’s construction. The goal is to send materials and equipment to the moon ahead of time, so humans can immediately start building the base when they arrive.

The CLPS 2 contract builds on the CLPS 1.0 contract to develop the infrastructure and vehicles, including cargo landers, necessary to continuously ferry supplies and crew between Earth and the lunar surface. To fund these efforts, NASA paired the $10 billion CLPS 2 budget with an expanded CLPS 1.0 budget, which increased from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion.

The cargo landers get cargo from space to the moon’s surface, but they also have to be transported there. NASA announced $1.3 billion in funding to Blue Origin, Arrow Science and Technology and Impulse Space to perform this step. They’ll make Orbital Transfer Vehicles, or OTVs, that act like “long-distance freight trucks” to carry the cargo landers and eventually deploy them safely to the moon’s surface.

In addition to building the vehicles that do this, NASA says three missions are slated for completion. First, research must assess how to reduce human risk and determine the best ways to deploy the CLPS landers. Second, NASA’s MoonFall drones will assess the moon and find the most optimal spot for a base. The third mission is to test the infrastructure to ensure it works as designed.

NASA took some time to talk about Promise, also known as Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping and In-Situ Exploration, an important vehicle for early moon exploration. The agency awarded Blue Origin a $94 million development contract, plus a performance-based $140 million for lunar delivery. Once deployed, the nuclear-powered rover will be managed by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory at Caltech, which oversees NASA’s other rovers, NASA’s Deep Space Network and the Voyager probes.

Unlike solar-powered rovers, Promise’s nuclear core allows it to operate continuously through two-week lunar nights and in permanently shadowed regions where the sun never reaches. Its goal is to analyze regolith, hunt for ice and conduct general exploration.

While most of NASA’s recent announcements focused on getting hardware to the moon, the final segment laid the groundwork for surface infrastructure, specifically, long-term habitability so astronauts can actually be there.

To power this presence, NASA awarded contracts for energy storage and transmission to Honeybee Robotics (a Blue Origin company) and Yank Technologies. Their solar arrays, batteries and wireless power hardware will culminate in the Mini-Communications and Solar Tower (miniCast), assembled at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, before being deployed to the moon.

NASA is also trying to tackle the myriad problems that must be solved for a moon base to succeed. One of the initiatives announced at Max Power is the Moon Base Student Challenge, which asks students to help build humanity’s future on the moon, with $1 million in prizes for winners with the best ideas.

“We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world,” Isaacman said during his speech, which was packed with students and kids, according to Space.com.

While the initiative isn’t aimed at anything specific, it challenges students to tackle whatever they can regarding lunar base problems. NASA has tapped students before to help solve problems such as dealing with lunar dust clouds and human-capable landers.

#3150. 6 default Pixel 11 settings I changed that made a big difference – and why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

I’ve been a dedicated Pixel user since the beginning, so I was naturally excited to get my hands on Google’s latest iteration, the Pixel 11 Pro XL. I’ve been impressed with it overall, but I noticed that, as Google has done before, the device isn’t set up perfectly out of the box.

Also: Pixel 11 is $200 off in this early Black Friday deal

After spending a few weeks with the device, I found that several features are either turned off by default or need optimizing to work in the best way possible.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

The camera was the biggest reason I first joined team Pixel back in 2016, so it’s one of the first places I looked on the Pixel 11 Pro XL. New this year is Camera Looks, a setting that changes how images will be processed before you take them. You can change a number of settings, including contrast, shadows, tint, sharpness, and warmth.

Also: A week with the Pixel 11 changed my mind about Gemini

I’ve always loved the camera on any Pixel I’ve had, but I’ll admit that images can look a little over-processed at times. If picture quality is important to you at all, it’s vital to set this feature right out of the box because it applies to every image you take from that point on. You can find Camera Look by opening the camera app, tapping the settings icon in the bottom-right corner, and making your changes.

Pixel’s “At a Glance” lock screen widgets are one of the most sneakily useful features, and you’re missing out if you’re not using them. These widgets are off by default, but when you enable them, you can see real-time information without unlocking your phone. You can see weather info, sports updates, flight information, rideshare and food delivery updates, fitness information, and more.

Also: These tech gifts topped our experts’ 2026 holiday wish lists

To use these widgets, long-press on an open space on your home screen. To customize your widgets, go to Settings > Wallpaper & style > More lock screen settings > Widgets on lock screen. To access your widgets, you just swipe left from your lock screen.

Out of the box, your Pixel 11’s display isn’t set to utilize its full capability. The Pixel 11 series comes with a fantastic low-temperature polycrystalline oxide (LTPO) display, but it’s slightly throttled in the name of battery life. You’ll notice the increased resolution most on text and in fine details. It won’t make a huge difference to your streaming or large display elements, though. If you read consistently, either articles or e-books, you’ll want to make the change.

To change this, head to Settings > Display > Screen Resolution. Bump the setting from “High resolution,” which is 1080 x 2404, to “Max resolution,” which is 1344 x 2992.

If you’re anything like me, your phone usually needs a quick charge some evenings. The Pixel 11 series introduced Extreme Charging Mode, which accelerates charging by pausing background activity and non-essential apps. Google says the mode should charge the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro to over 50% in 30 minutes, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL to 75% in 30 minutes. From my testing, that estimate was pretty accurate.

Also: After testing the Pixel 11, I feel fine about skipping the Pro models

There are a few caveats: this feature is only available when your phone is at or below 50% battery, and you do need to turn it on every time you use it. But after the first time you do it, it’s available in your quick settings. Head to Settings > Battery & charging > Extreme Charging to turn it on the first time.

If you have the newest Pixel, you might as well take advantage of one of its biggest selling points. I felt like this feature was gimmicky at first (and I’m still a little grumpy it replaced my beloved thermometer), but the more I use it, the more I like it. The multicolor LED on the phone’s rear camera bump can indicate who’s calling, serve as a status indicator for Gemini, and more — and it’s almost certain that more usability will arrive over time.

Where I found the most use was when I had my phone on silent. After assigning specific colors to contacts (you can do this from the contact information screen), I could easily see whether a call was worth picking up without reaching for my phone.

To make sure you’re getting the most out of your new device, head in and change your contact HiLight colors right away. It only takes a few seconds and makes deciding whether to answer a call a lot easier.

We’ve all accidentally swiped away an important notification or missed a notification in a sea of updates. The Pixel 11 offers two notification features to help you stay on top of things.

Notification History is a feature that logs every alert from the last 24 hours, including those you swipe away. This is off by default, meaning when you dismiss a notification, it’s gone forever. With this on, you get a searchable, chronological backup.

Also: Google’s big flagship is more Pro than ever

AI Notification Summaries, as the name implies, takes long multi-notification threads and stacked notifications and turns them into bullet points. This feature is powered by on-device Gemini Intelligence, and you can choose which apps to summarize.

You can find both of these under Settings > Notifications > Notification history & Notification Summaries.

#3149. Ring’s Flying Home Security Drone Is Finally Here, and It’s Surprisingly Affordable

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ring's $250 flying indoor security camera is set to arrive in January. We got a first look at the Drone Cam in action.

Ring Home Security has taken flight, and the brand’s tiny new home security drone is less expensive than we thought. The Ring Drone Cam, a $250 mini indoor drone camera, was announced on Tuesday as part of the brand’s new arm, Ring Robotics. It uses a learned map of your home to zoom around autonomously for up to 8 minutes at a time with custom routes to record places a couple of fixed cameras can’t.

The small drone weighs just 5.8 ounces and houses a pair of 2K-resolution cameras mounted on the front and bottom, respectively. The cameras use bright LED lights to enable day or night monitoring, sending a live feed or recorded video to your device. The LEDs are also meant to ward off potential intruders peering in from the outside.

You can program the flying cam to make regular flights or send it on specific missions to check on the dog or see if the stove was left on. The Drone Cam also syncs with other Ring cameras and sensors to respond automatically when windows and doors open at certain hours.

If you’re thinking, “Wait, didn’t Ring already launch a drone camera?” you’d be right — sort of. The brand “launched” the Ring Always Home Cam in 2020. The $250 indoor drone had a limited, invitation-only release but was never available for public sale. We’ve been assured this latest iteration is ready for prime time, though it’s still not available for preorder on Amazon.

Ring founder and CEO Jamie Siminoff demoed the drone, which has been in development for more than five years, in an event space set up to replicate a home. During the demo, the small drone lifted gently from the dock and rose to about eye level, where it hovered as if to say “hello” to the group of journalists gathered around.

Once airborne, the drone turned toward the adjacent room and whirred off to investigate. After a few seconds of scanning, the drone returned to the first room, docked and resumed charging.

While in flight, the Ring Drone Cam made a notably loud buzz reminiscent of a golf cart in reverse. Siminoff quickly noted that the sound was intentional, meant to deter potential intruders and alert home dwellers to the drone’s presence.

The 1-minute flight was enough to cover two medium-sized rooms, though the drone can fly up to eight minutes on a full charge before needing about an hour to recharge. Ring reps told me it can monitor a home up to 3,500 square feet – more than enough for most – but Siminoff says it plans to improve the range over time.

If you’re worried about the drone knocking over vases and flying into ceiling fans like I was, Siminoff assured us the preprogrammed coverage zone is tight.

The drone is powered by AI Pilot, “a custom-built system that uses the device’s cameras, specialized vision models, sensors and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.” (We’ll see for ourselves once we get a unit in for testing.)

To create your drone’s fly zone, you carry it through the space where it intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points like doors, windows or a nursery. You can add rooms and areas based on your home’s layout and security preferences.

The $250 Ring Drone Cam isn’t yet available for preorder, but Ring representatives at the launch event assured us it will be soon, and units are set to begin shipping in late January 2027. We’ll update this story when it becomes available for preorder or purchase.

#3148. 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Most HR professionals say they believe employees can be reskilled for AI jobs, yet companies still often seek outside hires. Here's why.

HR leaders are confident that current employees can be trained for jobs created by artificial intelligence. Organizations are hiring externally instead.

That’s the finding in new research from Careerminds, a global provider of workforce solutions. The study, published in Careerminds’ white paper, The AI Redeployment Gap: What Companies Lose by Hiring over Reskilling, reveals that 92% of HR professionals and 88% of people managers believe employees within their organizations could be reskilled for AI-related roles.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill

Yet 51% of HR professionals and 47% of people managers report that their organizations are hiring externally for new AI-related positions, compared with just 42% in each group who report redeploying existing employees.

The research was conducted in partnership with Censuswide and surveyed 595 US HR professionals and 547 US people managers, ages 25–65, working at organizations with 500-10,000 or more employees. The research was conducted May 15–26, 2026.

Also: Businesses finally seeing AI ROI, but 62% can’t handle the storage demands

“Companies are investing in AI while potentially overlooking one of their most valuable resources: the people they already employ,” said Mark Saddic, senior partner at Careerminds, in a press release.

“Our research shows that organizations largely believe their employees can adapt to AI-driven change, but that confidence isn’t consistently translating into opportunities. Before looking outside the organization, leaders need to understand the skills they already have, identify where employees can grow, and establish a clear process for making those transitions possible.”

Reskilling, especially for AI, isn’t easy to track. Limited visibility into individual skill sets and which employees should be reskilled was cited as a potential barrier by 43% of HR professionals and 34% of managers.

Also: Pearson’s Workera deal targets a big workplace problem: No time to AI upskill

It’s not the first time that the management of skills development has come up regarding AI. In September, educational giant Pearson agreed to acquire Workera, the AI-native skills platform used by organizations such as ServiceNow, Accenture, and the US Space Force.

Careermind’s data revealed that 87% of HR pros and 84% of managers believe their organizations are adequately considering reskilling employees for future roles. However, the findings suggest that these organizations may believe they are prioritizing internal talent development, even though their hiring practices reveal otherwise.

Response to AI-related workforce needs isn’t equal across the board. The findings reveal significant differences in how industries are responding to these needs.

Also: Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ new top stressor

For example, in the technology and telecom industries, external hiring outpaces redeployment by 15%. At the same time, media and entertainment is the only sector surveyed in which both groups report redeployment at least as frequently as external hiring. Among HR professionals in that industry, 56% report redeploying employees, compared with just 25% who hire externally.

Separate research from The Josh Bersin Company, cited in the Careerminds white paper, reveals that external hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally — and on average takes up to 20 days longer.

Jacqueline Shea: Good afternoon, and thank you to everyone for joining. I'd like to start today's call by highlighting the recent FDA approval of VOCERYQ, formerly known as INO-3107, under the Accelerated Approval Program as a new nonsurgical treatment option to reduce the frequency of surgery in adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, or RRP. In the press release it issued, the FDA stated that VOCERYQ was a groundbreaking therapy and that its approval represented a meaningful scientific breakthrough by offering patients a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that harnesses the body's own immune system to fight the underlying cause of RRP.

The accelerated approval for VOCERYQ and the broad indication included in its label for adults with RRP are an acknowledgment of the significant unmet need for nonsurgical treatment options for RRP and the potential therapeutic benefit that VOCERYQ can provide. We believe it has the potential to transform the treatment paradigm for this disease by delivering what we understand matters most to patients: reducing the need for surgery. This is a pivotal moment for RRP patients who have faced a relentless cycle of surgery for far too long with limited treatment options, and for Inovio, as we move forward into an exciting new chapter as a commercial-stage company.

Going forward, our primary focus will be maximizing the opportunity we see for VOCERYQ and executing our commercial launch with the goal of establishing it as the preferred first-line treatment for adults with RRP. To support those efforts, we recently completed an equity offering that provided approximately $80.5 million in net proceeds. These proceeds, together with our existing cash resources and subsequent warrant exercise proceeds, are expected to support operations into late fourth quarter 2027, past the launch of VOCERYQ, without taking potential expected product revenues into account. The approval of our first commercial product validates our platform and confirms our belief in the potential of our pipeline candidates to help patients suffering from other diseases.

While our initial focus is on the successful launch of VOCERYQ within our broad adult indication, we will also be looking to expand the potential of VOCERYQ to serve additional indications within the RRP marketplace, both here in the U.S. and internationally. We will also continue to prioritize partnerships to efficiently advance our clinical-stage candidates and look to establish new partnerships to advance promising earlier-stage candidates in our pipeline. This is truly a transformative time for Inovio and for DNA medicine, and we are excited about the significant opportunities ahead. I'll now turn it over to Mike Sumner, our Chief Medical Officer, to provide a few more details on the approval, product label and supporting clinical data. Mike?

Michael Sumner: Thank you, Jacqui. The approval of VOCERYQ is exciting on many fronts. It's Inovio's first approved product, the first FDA-approved plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy, and most importantly, an innovative and much-needed new treatment option for adults with RRP. I'd like to spend some time today providing a few highlights from the approval of VOCERYQ and its broad adult indication. VOCERYQ was evaluated in RRP-001, a multi-site clinical study designed to assess what matters most to patients, reduction in surgery. The study followed 32 adult patients who had 2 to 8 surgeries in the year prior to treatment. Patients had visible papillomas surgically removed before receiving their first dose of VOCERYQ. Patients then received 4 doses over a 9-week period.

The primary efficacy endpoint was a reduction in surgery following dosing initiation. In this trial, we counted all surgeries after the first dose against the efficacy endpoint. We also conducted study RRP-002, a retrospective assessment of treatment effect up to 3 years after initial dosing in patients who had participated in the 001 study. The full clinical data from these studies were published in 2025 in Nature Communications and in The Laryngoscope, the top journal for the specialists who treat RRP. An additional analysis of data was also recently published in The Laryngoscope, supporting the ability of VOCERYQ to generate an immune response that linked to durable clinical benefit over the second and third years following initial treatment.

These publications highlight the meaningful therapeutic benefit of VOCERYQ, with the vast majority of patients experiencing a 50% to 100% reduction in surgery in year 1, with durable responses and continued clinical improvement in year 2. The FDA's efficacy evaluation for Accelerated Approval focused specifically on the first year treatment effect for patients who required 3 or more surgeries in the 12 months prior to treatment. For those 26 patients, the median number of surgeries in the 12 months prior to the first dose was 4.5, which included the surgical debulking required immediately prior to treatment. FDA's efficacy analysis started at the end of the dosing window at week 9.

In the following 12 months, 27% of the patients achieved complete response, as defined by not requiring any surgeries to manage their disease. And as a reminder, this response was achieved without conducting any scoping or surgery during the dosing window. Patients going from needing 3 or more surgeries a year to needing 0 surgeries following treatment would not be expected as part of the natural history of the disease. In terms of safety, VOCERYQ was found in the clinical study to be well tolerated, with study participants experiencing mostly low-grade treatment-emergent adverse events such as injection site pain and fatigue, with the majority being grade 1.

This slide lists the most common adverse reactions occurring in greater than or equal to 5% of patients, as described in the prescribing information. Of note, because VOCERYQ is a drug device combination product composed of our plasmid DNA-based drug with delivery by our CELLECTRA device, this safety profile represents the combination product. For this approval, the safety data were further supported by data from prior clinical trials of VGX-3100, an HPV-16 and 18 related disease program, which included over 1,100 administrations and a placebo control. Delivery with our proprietary CELLECTRA device is well characterized and has also been shown in additional clinical studies to be well tolerated.

It is also important to point out here that reducing the need for surgery, both as part of or following treatment, is an important consideration for patients. Every surgery matters because every individual surgery comes with significant risk. Finally, I'd like to share a brief overview of our future confirmatory study. As VOCERYQ has received an Accelerated Approval, continued approval for this indication may be contingent on verification and description of clinical benefit in a confirmatory study. We expect to submit a draft protocol for this study before year-end with the goal of aligning with the FDA on a final protocol by mid-2027.

We have agreed with the agency that the study should enroll at least 50 adult and pediatric patients with RRP requiring 3 or more surgical interventions in the 12 months prior to treatment with VOCERYQ. Subject to further regulatory feedback, we expect the study to evaluate the number of surgical interventions required over at least 3 years following completion of treatment, and compare this to an appropriate external control group or scientifically justified threshold. We may also explore continued treatment in patients without a sustained complete response as part of the study. I will now turn it over to Steve Egge, our Chief Commercial Officer, for an overview of our commercial launch plans. Steve?

Steven Egge: Thank you, Mike. We're excited to launch VOCERYQ and are focused on ensuring eligible RRP patients can access treatment as quickly and efficiently as possible. Let's start by discussing the significant RRP market opportunity. Based on our ongoing analysis of claims data, we believe there's a prevalent population of at least 25,000 adult patients with RRP in the United States, with additional patients diagnosed each year. Most patients continue to be managed surgically, and every single surgery comes with a risk of permanent vocal cord and airway damage.

Key opinion leaders and the RRP Foundation stated in a position paper published in The Laryngoscope in January of this year that immunotherapy should be considered the first-line treatment for RRP, and that it should be started as soon as possible in the patient's disease journey to reduce the risk of permanent damage from repeated surgeries. This position paper also noted that should VOCERYQ be approved by the FDA, it would be recommended as first-line therapy. To date, only a small fraction of the prevalent population of patients have been treated with immunotherapy, indicating there is a significant market opportunity for a nonsurgical therapeutic treatment option designed to reduce the frequency of surgeries.

Our goal is to establish VOCERYQ as the preferred first-line treatment for adults with RRP by leveraging what we believe are the key differentiating strengths of the product. VOCERYQ targets the root cause of RRP to deliver compelling efficacy, reducing the need for surgery. VOCERYQ also has a favorable tolerability profile, with the potential to minimize disruption to patient lives. And for physicians, providing treatment is simple and straightforward.

The device is designed to be easy to use and has a standard refrigeration requirement for drug storage that allows for flexibility in the location of administration. These strengths are what we believe can enable VOCERYQ to become the immunotherapy of choice for both patients and physicians. Looking at the patient journey in more detail, physicians and patients can discuss treatment with VOCERYQ as soon as a diagnosis has been established through the first biopsy or surgery. Once prescribed, the patient would undergo initial papilloma removal and then complete a 4-dose treatment series over 9 weeks. As we've noted in the label for VOCERYQ, there's no requirement to conduct scoping or surgery during the dosing window.

This patient-centric approach helps to eliminate or reduce surgeries both during and after treatment. Looking ahead, I'd like to outline our priorities to support a successful launch. First, we're working to ensure patients can access VOCERYQ as quickly as possible. Payers recognize the burden of recurrent surgery in RRP and the need for additional treatment options. We expect insurers that cover approximately 80% of patients in the U.S. to have policies in place for coverage within 9 months of approval based on our payer research to date.

Third, we aim to make the treatment process as seamless as possible for both patients and physicians. We're launching the VOCERYQ Support Program with a single point of contact to provide support around product ordering, patient benefit investigation and verification, co-pay support and our patient assistance program. Our goal is to minimize the administrative burden and make access to treatment simple for both health care providers and patients. We aim to have the VOCERYQ Support Program in place once product is available.

To drive awareness and adoption, our strategy is focused on efficiently reaching the physicians who treat the majority of patients with RRP. The remaining 20% of RRP patients receive care in community hospitals and private group practices. Our field teams will plan to engage both of these important customer segments. #3145. Apple will monitor your public iCloud links now, starting with iOS 27.3

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Under Apple's new policy, the company will scan publicly shared iCloud links for harmful content - and possibly ban violators.

Be careful what you share in your iCloud. Apple announced it will start monitoring public iCloud links for harmful content — and potentially disable accounts that violate company policy.

Also: How to free up your iPhone storage almost immediately

The change comes with the impending release of Apple’s 27.3 build across its operating systems. If an iCloud user selects “Anyone with the link” when sharing something in a group chat or Discord server, it’s considered a public link; Apple is within its rights to scan for anything that violates company policy or is potentially illegal.

If you try to upload harmful content, Apple says it reserves the right to “move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete” your content at any time. Furthermore, Apple outlines possible actions it may take, including:

Apple’s announcement did not explain what “harmful content” would mean in practice. While there are obvious violations like drug sales and child sex abuse material, the new policy’s vagueness is concerning.

Once an iCloud link is shared under the “Anyone with a link” designation, end-to-end encryption is removed, even if either party has enabled Advanced Data Protection, which allows Apple to view the link’s content.

If you select “People you choose,” which limits access to users who have been invited or approved, the encryption remains in place, and Apple won’t be able to see what you’re sharing.

The new policy does not lay out an appeals process if you think your account or content has been falsely flagged as harmful. However, Apple does have a web page that provides information on how to appeal for other reasons. So there is a framework in place to push back if you think you’ve been caught in the dragnet by accident.

#3143. Thinking Machines’ new model takes the lead in western open-weight AI

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Another competitive model developed outside of China could change the open-weight landscape.

Thinking Machines Lab, a small AI startup from ex-OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has released its latest model, Inkling 2 Small — and according to third-party tester Artificial Analysis, it’s set to give Chinese models a run for their lead. It’s technically proprietary until now, but Thinking Machines said it will release its weights next week.

Also: Open weights vs. closed: An AI civil war’s afoot

Chinese companies have led the pack on open models over the last few years. Models from DeepSeek and Moonshot regularly top leaderboards and rival the capabilities of much more expensive, closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Since DeepSeek’s R1 performed similarly to OpenAI’s o1 in January 2025, Chinese open models have given investors and high-paying enterprise customers reasons to rethink their expensive contracts with US-based labs. Western labs creating more competitive open models changes the landscape.

Thinking Machines’ latest model has 594 billion parameters and supports image inputs but outputs only text. The company noted its web and game design capabilities and that it evaluated the model’s approach to coding problems alongside the code it generated during testing.

“The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops,” the company said.

Also: Nvidia takes another step forward for US open-weight AI

Inkling 2 Small scored a 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite test “for tracking progress toward artificial general intelligence” that combines benchmark scores spanning coding, science, and general categories. A score of 31 is above average for models in its class and is tied with Gemini 3.8 Flash. For context, Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 top the index at 60 and 59, respectively.

Thinking Machines said it will release the model’s weights next week, a practice that is becoming customary. Given the heightened security concerns around AI in general, AI companies spend a few weeks testing the to-be-open model with cybersecurity teams and safety reviewers before releasing the weights, rather than leading with the weights out of the gate.

French AI lab Mistral recently released its Le Chonk model via the same staggered process — it now keeps pace with OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra in coding abilities, which is rare for western-made open models.

Also: Mistral’s Le Chonk is now a top open model for coding

“[Thinking Machines’] plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings,” Artificial Analysis said.

“Inkling 2 Small is amongst the leading models in intelligence and reasonably priced when comparing to other models of similar price. It’s also notably slow per task and very verbose,” Artificial Analysis said. The organization also called Inkling 2 Small’s pricing “somewhat expensive” at $0.30 per one million input tokens, since the median cost for its class is $0.24.

Still, the model’s progress over its predecessor stands out to Artificial Analysis reviewers: Inkling 2 Small jumped 41% in automation capabilities and 20% in coding abilities. However, most models excel in certain areas or on specific benchmarks, making it hard to deem one or another the outright best coding model overall.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a local AI stack that’s completely free

Inkling 2 Small also made some gains in accuracy, Artificial Analysis said.

“On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small’s 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%,” its review reported.

#3142. Adobe Is Giving Its AI Agents Even More to Do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Across Firefly and Creative Cloud, apps are getting even deeper into creative work.

Would you use an always-on AI agent such as Claude Duet or OpenAI’s Dot to edit your photos? At Adobe Max on Tuesday, the company announced it’s expanding its local MCP integrations with more third-party companies to enable more autonomous creative work.

MCP, or Model Context Protocol, is an open-source protocol for connecting AI systems to external apps and databases. AI agents and MCPs act as a two-way street. Agents, or fancy bots, can complete tasks independently.

For example, if you wanted your OpenAI agents (or Dots, whatever you call them) to edit a project in Photoshop, the MCP pathway would allow ChatGPT to run agents to edit the design in the Photoshop beta desktop app — no need to search through the toolbar if you’re not familiar with it.

The new MCP integrations are in preview now. The idea is to give people more choice by letting them use their preferred AI app to help them work in select Creative Cloud apps.

Over the past year, Adobe has been working with AI companies to bring its creative knowledge and tech to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot as Adobe plugins. It’s also brought external models from AI companies into Firefly, Adobe’s AI hub. Now, Adobe is deepening its relationships with third-party AI vendors to adapt to the agentic AI era.

Bringing your own agents offers a degree of user control, according to Shilpa Anand, vice president of global strategic partnerships. “These new models allow me to actually do things faster, experience the full power of the application and really make it more accessible to a broader set of users who are not experts in our workflow,” Anand told me.

Agentic AI has been a huge focus for tech companies this year. It’s the next step for companies that want to move beyond mere chat and information-gathering AI capabilities.

Adobe has been driving toward this vision for a while. It released AI assistants in Photoshop and Adobe Express that set the foundation for June’s official launch of Adobe creative agents.

But AI agents from frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic caused trouble this summer when they escaped testing environments and hacked real websites. Anand told me that safety and security are “table stakes” for Adobe and that there haven’t been any issues aligning with other AI companies on safety precautions.

When considering partnerships, the company also considers which AI models will be most useful for Adobe’s creative customers, which is why Firefly includes models from big players including Google, as well as more specialized AI companies, such as ElevenLabs for AI audio tech. (Adobe acquired Topaz Labs, which makes AI photo editing software, earlier this year.)

Those creative AI agents are getting new capabilities across Creative Cloud apps, too. In Firefly, the company’s AI hub, its AI assistant should now be better at multistep or more complex tasks, and it has a new “plan mode” in preview that lets you review the agent’s plan before it starts running.

New “always-on” Firefly AI agents do exactly what the name implies: They’re always working and can handle predefined tasks, such as assessing image quality in new asset uploads. They’re in preview now, too. And across Illustrator, InDesign, Premiere, After Effects and Frame.io, those AI assistants are getting upgraded capabilities as well.

Adobe is also expanding its partnerships. Microsoft Photos will have a built-in Adobe Express integration, and Microsoft’s Arm-based Windows PCs are getting “optimized” Adobe apps. Disney is also deepening its relationship with Adobe, bringing Adobe’s Firefly AI tech to its creative teams.

Partnerships with AI companies and the integration of agentic capabilities will continue to be a focus for Adobe next year, Anand told me. “Agentic software is really going to enable us to reach more users and empower everyone to create, which is our mission.”

#3141. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

At the same time, we ended the quarter with $75.7 million in cash and cash equivalents and reduced our outstanding debt by approximately 76% since year end as we continue to bring our Livermore production campus to full operation. Third quarter 2026 revenue was $20.5 million up 50% compared to $13.6 million in the year ago quarter.

Revenue from 3 d printers and parts was $18.8 million an increase of 57% compared to $12 million in the third quarter of 2025. The increase was driven by a higher number of 3 d printer systems sold higher average selling prices and a product mix, as well as an increase in Rapid Production Solutions or RPS revenue resulting from higher production volumes. We are encouraged by the continued strength in revenue across our business. Our results reflect ongoing demand for our systems, and production capabilities, as well as progress in expanding our RPS offering.

We believe the combination of system sales and production related revenue provides a foundation for continued growth as customers increasingly adopt metal additive manufacturing for more demanding applications. Gross margin for the third quarter was 26.5%, compared to 3.2% in the year ago quarter. The improvement reflected higher average selling prices, a more favorable product mix improved manufacturing efficiencies and increased production volumes that improve the absorption of fixed manufacturing costs. Results also benefited from adjustments to our excess and obsolete inventory reserve attributable to the current period. As well as the changes implemented in the second quarter to the allocation of certain labor and overhead costs between cost of revenue and operating expenses.

Looking forward, we believe continued improvements in manufacturing utilization, production efficiencies, product mix and the scaling of RPS will support gross margin performance. Operating expenses for the third quarter were $22.7 million compared to $10.4 million in the third quarter of 2025. The increase primarily reflects our continued investment in the Livermore production campus as we prepare the facility for expanded production along with investments in technology, manufacturing readiness, and the operational capabilities required to support our growth strategy. On a non-GAAP basis, excluding stock-based compensation, recorded in operating expenses of $5.7 million. Adjusted operating expenses were $17 million compared to $9.1 million in the prior year quarter.

GAAP net loss for the third quarter was $16.7 million or $0.52 per basic and diluted share, compared to a net loss of $11.2 million or $0.65 per basic and diluted share in the year ago quarter. The increase in net loss reflects in part the higher operating expenses associated with our continued investments in the business. Non GAAP net loss for the third quarter was a non-GAAP net loss of $10.8 million compared to a non-GAAP net loss of $9.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. These non-GAAP results exclude stock based compensation, and other specified items as detailed in our earnings release.

Non GAAP adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter was a negative $9.8 million compared to negative $7.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. As we continue investing in our production infrastructure and operational capabilities, our focus remains on balancing these investments with revenue growth, improved gross margins and disciplined expense management. These efforts are important as we work towards our objective of achieving positive EBITDA and positive net cash provided by operating activities in 2028. Turning to bookings and backlog.

We generated $28.9 million in new bookings during the third quarter and ended the period with a backlog of $40.1 million Moving on to the balance sheet, we ended the third quarter with $75.7 million in cash and cash equivalents compared to $39 million at the end of 2025. Our cash position reflects the financing activities completed earlier in the year partially offset by cash used to fund our operations and investments in the business. At September 30, 2026, total outstanding debt was $7.4 million compared to $31 million at the end of 2025. The combination of our cash position and reduced debt provides additional flexibility as we continue executing our strategic priorities.

Overall, the third quarter reflected continued progress across the business. We delivered strong year over year revenue growth, improved gross margin compared with the prior year period, generated bookings in excess of revenue and strengthened our balance sheet. We also continued investing in the manufacturing infrastructure and operational capabilities needed to support our long term growth strategy. With that, I will turn the call back over to Arun.

And our priorities remain clear. Execute with discipline, strengthen customer relationships and partnerships, scale our production capabilities, and build a business that delivers sustainable long term growth and profitability. The DJ's voice feature can now be disabled but what's the fun in that?

Music streaming service Spotify has unveiled new abilities for its popular AI-powered DJ feature, including new hosts — speaking in Spanish and English — and an on/off announcer toggle. The update rolls out to existing DJ markets starting Tuesday.

The lineup includes seven new English voices with British, American, Irish, Australian and Indian accents, as well as two new Mexican-accented voices that speak in Spanish.

The personalities also differ by announcer, too — for instance, Spotify says American Tess is “direct but inviting, has a bit of an edge. In-the-know” while Australian Sam is “gregarious, fun, likes to keep things not-so-serious.”

You can also turn the announcer off, but it would then be hard to tell how a Spotify DJ mix differs from a random mix. The company says you’ll still hear a “brief acknowledgment” when you start the DJ or press the DJ button to switch modes.

Spotify’s DJ was introduced in 2023 and is a way to set up your own radio station with a dynamic announcer. In addition, Spotify is the most popular music streaming service, with over 100 million tracks and a plethora of features including audiobooks, podcasts and the end-of-year Spotify Wrapped. #3137. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.
