#3135. Your November Stargazing Calendar: Meteors, Morning Planets and a Supermoon

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Darker evenings after the end of daylight saving time, plus a crowded morning sky, give you plenty of chances to look up this month.

Looking to see some amazing sights in the autumn sky? You’re in luck. November is the final full month of fall, and with daylight saving time having ended on Nov. 1, the sun has been setting even earlier. That’s good news, since some of November’s best views come before sunrise.

Venus, Mercury, Mars and Jupiter all appear in the morning sky this month, with Mars and Jupiter drawing close together around Nov. 15–16. The Leonid meteor shower peaks a couple of nights later, and the hours after moonset on Nov. 17–18 offer the darkest window to catch it. Evenings have their own highlights, from Saturn after dusk to the Beaver Supermoon on Nov. 24.

Below, find some of the remaining sights you should catch in the night sky throughout the rest of November.

Every planet is visible during the month of November, though depending on the time and day, you’ll get a better or worse view of them. Mercury and Venus are the most difficult to see due to their proximity to the sun.

Mercury: Mercury was at its eastern elongation during October, so it starts November a bit too close to the sun to see safely. It reaches western elongation on Nov. 20, when it’ll be easily visible just before sunrise for the rest of the month.

Venus: Venus starts the month just ahead of the sun at sunrise, technically making it possible to see every morning in November. It gets further from the sun as the month goes on, making it easier and safer to see toward the end of the month.

Mars: Mars is high in the sky all month. It rises out of the eastern horizon shortly after midnight at the start of November and rises earlier as the month progresses. Early morning is the best time to see it, or right around midnight toward the end of the month.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are close pals for all of November, rising at roughly the same time and right next to each other in the sky. The star Regulus joins in to form a trio, which is visible to the naked eye the entire month.

Saturn: Saturn is also visible every night in November. It’s in the eastern sky when the sun sets, and sets on the western horizon shortly before sunrise. Right after dark is the best time to see it, but you’ll need binoculars or a telescope to capture its glorious rings.

Neptune: Neptune and Saturn are teamed up for November, with both of them being very close in the sky and following a similar trajectory. Bring binoculars or a telescope.

Uranus: Uranus is in the night sky every day in November, rising in the east shortly before sunset and setting in the west right around sunrise. It reaches opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s as far away from the sun as it can get, and will be the most visible. You’ll still want to bring some binoculars or a telescope for best results.

Most of the planets are visible in the night sky almost every night in November, but on Saturday, there’ll be a fun little planet parade. It’ll take place just before sunrise, so it’s mostly for early risers. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter are set to line up nicely, making them easy to spot. This is especially true for Jupiter and Mars, which should be right next to each other that night.

The show will start around Saturday and will last until around Nov. 25, depending on your location. The tricky part is catching Mercury in the sky before the sun comes up. It’s only about a 30-minute window since the sun closely follows Mercury up over the eastern horizon. The single best day to view it is Nov. 20, when Mercury is at its western elongation — as far from the sun as it can get.

Uranus is also visible at this time, bringing the number of visible planets to three. Saturn and Neptune are below the horizon. Uranus is on the other side of the sky, however, so it’s not technically part of the alignment.

If you miss the Southern Taurids, you only have to wait a week to catch a glimpse of the Northern Taurids meteor shower. This is another long-lasting meteor shower that started on Oct. 20 and runs until Dec. 10. It peaks on Wednesday and Thursday morning. The American Meteor Society notes that the moon is only 5% illuminated on Wednesday, giving viewers even better conditions than during the Southern Taurids.

It is otherwise virtually identical to the Southern Taurids. The shower appears to originate from the same constellation, Taurus, which rises and sets at almost exactly the same times as it did a week earlier. The Northern Taurids promise about five meteors per hour under optimal conditions, with an increased chance of fireballs. Both showers are even fueled by the same comet, 2P/Encke. It’s the space equivalent of a sitcom rerun airing just one week later.

Leonids is usually the most active meteor shower in November. It started on Nov. 6 and runs until Nov. 30, making it shorter than both Taurids meteor showers. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 16 and the morning of Nov. 17.

The good news is that the meteor shower is very easy to find. Meteors from it will appear to originate from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars and Jupiter, which are visible in the night sky.

The bad news is that this part of the sky doesn’t rise until around midnight, making this a meteor shower for night owls. It should produce about 15 meteors per hour under optimal conditions, though you can expect slightly fewer because the 41% illuminated moon will create enough natural light pollution to obscure fainter meteors.

The Leonids have produced exceptional meteor storms in the past, with hundreds of meteors per hour. That isn’t expected to happen in 2026, but the odds aren’t zero. They may improve after the comet loops around the sun again in 2031.

A micro moon is noticeably smaller and less bright than a supermoon or even a regular full moon.

November’s Beaver Moon takes place just two days before Thanksgiving. It is also the first of a string of four consecutive supermoons that will close out 2026 and begin 2027. This happens when the moon is within 90% of perigee — its closest point to Earth. The phenomenon makes the moon appear about 7% larger than a regular moon and 14% larger than a minimoon — and noticeably brighter than both.

Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the Beaver Moon reaches its peak illumination on Nov. 24 at 9:53 a.m. ET, which is after sunrise for most people in the US. That means the best time to see it is either the night before (Nov. 23) or the evening after (Nov. 24). The moon remains over 90% full from Nov. 22-27. If you plan on going skygazing, avoid those days like the plague, since the moon creates a ton of light pollution.

It’s not often that the same event happens twice in a single month, but it turns out Jupiter, Mars and the moon just can’t seem to get enough of each other. The trio closes out the month the same way it started: hanging out very close together in the night sky. And yes, Regulus will once again tag along.

Unlike the prior meetup, this one only lasts for one night before the moon dashes away. Since all four of them are visible with the naked eye and the moon is still mostly full, people shouldn’t have any trouble finding them. Eagle-eyed stargazers may see Algieba nearby as well. It’s the second brightest star in the Leo constellation (behind Regulus), and it’s also visible without binoculars or a telescope.

The constellations continue their summer-to-winter shakeup. Prominent constellations in the sky include Taurus, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquila, Pisces and Aries. Mainstays such as the Big Dipper and Little Dipper are still out there, but can be difficult to see if you live too far south. As a rule, we recommend using a sky map or a tool such as Stellarium to pinpoint each object.

There are also some lesser-known asterisms to seek out, such as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters), the Great Square of Pegasus and the Circlet of Pisces. The Summer Triangle is still visible, while the Winter Triangle becomes much easier to spot as it rises above the horizon earlier in the evening.

#3134. Samsung mulls Galaxy AI usage limits and subscription tiers – what we know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Galaxy device owners who are heavy AI users would likely start paying for some features they've long enjoyed for free.

Samsung is reportedly planning a shift from free unlimited Galaxy AI tools to a tiered subscription plan. This would be a major adjustment for Galaxy device owners who are heavy AI users, as they’d likely have to pay for some features they’ve long enjoyed for free.

Also: 7 Samsung Galaxy settings I always change

Tools like Photo Assist, Now Brief, and Creative Studio will still remain free, according to reports — they just won’t offer unlimited usage. Once the allotted number of free credits runs out, Samsung plans to introduce either standalone packages to top up AI credits or a monthly or annual subscription for users to continue using these features.

No free usage limit has been specified for users, but the highest-tiered subscription claims to offer usage limits four times higher than the free plan. A subscription would also give users access to exclusive features, presumably high-compute and newer processes.

The Galaxy AI Premium subscription would start at $4.99 per month or $47.99 per year, and reports indicate it would go up from there.

Samsung is planning to roll out a paid subscription model for the Galaxy S27 series, according to code references in 2027 Samsung devices. The company is reportedly planning to expand the plan to older devices through One UI updates, including S24 series models and newer devices, as well as Fold and Flip series phones.

If you’re an occasional Galaxy AI user, you probably won’t ever need to pay to use your preferred AI features. This would include those who edit a photo or summarize an email every now and then.

Power users and those who rely heavily on Galaxy AI daily will need to decide whether yet another subscription is worth the money. Aside from a higher token limit, these features would include AI-generated videos, Bixby Action, and Daily Briefing.

Samsung hasn’t announced a release date for the Galaxy S27 Series phones, but the company typically holds a Galaxy Unpacked event in January or February.

#3133. Stereotaxis (STXS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Supply constraints and new financing shape the next phase for robotic catheter growth.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Stereotaxis, Inc. (STXS -9.65%) reported third quarter results that focused on two structural transformations: a shift toward more accessible robotic capital systems and the expansion of its recurring revenue through a proprietary portfolio of interventional catheters. Management reported that revenue growth was driven by the initial commercial impact of the GenesisX and Synchrony systems, even as supply constraints for the MAGIC catheter created a $1.9 million order backlog. The company stated that the acquisition of Robocath has closed, adding a mechanical robotic system designed for cardiology and neurointerventional fields to its portfolio. To support these transitions, the company secured up to $24 million in convertible note financing, providing a pro-forma cash balance of $16 million and a total liquidity of $28 million. Management indicated that it expects a pathway to cash-flow profitability within the next year, supported by stabilized operating expenses of approximately $8 million per quarter.

Operator: Good afternoon. Thank you for joining us for Stereotaxis Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Certain statements during the conference call and question and answer period to follow may relate to future events expectations, and as such, constitute forward looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 2000. Such statements involve known and unknown risks, uncertainties, and other factors that may cause the actual results, performance, or achievements of the company in the future to be materially different from the statements that the company's executives may make today. These risks are described in detail in our public filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission including our latest periodic report on Form 10-K or 10-Q.

We assume no duty to update these statements at this time. All participants have been placed on a listen only mode. The floor will be open for questions and comments following the presentation. As a reminder, today's call is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to turn the floor over to your host, David Fischel, Chairman and CEO of Stereotaxis.

David Leo Fischel: Thank you, operator, and good afternoon, everyone. On our last few calls, I provided significant background on our innovation and commercial strategy. I want to keep today's prepared remarks more focused on our near term priorities key updates from the past quarter and expected upcoming milestones. it is a busy and exciting period. Our near term priority is to drive forward 2 major business model transformations. The first is shifting from capital systems that require long sales construction timelines to having a portfolio of systems that can be easily installed and are therefore significantly more accessible and scalable.

The second is developing and commercializing a portfolio of disposable interventional catheters that enhance the value of our robots and provide us with a robust recurring revenue opportunity. We are fully focused on pushing these 2 major structural transformations forward, such that they are established realities and a solid foundation upon which to build a healthy, high growth, profitable company. On the capital side, the 2 primary innovations that are beginning to have a commercial impact and advance this structural transformation are GenesisX and Synchrony. GenesisX is our newest robotic system for minimally invasive procedures. It can be installed in existing operating rooms, without the need for construction or the purchase of a specific integrated X-ray.

Synchrony is our consolidated digital cockpit for the operating room. Enhancing procedure workflow and introducing intraoperative connectivity and augmented intelligence. Our revenue growth in the third quarter benefited from the initial commercial impact of these 2 technologies. System revenue of $3 million in the quarter was up 60% compared to the third quarter of last year. We benefited from partial revenue recognition from the first GenesisX system sale in the US, the first Genesis system sold in China, and multiple Synchrony systems sold and installed in the US. Installing the first GenesisX system and demonstrating their performance and reliability in the real-world settings will be significant milestones.

We are prepared to install the first GenesisX system in the US this month, and expect to install the first GenesisX system in Europe soon afterwards. A clear requirement for the broad adoption of GenesisX by hospital customers is ensuring it can be used interoperably with various standard X-rays. We have 2 significant recent milestones supporting this broad interoperability. In August, we received FDA clearance for an upgraded version of Genesis X approved to work in a compatible fashion with any nonmodified, nonintegrated X-ray. Our systems have never had this capability or broad regulatory label, with all our previous robots being tied to a specific X-ray modified to work with us.

Then at the end of October, we were delighted to enter into a collaboration with Canon. A global leader in X-ray technology. Our collaboration supports compatibility of GenesisX with their X-ray, along with co marketing of our systems together and opportunities for other technology and commercial collaborations. The first US GenesisX system will be installed alongside Canon's X-ray and we are looking forward to this first commercial installation together. Beyond the already announced first US and European GenesisX systems, We have visibility to an additional GenesisX installation early in 2027. That will work in a compatible fashion with an X-ray system from another major manufacturer.

We have a pipeline of a couple dozen GenesisX opportunities and expect commercial activity to increase meaningfully as the first systems demonstrate their performance in real-world use. The second key capital system in our portfolio is the Synchrony digital operating room system. This past quarter was the first full quarter of commercialization following FDA approval in spring. We have multiple Synchrony systems ordered, sold, and installed in the quarter. Alongside robots, but predominantly as standalone systems installed in non robotic cath labs.

We were particularly excited by the first multilab installation of Synchrony with Abbott Northwestern Hospital in Minneapolis becoming the first hospital in the world to adopt the Synchrony system as a standardized technology across its 4 cardiology catheterization labs. We have a robust pipeline of Synchrony systems with a few dozen identified as actionable within the next year. Genesis and Synchrony GenesisX and Synchrony, are independent, though synergistic, opportunities to grow capital revenue significantly. We are just in the earliest stages of commercializing these systems, but are excited by the recent accomplishments and near term milestones. And expect more consistent and substantial capital activity in the coming months.

The development and commercialization of a portfolio of robotically steered interventional catheters is the other major transformation we are driving forward. We will have several million dollars in robotic catheter revenue this year, up from just a few hundred thousand dollars last year. And this is despite significant supply constraints and the challenge of our customers needing to transition relatively abruptly from the historic change in ecosystem they have been dependent on. Robotic capital revenue in the third quarter was up over 20% sequentially from the second quarter and up over 400% from a year ago. But underperformed our expectation. Osypka, our contract manufacturer in Germany, has not been able to meet its forecast for production of MAGICatheters.

We saw no increase in MAGIC shipments in the third quarter versus the second quarter. In Europe, we are fortunate to have 2 other robotic magnetic catheters we can offer to customers through exclusive distribution rights we established with industry partners. We have pivoted to fully focusing on these catheters in Europe, and by doing so will better serve our European customers and will preserve limited magic production from Osypka for the U.S. In The US, MAGIC remains the only available catheter for customers, and we have worked hard alongside our customers to manage the painful reality of limited supply.

We entered the fourth quarter with a backlog of approximately $1.9 million in disposable orders we could not convert to revenue due to supply constraints. While continuing to work with Osypka to improve their processes, we are also fully aware of the need to establish additional supply capacity. We reached significant regulatory milestones in that effort, in recent months and see the opportunity for the shortage to be resolved in the earlier parts of 2027. Even with no improvement in shipments from Osypka, we are confident in achieving a high watermark of recurring revenue this quarter primarily driven by the shift to our alternative catheters in Europe.

It is important to keep in mind context for our annual growth in disposable revenue. It reflects significant contribution from improved razor blade business model, counteracting significant procedural pressure from limited catheter supply, and a challenging transition away from J and J. As we continue to address these headwinds and constraints, expect the power of the attractive recurring revenue business model become much more visible and impactful. While these 2 structural transformations in capital systems and disposable revenue are our clear near term focus, we continue to advance a broad innovation pipeline that will enhance our clinical impact and commercial opportunity.

This progress is often underappreciated but is a source of significant excitement internally and among our physician customers and the industry partners. Several of the most impactful innovation efforts internally include a future generation of GenesisX that will be fully wireless, battery-operated, mobile, a more robust portfolio of electrophysiology catheters including robotic pulse field ablation, a pipeline of robotically steered wires and catheters for the cardiology and neuro fields, and AI efforts that will incorporate intelligent decision support features into Synchrony and automation to our robotic platforms. In addition to these internal efforts, most notable contribution to our innovation pipeline came with the closing of the Robocath acquisition last quarter.

We have been busy working alongside our new Robocath teammates to develop their next generation robot. The R-Star system is a mechanical robot with essentially human like fingers that can hold and manipulate 5-path catheters and interventional devices in tandem. It is being designed to work as an independent robotic system for the interventional cardiology and neurointerventional fields, but will also work synergistically with Stereotaxis' robotic technology. Clinical data from a first in human study performed with the R Star system was presented a week ago at the TCT conference. It showed superb clinical results and safety across a full range of complex coronary angioplasty procedures. Our near term work with Robocath is focused on 4 specific efforts.

Addressing remaining engineering work needed to reach formal design freeze, establishing a reliable supply chain, defining more clearly a continuous innovation pipeline for R-Star, following initial launch, and enhancing R-Star with Stereotaxis' existing advanced software architecture Synchrony Digital Cockpit, and Sync Telesurgery system. All these innovations I just shared are relatively advanced. Some will have an initial commercial impact in 2027, and all of them are in a maturing stage where they should have a commercial impact within the next 2 years. Our ability to advance so many complex technologies in parallel is a testament to the strength of our team.

It highlights our global leadership in the technological race, to make endovascular robotics an impactful reality in the large unaddressed markets of electrophysiology, interventional cardiology, and neuro interventions. Before handing the call to Kimberly, to discuss our financial results, I want to step back for a moment and make 1 general comment. I know that it may not feel like it, from the vantage view of the capital markets but this is a highly exciting period for stereotaxis. In my nearly 10 years here, I have never felt as proud of what we have accomplished and as confident about the opportunity ahead of us.

There are obviously stresses and challenges that weigh on us, but these are being addressed in a diligent fashion. It has been a long journey with some bumps on the path, but what we have brought together is remarkable. The core technology ecosystem we developed, and our in house capabilities to expand on those technologies are a very solid foundation. Our vision for what Stereotaxis can accomplish is becoming increasingly clear and tangible. We are enthusiastically advancing forward. Kimberly will now provide commentary on our financial results and then I will make a few financial comments as well before opening the call to Q&A. Kimberly?

Kimberly R. Peery: Thank you, David, and good afternoon, everyone. Revenue for the third quarter of 2026 totaled $8.9 million a 20% increase compared to $7.5 million in the prior year third quarter and a 16% increase sequentially compared to $7.7 million in the second quarter of 2026. System revenue for the third quarter was $3 million compared to $1.9 million in the prior year third quarter. System revenue in the current quarter benefited from partial revenue recognition on the shipment of the first Genesis X system sold in the United States the first Genesis system sold in China, and the first full quarter of Synchrony system sales. Recurring revenue for the third quarter was $5.9 million.

An increase of 6% compared to the prior year third quarter and a decline of 4% sequentially. Recurring revenue in the quarter benefited from a significant increase in revenue from our new portfolio of robotically navigated catheters, countered by general pressure on procedures due to supply shortages of the magic catheter and the transition away from Johnson and Johnson. Gross margin for the third quarter of 2026 was 45% of revenue. System and recurring revenue gross margin were 15%, 59%. Gross margins for both system and recurring revenue are impacted by overhead allocation over low manufacturing volume.

While we expect margins to remain at these approximate levels over the near term, we see significant opportunity for margin expansion in 2027 and 2028. Operating expenses in the quarter of $10.4 million included $1.3 million in noncash charges for stock compensation expense, mark to market adjustment for acquisition related contingent earn out consideration, and amortization of acquired intangible assets. Excluding these noncash charges, adjusted operating expenses were $9.1 million an increase from $6.6 million in the prior year third quarter due to 1-time transaction costs and higher expenses following the acquisition of Robocath. We believe it is reasonable to model future adjusted operating expenses excluding noncash and onetime item, at approximately $8 million per quarter.

Operating loss and net loss in the third quarter of 2026 were both $6.5 million consistent with the prior year. Adjusted operating loss and adjusted net loss for the quarter excluding noncash charges, were $5.1 million and $5.2 million compared with $2.5 million and $2.4 million in the previous year with the increase predominantly driven by 1-time transaction costs and higher expenses following the acquisition of Robocath. Negative cash flow for the third quarter was $6.5 million of which $2.6 million was associated with the Stereotaxis core business and $3.9 million were payments associated with the acquisition of Robocath. At September 30, Stereotaxis had cash and cash equivalents of $4 million.

Concurrent with today's financial results, we announced the convertible note financing with $12 million funded upfront and an optional additional $12 million available at Stereotaxis' discretion following certain regulatory milestones. On a pro forma basis, taking into consideration the proceeds of this financing, Stereotaxis would have $16 million in cash and cash equivalents. I will now hand the call back to David.

David Leo Fischel: Thank you, Kimberly. As Kim just mentioned, concurrent with our quarterly results, we announced the closing of a financing for up to $24 million. We appreciate the strong support we received from our long term investors. The structure of the financing is a convertible note with an initial $12 million upfront investment and then an additional $12 million optional draw. This structure reflects our belief that the financing bridges us to profitability within the next year. The conversion price of the note is at a 30% premium to our recent stock price, and interest is due at maturity in 3 years.

The incremental $12 million optional drop is contingent on a regulatory milestone we expect in the coming month, that addresses the supply constraint we have experienced with MAGIC. Upon achievement of the milestone, we would have the option but not the obligation to draw the additional $12 million in funding. With this financing, we have $16 million in pro forma cash on our balance sheet, and access to an additional $12 million for total availability of $28 million. We had significant nonrecurring expenses in the quarter related to the closing of the Robocath acquisition. The ongoing costs will be more modest. Even as we aggressively advance development of the next generation R-Star system.

Having Robocath under our belt for the past 4 months I am delighted that we made the acquisition. it is an attractive and differentiated technology, with Stereotaxis adding significant value through our expertise and synergistic capabilities, and I am confident we will turn the technology into a highly impactful and valuable asset. We expect growing recurring revenue and more consistent capital sales in the coming quarters. 2 near term milestones that support this include installing the first commercial GenesisX system, and resolving the supply constraints with Magic. We expect the coming months to be an event rich period.

With expected growth in recurring revenue and a more reliable tempo of capital sales, we see a clear pathway to profitability next year. We will now take your questions. Operator, can you please open the line to Q&A We will now begin the question and answer session.

Operator: If you would like to ask a question during this time, simply press star, followed by the number 1 on your telephone keypad. We will just take a brief moment to compile the Q&A roster. First question comes from the line of Joshua Jennings from TD Cowen. Your line is live.

Joshua Jennings: Hi. Good afternoon. I wanted to, David, just how are you doing? Touch base on just your sense of the EP community's reception to robotics, how that is been evolving over the last 12 months. I mean, just my own personal view and experience has been just thinking about the robotic symposium at HRS, you know, some of the panels at HRX Live, and then you just had SCRN within the last couple of weeks. It seems as if the interest level is percolating but wanted to get your view and your experience and whether mine is the right interpretation.

David Leo Fischel: Yeah. Sure. Happy to answer that. Thanks for the question. I think both those 2 conferences that you mentioned, both the robotic symposium at HRS in the springtime. And then just a month ago, we had the SCRN Society for Cardiac Robotic Navigation Conference. in Europe. Both of those were very well attended, far better attended than ever in the past. And we had an enthusiastic kind of physician base attending it. So, those were both very uplifting events.

I would say that there is generally among our existing user base, there is all of them are going through the process of switching from an ecosystem that they were long used to the new ecosystem with our own catheters and with different mapping systems shifting away from Johnson and Johnson. And that is a great and smooth process for some. For others, it is more challenging. But we have been working with site-by-site to get through whatever administrative hurdles work in that process. And to make sure they are comfortable with the new technology setup.

I feel that kind of we are overall working through that process in a diligent, thoughtful fashion, and I feel kind of it is always tough to change things in health care. To change things that have been working for them for many years, but I think overall, we are working through that in a good fashion. The shortage of catheters in the US does create an additional layer of stress for those sites. We are fortunate that those sites then understand our situation, understand the difficulty, and overall, we are able to work with them despite that challenge.

And I think if you look at kind of the overall space beyond our existing users, you have many physicians that are starting to look at us again given the new technologies that we received approval for over the recent months. And are intrigued by our innovations, are engaging with us more. We definitely have a pipeline that is more exciting than it is ever been in the past. There is an aspect of proving that pipeline works, making sure we can supply that pipeline, and then and then capitalizing it through actual orders and new installations.

And if you have been following us, kind of our press release and social media, we obviously had 2 new installations, new launches of robotic labs in Europe over the over the last quarter, both of them in greenfield sites, Both of those launches have gone very well so far. We see kind of a pipeline with GenesisX that we believe we will be able to capitalize much more meaningfully as we demonstrate GenesisX working in the real world. As we demonstrate compatibility with multiple different X-ray systems in these next few months. And so, overall, it feels relatively good.

I would say the 1 big macro pressure to some extent on the space, and you see it with others in the electrophysiology. Field. If you look at, let's say, you know, companies, let's say, the surgical ablation space or some others, is that the rise of PFA has definitely served as a bit of a distraction for many physicians. And so we have made significant progress even just in most recent weeks on pairing PFA with our robotic system, particularly first in Europe, but whatever we do in Europe, will come ultimately to the US. #3132. Samsung’s new SmartTag 3 debuts with next-gen Bluetooth – and one big problem

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 supports emerging Bluetooth tracking tech, but it's not a match for Samsung's OS exclusivity.

Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is now available for purchase in the US, promising a smaller, lighter design than previous generations, compatibility with iOS devices, 550 days of battery life, an NFC-powered Lost Mode, Left Behind Alerts, and an IP67 dust- and water-resistant rating.

Though the Galaxy SmartTag 3 is compatible with iOS devices, the features available to Apple fans are limited, with Ring Phone, Left Behind Alerts, and Compass View reserved for Galaxy users. Compass View is enabled by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, an upgraded Bluetooth distance-finding technology. Despite Samsung embracing a low-cost boost to device tracking, Channel Sounding is locked inside the Galaxy ecosystem, a blow to the technology’s intended purpose.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Channel Sounding is also Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2, but these manufacturers open the technology to all compatible Android phones. However, Samsung’s SmartTag 3 doesn’t rely on Android’s vast but fragmented Find My Device network; instead, Samsung’s take on Channel Sounding will rely exclusively on the Galaxy Find Network. If a semi-closed ecosystem can help make evolving Bluetooth tech more reliable, does it matter that its implementation is counterproductive?

Samsung is the Goldilocks of device ecosystems. It’s not considered a walled garden like Apple, but it’s not as open to full third-party interoperability as Google. Many of Samsung’s most useful features are reserved for use within its Galaxy ecosystem. However, Samsung’s OS is built on top of Android, allowing for more flexibility than iOS, but still offering OS-exclusive features and, more importantly, feature reliability.

Full access to Samsung’s Galaxy Find Network is exclusive to Galaxy devices, similar to how full access to Apple’s Find My tracking features is reserved for Apple devices. On the other hand, Google’s Find Hub can accommodate Android phones from several manufacturers, including Samsung.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect

According to a press release, nearly 900 million Galaxy devices exist on the Galaxy Find Network. Each one’s constant Bluetooth signals contribute to an expansive network of crowdsourced data, extending the Galaxy FindTag 3’s reach and surfacing location data faster.

Google’s Find Hub’s greatest benefit is its scale: it can work with headphones, earbuds, Bluetooth trackers, smartphones, and smartwatches from multiple manufacturers.

However, different ecosystems limit tracking features to basic functionality, showing only where a device was last seen before it was powered off, or emitting a chime if you lose it. Live location data and accurate direction and distance finding from your smartphone aren’t possible.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Implementing Bluetooth Channel Sounding aims to break down ecosystem-specific barriers, especially in a device-tracking context. If your smartphone, headphones, and smartwatch all support Channel Sounding, you could access fine-ranging tracking on all of them, regardless of device manufacturer.

Despite Samsung’s ecosystem providing it a device-tracking advantage, it defeats the purpose of Bluetooth: democratization. Basic Bluetooth connectivity allows any Bluetooth-compatible device to connect to another; that’s why you can wirelessly pair a pair of AirPods with a Lenovo laptop.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

Channel Sounding’s goal is no different in that it aims to bring more accurate distance awareness to Bluetooth-enabled devices, allowing you to finely track a pair of Sony headphones with an iPhone — that’s the goal, but not yet reality.

Samsung instead adopted Channel Sounding for its first consumer-ready endpoint within the boundaries of its ecosystem. Only Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Galaxy S26 Plus users can unlock the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding capabilities when engaging its Compass View feature.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

All of these phones support Bluetooth 6.0 and Channel Sounding, but the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding abilities will only be available to them and future Galaxy phones with Channel Sounding.

Conversely, Google’s Pixel Tag offers Channel Sounding to all Android phones that support it, including Galaxy phones. The result is that the Galaxy SmartTag 3 will operate just like any other Bluetooth tracker when paired with a base-model flagship phone, an older Galaxy phone, or an iPhone.

During this year’s WWDC, Apple announced Channel Sounding support for iPhones with its N1 networking chip and third-party Bluetooth 6.3 devices. Bluetooth 6.3 devices aren’t on the market yet and won’t be for a few years.

I assume Apple’s announcement of faraway future support is to give itself time to decide how Channel Sounding will fit into its walled garden, similar to Samsung’s implementation in the Galaxy SmartTag 3.

Also: How to tell if a hidden AirTag is tracking you – and disable it ASAP

Sure, Google’s Find Hub still needs some maturing; just last year, Google boosted the opt-in opportunities to add more devices for crowdsourced data, Find People is coming to Wear OS, and Find Hub is getting “Notify when left behind” alerts soon.

Apple’s and Samsung’s device location networks may be more feature-rich thanks to their closed ecosystems, but Google is working toward a truly open, easy-to-use network of devices powered by Channel Sounding. Which one is more important to you is for you to decide when it’s time to make a purchase.

#3131. Apple TV Adds Sign Language Interpretation, Starting With Original Film ‘Being Heumann’

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Streaming Services

It's the latest streaming service to add American and British Sign Language options, making movies more accessible and enjoyable for a wider audience.

Apple TV is adding sign language interpretation for a handful of supported streaming titles, beginning with the Apple original film Being Heumann, which premieres on Friday.

With iOS 27.2, you’ll find new options for American Sign Language and British Sign Language within Apple TV’s app settings. When you select one of these languages, a new button will appear on supported Apple original titles indicating sign language availability. You can also turn off or change your language selection directly within the player.

Titles that support sign language interpretation will have a sign language icon displaying an image of a hand. This icon appears on the title page of a show or movie, next to other accessibility options like closed captions and audio descriptions.

Being Heumann is an apt pick for debuting this accessibility feature. The film centers on the true story of disability rights activist Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) and her leadership in the historic 1977 protest that helped advance equal rights and protections for Americans with disabilities. Sign language support will also roll out to other Apple TV titles starting with F1 The Movie, followed by Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid (which debuts Nov. 25) later this year.

Apple TV is adding a dedicated collection called Movies & Shows with American Sign Language to make it easier to browse supported content. That collection will include movies where sign language is part of the story, such as 2021’s Oscar-winning film CODA. You can also look up “with ASL” in the app’s search bar to find relevant titles.

“We believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment,” Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives, said in a statement. “Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences.”

Apple TV joins a handful of other streaming platforms with sign language options, including HBO Max and Prime Video. Netflix also features sign language interpretation for dozens of kids and family titles through a partnership with SignUp Media, which built a Chrome extension that overlays an interpreter onto supported shows and movies. SignUp is also available on select Disney Plus and Peacock content.

While closed captioning can help some deaf and hard-of-hearing people better understand what’s happening on screen, many viewers prefer watching with sign language interpretation, which can better convey emotion and expression.

“For the deaf community, our first language is ASL,” Nakia Smith, a deaf storyteller and an interpreter for the HBO Max series It: Welcome to Derry, told me in an interview earlier this year.

Unlike closed captioning, which has become nearly ubiquitous across streaming and television, sign languages like ASL are slowly making their way into more entertainment spaces, from sports broadcasts to awards ceremonies and red carpets. But there’s still a long way to go.

The challenge is that sign language interpretation requires skilled human professionals who can capture context and nuances, which takes time and resources. More companies appear to be making the effort. And while some studios are exploring AI to automate captioning, the complexity and diversity of sign languages suggest this will remain a largely human-driven endeavor for the foreseeable future.

For its part, Apple worked closely with the deaf community, partnering with Directors of Artistic Sign Language to ensure they matched the tone of the films and maintained authentic representation.

“It’s incredibly meaningful to see our beautiful language authentically represented onscreen,” Daniel Durant, who appears in Being Heumann and who directed the film’s sign language interpretation, said in a statement. “Bringing this experience to life required a lot of care to ensure every translation captured the emotion and meaning of the story. I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences.”

#3130. Suja Life (SUJA) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Softer store traffic and competitor price cuts are eroding Suja's promotional returns.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

In response, the company lowered its full-year outlook to reflect current macroeconomic conditions and shifted marketing investment toward retail trade promotions to maintain competitiveness.

Club is our clearest win so far, driven by incremental programming on Suja organic green juices and wellness shots.

We also said we would work arm in arm with our retail partners. And we did. Through top to top sessions with several of our largest customers. Where we have the most work to do is conventional grocery, our largest channel. Weaker store traffic across the industry continues to weigh on our sales velocities. Despite that headwind, we grew distribution nearly 10% in the quarter. Which tells you retailers continue to want our brands on their shelves.

Distribution only creates value when it turns. So our focus is on both. But the grocery pressure that began in July has intensified.

Store traffic is softer. Retailers are cutting prices more deeply and promotions are delivering lower returns. As a result, we no longer expect the fourth quarter step up we planned for. And our larger multi serve formats continue to build in the quarter. Green juice, the platform that started this brand, softened in grocery in the quarter. Even as it helped drive our club growth. While expanding profitability this year. Our priorities ahead are clear. First, building velocities across our portfolio. Including in our core greens juices, single serve shots, and vibe.

And it reaches consumers where they spend their time. Most consumers discover us at the shelf, or through word-of-mouth. And so that is where we are focused. The experience at the shelf, and what people hear about us from their friends family, and trusted sources. Having marketing sales, and innovation in 1 commercial organization is what makes that possible. Second, deepening our penetration in existing accounts and capturing white space in channels where we are underdeveloped.

We are in the selling season for 27 placements, we are encouraged by the early progress. Third, innovating to capture new consumer opportunities with new formats and adjacent categories that build on our platform. And throughout, grow profitably through scale These priorities will take time to show up in our results, so I want to be clear about how we see the next several quarters. We expect net sales to grow by roughly 8% this year, but we will exit 2026 at a softer run rate. Looking beyond 2026, we expect continued pressure in grocery, and difficult comparisons in the first half of 27. Particularly in the first quarter.

Our new programs and innovation are expected to reach shelves over the course of the year with their contribution building progressively. So we expect a slower start to 2027. But top line growth improving as the year progresses. Through this period, we expect to continue gaining share. And when the category picks back up, we believe we will be in a strong position to benefit. We will provide our formal outlook on our fourth quarter call in March. That said, our conviction in the long term opportunity has not changed. We are not just taking share in an existing category. We are helping build a new segment of the beverage aisle.

Household penetration rose to 11.2% from 9.6% a year ago. And spend per buyer grew 9%. To nearly $31. Even so, only about 11% of US households buy our brands today, which leaves substantial room to grow. Consumers continue to look for beverages that do more for them, and taste great. And that is exactly where our brands compete. We have leading brands, a vertically integrated platform built over a decade, and retail partners who rely on us to grow the category. Our focus now is on turning those strengths into more consistent profitable growth. We have work to do, and I am confident in our ability to deliver. With that, I will turn it over to Jeff.

Jeff Pedersen: Thank you, Maria. Good afternoon, everyone. I will start with detail on our third quarter results, and then walk through our updated outlook for the full year. In emerging brands, slice net sales increased 3% to $2.7 million. That said, growth in Better For You soda has slowed this year, and new distribution has built more slowly than we expected.

Gross profit was $33.5 million or 43.9% of net sales. Compared to $34.3 million or 46.3% in the prior year period. That was below the approximately 47.8% we estimated in August. Historically, the third quarter has been our lowest gross margin quarter. Given a lower mix of wellness shots. 3 factors drove the decline. First, higher promotional investment in a more competitive environment. Second, unfavorable fixed cost absorption in our supply chain as category softness reduced production volumes. Ongoing efficiency improvements across our operations along with favorable purchase prices on key produce inputs are partially offsetting these pressures.

We expect gross margin to improve sequentially in the fourth quarter as production volumes rise seasonally and these efforts continue. SG and A expenses were $36.5 million or 47.8% of net sales. Partially offset by lower gross profit and higher freight costs. On a segment basis, Suja Core adjusted EBITDA increased 4% to $13 million. In August, we completed the refinancing we mentioned on our last call. It includes a new $165 million term loan that matures in 2031. Our effective interest rate is now 5.7%, compared to 9.7% at the end of last year.

As we said at the time, this was a cost of capital transaction. And we did not add leverage. Interest expense in the quarter was $3.3 million compared to $7.6 million a year ago. Connection with the refinancing, we recognized a $1.8 million loss on debt extinguishment which is excluded from adjusted EBITDA. As of 09/28/2026, we had cash of $15.5 million and total debt of $163 million, with $100 million of undrawn capacity under our revolving and delayed draw facilities. Capital expenditures were $18.6 million year to date, as we continue to expand our capacity adding our 6th HPP machine in our Oceanside, California campus by year-end. Turning to our outlook.

For the full year-ending 12/28/2026, we now expect net sales of $351 million to $354 million and adjusted EBITDA of 68 million to $70 million We continue to expect net interest expense of $18 million as previously communicated in our August refinancing announcement. And a base tax rate of 26.1%. To help with your modeling, our outlook implies fourth quarter net sales of $83.7 million to $86.7 million and adjusted EBITDA of 17.8 million to $19.8 million A few things shape the fourth quarter. About $2 million of shipments moved into the third quarter.

We expect trade investment to stay well above last year's level in a highly promotional environment, which weighs on both net sales and gross margin. And our outlook assumes today's grocery conditions hold through year-end. Against the fourth quarter last year that benefited from stronger velocities. We also expect marketing to be lower as a percentage of net sales in the fourth quarter. As we redeploy upper funnel marketing dollars into trade programs, to stay competitive in a heavily promoted category. As we outlined in August, we have been shifting investment from upper funnel marketing into trade.

Together with cost actions across the company, including freight optimization and tighter management of operating expenses, that supports adjusted EBITDA margin expansion despite lower gross margin. #3129. Android Auto requires Android 11 or higher now – check your compatibility

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Android Auto's minimum requirements have changed. Here's what to know.

Google has officially phased out support for Android 9 and Android 10 for wired Android Auto use — so you’ll need Android 11 at a minimum to connect an Android phone to a compatible car via USB, according to an update to Google’s Android Auto support page spotted by Android Authority. Android 11 through Android 17, the most up-to-date version, are fully supported for Android Auto (though Android 17’s adoption rate remains quite low).

These changes confirm early reports that Android 10 users saw warnings that their devices would soon lose Android Auto support, even before Google’s documentation had specified the change.

Also: Got an old car? Android Auto is easy to add: 2 ways, starting at $20

It’s not uncommon for Google to drop the oldest Android versions that can still run Android Auto every few years. In 2024, Android 8, released in 2017, was dumped from service. Android 11 was first released in 2020.

Android Auto brings apps to your car display so that drivers can focus better on the road. It allows you to control features such as navigation, maps, calls, text messages, and music, and is the Android equivalent of Apple CarPlay.

Also: 5 Android Auto apps that make my life easier on the road

The requirements have changed little since last year, aside from the new minimum software requirement. The new instructions for wired Android Auto support are straightforward: Phones must be running Android 11 (Red Velvet Cake) or newer, have an active data plan, and be supported by a compatible car. Google also recommends a quality USB cable.

Android Auto is integrated into compatible phones, so you do not need to download it. Android Auto isn’t available on devices that run Android (Go edition).

Also: I was a big wireless Android Auto fan, until I tried wired – now I won’t go back

To find out if your car or stereo is compatible with Android Auto, Google has a hub page to help. For more information about your car’s compatibility with Android Auto on your car display, it’s best to contact your vehicle manufacturer.

For drivers still using older phones running Android 9 or Android 10, getting Android Auto back will require either replacing a current device with one that runs Android 11 or newer, or installing an available software update on a current device.

Also: Gemini on Android Auto can access my photos, emails, and calendar – why I’m OK with that (mostly)

#3128. Google Pixel Tag Hands-On: The AirTag for Android Fans

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Google’s own tracker adds a few welcome details to the smart tracker field.

When a company comes out with its own version of a product in an established market, there has to be a good reason. Maybe it’s created a design that sets the product apart, or it’s included features that none of the competition has.

If you think I’m talking about Apple and Google, you’d be right – but this isn’t the iPhone Duo muscling into the folding phone fray. This time, the roles are reversed: Google is releasing the Pixel Tag, a small Bluetooth tracker that it hopes will be the Android ecosystem’s answer to Apple’s near-ubiquitous AirTag.

The Pixel Tag is available starting Wednesday for $30 each or $100 in a pack of four. It works with Android phones and uses Google’s Find Hub technology for tracking over distances beyond Bluetooth range. If you use an Android phone and have wanted the capability to track things such as keys, bags, bikes, vehicles and other indispensable items, and you want the tech to come from the company that designed the system, the Pixel Tag is an excellent choice.

It isn’t the first Android-compatible tracker. Motorola introduced its Moto Tag 2 earlier this year, and Tile has been the de facto AirTag alternative for several years. There’s also now a growing ecosystem of other items that tap into Apple’s Find My and Android’s Find Hub networks, ranging from slim credit-card-sized devices like the Rolling Square AirCard Pro and Peak Design’s Beacon Finder Card, to novel approaches like Falcam’s TagBatt, a battery for some Sony and Canon mirrorless cameras that integrates Apple Find My tracking.

Google jumping into this more crowded field tells me the company thinks there’s profit to be made by manufacturing its own hardware and software. It’s also investing in the infrastructure it’s already built out, and not leaving the hardware side to a constellation of other vendors.

Trackers like the Pixel Tag and AirTag can be a surprisingly deflating purchase: You pair them with your phone, put them into something you don’t want to lose track of – then forget about them. They’re usually not tactile the way a phone, watch or laptop is each day. And their value doesn’t kick into action until you think an item has gone missing.

After slinging AirTags into bags and dangling them off keychains, one thing I really appreciate about the Pixel Tag is its thinness. Apple chose a small, round footprint, even keeping the exact design for the second-generation AirTags. Google instead opted for a longer lozenge shape, at 1.8 inches (46.1mm), that is about two-thirds the height of the AirTag at 0.2 inch (5.4mm).

Google sent a Bellroy leather keychain as a sample accessory for review, and paired with the Pixel Tag, the two are a fine size for a pocket or clipped to an inside bag pocket. I thought the longer design would get in the way, but it’s not bad at all.

The Pixel Tag uses a CR2032 coin-sized battery that should last about a year (the same as the AirTag). It also has an IP67 rating, which is durable in 1 meter of water for up to 30 minutes.

Another departure from the AirTag is a physical button, making the Pixel Tag even more tactile. When you’re using Find Hub on your phone to locate it by sound, press once to stop the chirps it makes. Or, if you have the tag in hand (on a keychain, for example) and need to find your phone, press twice to ring the phone – it makes a pleasant sing-songy chime that gets louder and more intense as it continues, so I’m confident it’ll be easy to locate, even among couch cushions.

Speaking of the chimes, credit to the Google sound designers who came up with the Pixel Tag’s tune. It has three levels of loudness you can set, and seems plenty audible enough when you’re spelunking the living room for it. I measured it at 80 decibels, which when compared to the second-generation AirTag volume, is 7 less than the 87 decibels of Apple’s tracker.

One more nice touch compared to the AirTag: the Find Hub app shows the tag’s battery status. If that gets to Low or Very Low, the app sends you notifications every two weeks until the battery is replaced. After Apple showed battery statuses on AirTags in early versions of the Find My app, the company changed the Find My app so it only indicates battery when it’s low and needs to be replaced.

The best feature of either tracker is the ability to locate its exact location – not which building or room it’s in, but to tell if the item fell behind the couch or was accidentally dropped in the driveway. (Yes, I’m making up these examples from personal experience.)

Precision Finding uses a combination of Bluetooth 6.0 (via a feature called Channel Sounding) and the ultra-wideband chips inside the tag and the phone to directionally find the tracker when it’s within Bluetooth range. You hold the phone upright, perpendicular to the ground for the best connection. Then you wander your space, watching the indicator change as you get closer to the tag.

On the Pixel Tag, that indication is a wobbly circle shape that fills in as you get closer; when you’re on top of the tracker, the shape is fully filled. The Find Hub app also uses the camera and UWB chip to include an estimated distance in feet and inches (or meters and centimeters). When you’re close enough, the tracking shape becomes a directional arrow to point you the right way. UWB is compatible with the Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8 Fold and newer Pixel phones.

In my testing, the Find Nearby feature performed fairly well. Find Hub using a Pixel 11 Pro XL connected from within about 25 feet, including on multiple levels of a house when I was above or below it.

Perhaps because I was raised on science-fiction devices like the trackers in Aliens, though, I expected more consistent readings. There were times when both I and the tag remained stationary. The distance estimates would fluctuate by several feet.

Since I’ve had this review unit for only a couple of days, I haven’t yet had a chance to send it off with someone else and see if I can track it remotely using the Find Hub network. When nearby Android devices detect the Pixel Tag’s presence, they should securely and privately relay the tracker’s location to Google’s servers. (Apple’s Find My network operates the same way.) I’ll update this article once I’ve taken the tag on such an adventure.

Tracking all your stuff is invaluable – I learned this first-hand earlier this year when I left a small bag containing my passport in a hotel room, and was able to convince the hotel that the bag was still on the premises. But unfortunately, smart tags are being used to track people without their knowledge.

Google is taking the same approach as Apple to help thwart this type of tracking. If a tag is separated from the phone it’s paired with (or the phone of someone else you’ve chosen to share the tag location with), and the tag is moved, its chime activates.

The idea is that you’ll hear an unfamiliar chirp and investigate. It has an NFC chip that displays its information when you tap it using the NFC built into a phone.

#3127. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.
