#3082. Reddit’s New AI-Powered Reviews Are Already Controversial

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Online > Online Services

The platform's test of automated product review summaries is sparking concern that advertising will replace human advice.

Reddit announced on Tuesday that it’s testing Reviews, an AI-powered shopping feature that aggregates user comments into product summaries, commerce links, and pros-and-cons breakdowns. In a blog post, the company said it wants to organically use discussions on the platform, from conversations about skin care treatments or coffee to headphones, to help people “understand what a product is really like and feel confident deciding whether it’s right for them.”

The Reviews feature promises to make product research easier on a site that’s increasingly focused on shopping recommendations. But the announcement immediately rankled some Reddit users who are concerned it will degrade authentic human-to-human discussion and advice. Many Reddit moderators, or “mods,” tasked with keeping order of communities called subreddits, believe it’ll be hard to distinguish real opinions from straight-up advertising.

According to Reddit, the upcoming feature will surface product reviews in search results and through highlighted product mentions in comment threads, regardless of a group’s rules preventing the promotion of products by users or brands.

The test launch of Reviews, which was previewed in February and focused on electronics, will start with about 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel. If the experiment works, Reddit plans to expand the feature outside the US and also increase the range of categories and products.

In a Reddit community for the moderators who enforce platform and subreddit rules, the new AI-powered shopping feature was greeted with skepticism and criticism. Writing in modnews, ProudnotLoud dubbed early tests “an ad-ridden, distracting mess” that made reading threads nearly impossible.

For moderators who work to keep commercial spam out of their subreddits, the feature poses an existential threat. User nerdshark warned that communities are already being actively targeted by stealth corporate campaigns, arguing that forcing Reviews into these spaces “does vulnerable communities a huge disservice,” especially without an opt-out mechanism.

Some Reddit admins have pushed back against the backlash, clarifying that the embedded product links are search shortcuts rather than paid placements. Yet users remain unconvinced. As CouncilofStrongs countered: “From a user experience, it is an ad.”

Reddit has also recently been testing advertising in search results, which could be a way for brands to reach Reddit users who click a product name even if they aren’t paying for placement in Reddit Reviews.

Given the amount of sites that focus heavily on human-centered reviews (you’re reading one of them), Reddit’s intent to aggregate product information through AI summaries could be seen as another way for traditional media publishers to have their content used without compensation.

But Reddit maintains the feature is purely informational. In a statement to CNET, a Reddit spokesperson said that Reviews relies exclusively on internal platform content and “does not source, scrape or republish third-party content.” The company said that because each review links to the original discussion, users on the platform “can explore the context and go deeper. “

Reddit also said that brands can’t buy ads to get into Reddit Reviews. “What appears in Reddit Reviews is shaped by Reddit communities, not paid placement,” the spokesperson said.

However, that reliance on organic Reddit activity brings its own vulnerabilities. One challenge Reddit may face with Reviews is trying to keep its AI focused on authentic human-written reviews versus posts that might come from marketers, coordinated astroturfing or AI-generated spam. Because the platform operates on anonymity, it’s facing an uphill battle with a massive influx of AI bots that could try to game content in Reviews.

The new feature comes alongside Reddit’s recent changes to the platform to detect spam or other manipulated content and keep bots out, including discontinuing support for RSS feeds and limiting access to its content API. The company is also restricting Old Reddit, a previous design version of the platform that has fewer ads.

A Reddit spokesperson told CNET that the platform has “the least amount of AI slop relative to other[s]” and that it is taking “numerous steps to prevent and enforce against inauthentic content.”

But while Reddit insists that Reviews will be centered on personal experience and uncorrupted by advertising dollars, many are worried the feature could blur the line between community research and automated e-commerce.

#3081. Gaining Financial Control Requires More Than Just a High Income

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Income is one factor to feeling financially in control, but your approach to managing your money is crucial, too.

Earning more money can boost your feeling of financial control.

Nearly 9 in 10 (89%) Americans with a household income of $100k-plus say they feel in control of their day-to-day finances compared with 62% of Americans with a household income of less than $50k, according to NerdWallet’s October 2026 Financial Resilience Index survey conducted by The Harris Poll.

But getting a raise or a higher-paying job isn’t a surefire way to feel in control. Pairing your paycheck with good financial habits is a more robust approach.

Nearly 4 in 5 (78%) Americans feel in control of their day-to-day finances, according to the survey. That’s up from 73% in September.

There’s no single external measure for what makes someone feel in control of their finances. If you swap financial positions with someone else who feels in control, for example, there’s no guarantee you would feel the same way.

That said, a person who lives comfortably with what they have and who has the ability to withstand unexpected expenses has a good chance of feeling in control.

Americans with lower household incomes are much more likely to feel a lack of control in their day-to-day finances compared with those with higher household incomes.

That may seem intuitive. Someone with a high income is more likely to be able to cut back on luxuries, such as dining or vacations, when the costs of groceries and healthcare rise. Someone whose income is lower might not have expenses to cut.

However, that narrative is an overgeneralization.

If feeling in control of your finances depended entirely on having a high income, you might expect to see a much higher share of Americans with low incomes who feel they aren’t in control of their day-to-day finances.

But in fact, the majority (62%) of Americans with a household income of less than $50k do feel in control of their day-to-day finances. At the other end of the income spectrum, it’s clear that money doesn’t automatically result in feeling in control: About 1 in 10 Americans (11%) with a household income of $100k+ say they don’t feel this.

A high income alone won’t offset spending more than you earn, and it isn’t a substitute for an emergency fund. Good financial habits are an important component of financial control, too. They may look like:

Preparing for an emergency: Car repairs, medical bills, broken appliances: There are plenty of expensive emergencies that can pop up, even if you’re doing everything right. One-third (33%) of Americans don’t have enough cash on hand to cover an unexpected $1,000 expense if it popped up this month. Those who have an emergency fund can avoid relying on credit.

Managing debt: Monthly expenses that exceed income indicate a shaky financial footing — not great for developing a feeling of control. Nearly 2 in 5 Americans (38%) say they’ll have to rely on credit to manage expenses in October. Managing debt goes beyond paying your credit card bill each month. For example, if you get the maximum car loan or mortgage that lenders approve, a large portion of your paycheck is committed to debt payments. Keeping your overall debt load low gives you flexibility if your situation changes in the future.

Avoiding expensive mistakes: Saving money takes time. Spending it can happen quickly. A separate recent NerdWallet study found that 3 in 5 Americans (60%) say they’ve spent money on something expensive and later regretted it. Luxury items, gambling and vehicles topped the list of regrettable purchases. Pump the brakes on avoidable expensive purchases. For any big buy, take a day or two to mull over your options, especially if you have outstanding debt or if your emergency fund is low. Considering spending decisions carefully is another way to feel more in control.

The feeling of control is likely to emerge over time. Build momentum by making progress on one tangible financial goal — saving money or paying down debt, for example — before adding another.

Yes, Americans across a range of incomes report feeling in control financially. But it would be glib to suggest that this demonstrates that the feeling of financial control can be flicked on like a light switch, if only people tried harder.

There are plenty of reasons why the road to feeling in control can be arduous. Family obligations, medical concerns, affordability issues and limited opportunities can all present real obstacles, even for those who strive to practice sound financial habits along the way.

If you’re struggling and need assistance, start with these resources:

#3080. Grove (GROV) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Grove reports first quarter of positive GAAP net income and adjusted EBITDA

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Grove Collaborative Holdings, Inc. (GROV -5.46%) reported positive GAAP net income and adjusted EBITDA for the same quarter for the first time as a public company. Management attributed the results to a stabilized top line and continued cost discipline, including a 22.1% reduction in operating expenses. The company is shifting its strategic focus toward human health through the implementation of the Grove Standard and an expanded assortment via dropship capabilities. Management indicated that 2027 is the target year for returning to year-over-year revenue growth.

Operator: Good afternoon, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to Grove Collaborative Holdings, Inc. Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all lines have been placed on listen only mode to prevent any background noise. Following the speakers' remarks, we will open up your lines for questions. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded. Hosting today's call are Grove's CEO Jeff Yurcisin and Principal Financial Officer, Flip van den Bosch.

Jeff Yurcisin: Some of the statements made today about future prospects, financial results, business strategies, industry trends and Grove's ability to successfully respond to business risks may be considered forward looking. Including statements relating to growth making it easier for customers to see why each product earned its place on the Grove platform and to swap for healthier options. The plan to reinvest part of GROW's savings into acquiring and reactivating customers. The expectation that inventory comes down in the fourth quarter the launch of Grove's AI shopping assistant and its features, improvements to Autoship, the expectation that Grove Amazon sale, will grow in the fourth quarter.

Projected higher lifetime value and a platform Grove can use to scale advertising onto acquiring new customers efficiently. Grove's guidance for 2026 including guidance for full year 2026 net revenue and adjusted EBITDA. Fourth quarter net revenue being modestly below the third quarter. The expectation that Grove's DTC channel will be approximately flat the fourth quarter compared to the third. Continued stabilization of the DTC business. Such statements are based on current expectations and beliefs and are subject to a number of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially including those risks discussed in Grove's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

All of these statements are based on Grove's views today, and Grove assumes no obligation to update any forward looking statement. Whether as a result of new information, future events, or otherwise, except as may be required under applicable securities laws. During today's call, Grove will also discuss certain non GAAP financial measures, which adjust GAAP results to eliminate the impact of certain items, will find additional information regarding these non GAAP financial measures and a reconciliation of these non GAAP items to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures in Grove's earnings release, which is also available on Grove's Investor Relations website.

Operator: I would now like to turn the call over to Jeff Yurcisin to begin.

Jeff Yurcisin: Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us. Inside Grove, we have started calling this moment a new Day 1. After years of transforming and stabilizing the business, we are entering a new chapter, the results are starting to show it. Revenue grew sequentially for the second straight quarter and we have delivered positive GAAP net income alongside positive adjusted EBITDA, the first time we have done both in the same quarter as a public company. Today, I want to focus on where growth is headed, that starts with human and environmental health. This new Day 1 is about doubling down on human health. We believe 57 million consumers want a trusted guide to healthier products.

And Grove is uniquely positioned to be that guide. With ingredient standards, we believe are among the highest in our industry. A curated assortment and years of customer trust. Planetary Health will always be a part of who we are, but our focus is helping customers build healthier homes for the people they love. In September, we published the Grove Standard, developed with guidance from our Independent Science Council. Every product we sell is screened against thousands of restricted chemicals. Including PFAS, phthalates, and bisphenols. We do the hard work on ingredients so our customers do not have to. And the standard is not static. Our science council reviews it as the research evolves. evolves.

Our customers want more than a list of what is been left out. They wanna know what is actually good for their family. Parents are reading labels on everything from dish soap to snacks. And concerns about chemicals like PFAS are now mainstream, not niche. that is why we are expanding from a clean home to the health of the whole household. With the same standards and the same trust. Over the coming quarters, we plan to make it easier for customers to see why each product earns its place on the Grove platform and to swap within their home for healthier options. Building on product pages, we relaunched the quarter to educate, not just sell.

That trust is our advantage. In a Grove survey this year, 94% of more than 1000 Grove customers said they trust Grove more than Amazon to sell products that are safe for their families. And it shows up in how they shop. Customers who buy wellness products from Grove have had 33% higher average order values. And purchased twice as often based on an internal analysis of Grove customer orders in 2025. We are not trying to be everything to everyone. We are building a business that matters in the lives of a highly valuable group of customers, people who trust us with their homes and their families, that is the foundation durable growth is built on.

Before turning to the other 3 pillars of our turnaround, profitability, balance sheet strength and revenue growth, want to talk about what is accelerating our progress. Artificial intelligence. Let me start with a story. A colleague on our people team who supports our fulfillment centers and has no engineering background used Claude to build a tool that replaced 7 manual workflows. The initial build took her about 10 minutes, and the whole project took a couple of hours. She estimates it will save roughly 1000 hours of work a year across our 2 fulfillment centers. that is an extraordinary return, and it reflects a broader shift at Grove. Our teams can increasingly turn their own ideas into working solutions.

We are truly changing how we work. Smaller, more autonomous teams are improving the customer experience faster, than we could have imagined even 3 months ago. And we are getting better at the fundamental job of retail, putting the right product in front of the right customer at the right time. With the correction of the issues we experienced in connection with our platform migration, we have the platform and the team ready to accelerate into this new era. Now let's get to our remaining pillars. Sustainable profitability. Grove reported positive GAAP net income this quarter, together with positive adjusted EBITDA, was the first time we have achieved both as a public company.

This quarter included a $1.2 million tariff refund, but adjusted EBITDA was positive even excluding the refund. A profitable quarter does not happen by accident. It reflects years of resetting our cost structure. Operating expenses fell 22% year-over-year to $20.3 million driven by lower personnel costs and lower fulfillment and shipping costs from our updated carrier strategy. We plan to stay disciplined, reinvesting part of those savings and acquiring and reactivating customers where the return is supported. Balance sheet strength. We ended the quarter with $11.1 million in cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash compared with $11.4 million at the end of the second quarter.

Operating cash flow was positive $0.2 million including the tariff refund compared with negative $1 million a year ago. We achieved that while rebuilding in stock levels and bringing in holiday assortment, and we expect inventory to come down in the fourth quarter as that assortment sells through. The modest decline in cash reflects investments in our web and app infrastructure, and payments on financing agreements. Revenue growth. Net revenue was $36.8 million down 15.8% year over year, but up 0.7% from the second quarter. Sequential growth has always been our first step back to year over year growth. QVC drove the increase, partly offset by a slight decline in DTC.

The year over year decline still reflects a smaller active customer base, the compounding effect of lower advertising in prior years and attrition from our 2025. Platform disruptions. We are working 4 levers to turn that around. First, a broader assortment. Our drop ship assortment recorded its first sales this quarter. It lets us offer healthier options in categories where holding inventory does not make sense, such as air and water filtration, whose replacement filters fit naturally into replenishment. By offering customers more options to shop throughout their home, we believe drop ship will enable more frequent orders and larger basket sizes. Second, a better experience.

Since July, we have shipped 6 iOS app releases, relaunched our homepage and product pages around health, and released a redesigned cart. Customers are noticing. Since September 1st, we have averaged 4.9-stars on our app review and we are seeing gains in conversion and subscription penetration. In the fourth quarter, we plan to launch our AI shopping assistant which answers questions using our product knowledge, real customer reviews and the Grove Standard personalized to each customer's cart, orders, and subscriptions. We will also make Autoship simpler and more transparent. Third, bringing customers back. More than 5 million customers have shopped with Grove. They know the brand. And we often know why they left.

This quarter, we began testing reactivation off including membership trials and rewards to show them a faster app, a broader assortment and our Grove rewards program. Early signs are encouraging. Fourth, Amazon. We added selection, refined pricing and promotion, and we expect Amazon to grow in the fourth quarter. It extends our brands to shoppers who want trusted, healthier products that start their shopping on Amazon. All 4 point to the same outcome. Higher lifetime value from a loyal customer base and a platform we can scale advertising on to acquire new customers efficiently. It is a new Day 1 at Grove.

We have a clear mission in human health, a more efficient cost structure, and a team building faster than ever. I will now turn it over to Flip to review our financial results for the third quarter in more detail.

Flip van den Bosch: Thank you, Jeff, and welcome, everyone. Our third quarter results reflect continued cost discipline and a stabilizing top line. We grew revenue sequentially, our cost structure is leaner, we delivered positive adjusted EBITDA for the fourth consecutive quarter along with positive net income. Before I walk through the details, I will start with the tariff refund because it affects several of the lines I will cover. During the third quarter, we received a refund of approximately $1.2 million in tariffs we had previously paid. We recorded it as a reduction in cost of goods sold. It is included in reported gross margin and reported adjusted EBITDA. I have not adjusted it out of adjusted EBITDA.

Consistent with how we treated tariff costs when they were incurred. The gross margin net income adjusted EBITDA and operating cash flow figures I cite today include this refund. Starting at the top line. Net revenue for the third quarter was $36.8 million down 15.8% year over year, but an increase of 0.7% quarter over quarter. The year over year decline was primarily driven by a smaller active customer base than a year ago. Reflecting the compounding effects of lower advertising investment in prior periods and customer attrition tied to the e commerce platform disruptions experienced throughout 2025. This was partially offset by an increase in D2C net revenue per order. Sequential increase was driven by QVC revenue.

Including $1.2 million from a today's special value program. Partially offset by a slight decline in DTC net revenue. Active customers totaled 458,000 as of September 30, 2026. A decrease of 30.6% year over year. These declines reflect the lightning effects of reduced advertising investments and customer attrition tied to the e commerce platform disruptions we experienced throughout 2025. DTC total orders were 473,000 a decline of 23.6% year over year an increase in frequency of orders per active customer partially offset the decline in active customers. DTC net revenue per order was $70.85 an increase of 6.1% year over year.

The improvement was primarily driven by continued efficiency in promotional spend following the launch of our new loyalty program in the fourth quarter of 25. A larger mix of higher priced items and customer orders. Reflecting continued category expansion into higher priced assortment. In addition to an increase in shipping revenue per order. Gross margin was 55.8%. An increase of 250 basis points compared to the 53.3% in the third quarter of 25. The increase was driven by the tariff refunds and more targeted promotional spend. Partially offset by a higher mix of QVC revenue during the quarter, which contributed a lower margin than our DTC business. Turning to advertising.

Invested $1.8 million in the quarter, a 43.3% decrease year over year. But an increase compared to the second quarter. Increasing advertising spend from 3.4% of revenue to 4.9%. An enhanced customer experience in place, we are increasing advertising spend with discipline, including testing new channels for new customer acquisition, reengaging lapsed customers, and supporting growth on Amazon. Product development expense was $1.5 million down 8.6% year over year. Reflecting lower personnel spend on brands development. At present, we have been more selective in own-brand innovation. Prioritizing resources towards improving our customer experience. SG&A was $17 million, a 19.9% decrease versus the prior year.

The decrease was driven by improvements to our personnel cost structure lower fulfillment costs from fewer orders, lower outbound shipping rates. Tied to our carrier change. As well as continued ongoing cost optimization across the organization. Net income was $0.1 million or a 0.3% net income margin. Compared to a net loss of $3 million or a 6.8 net loss margin in the prior year. The year over year improvement reflects lower operating expenses and the tariff refund. Offset by the decline in revenue. Adjusted EBITDA was positive $1.4 million or a 3.7% margin. Compared to negative $1.2 million or a negative 2.7% margin in the prior year period. This marks the fourth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA.

And reflects continued operating discipline while investing in the customer experience. Turning to the balance sheet and liquidity. We ended the quarter with $11.1 million in cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash. A decrease from $11.4 million at the end of the second quarter. Primarily reflecting capitalized expenditures as a result of continued investment in e commerce platform enhancements and payments on financing agreements. Partially offset by positive operating cash flow. Operating cash flow was positive $0.2 million for the quarter.

Reflecting positive net income net of non cash expenses inclusive of the tariff refund, partially offset by net use of working capital primarily from the timing of inventory purchases, as an increase in inventory was largely offset by an increase in accounts payable. This compares to negative $1 million in the prior year period. Now turning to our outlook. We are narrowing our full year 2026 guidance. We now expect full year net revenue of $144 million to $146 million within our prior range of $142.5 million to $152.5 million. adjusted EBITDA of $1 million to $2 million within our prior outlook of breakeven to positive low single digit millions.

Last quarter, we said that we expected sequential revenue improvement in each remaining quarter of 2026. We now expect fourth quarter net revenue to be modestly below the third quarter. Third quarter net revenue included $1.2 million from a today's special value program on QVC. We do not expect a comparable program in the fourth quarter. We expect our DTC channel to be approximately flat in the fourth quarter compared to the third quarter. Reflecting continued stabilization of the DTC business. In closing, we are continuing to see progress on stabilizing the top line while executing with the financial discipline we committed to at the start of the year.

Our cost structure is more efficient, unit economics continue to improve, and we are managing cash flow consistent with our liquidity. I am encouraged by the discipline, we have built the foundation we are putting in place to support profitable durable growth in 2027. With that, I will turn the call back over to Jeff for closing remarks.

Jeff Yurcisin: Thank you, Flip. 3 quarters into 2026, we are seeing our discipline translate into results. 2 consecutive quarters of sequential revenue growth, 4 consecutive quarters of positive adjusted EBITDA and a customer experience where we have meaningfully transformed, including category expansion, loyalty program, the improved platform experience and an updated subscription experience. As we look to 2027, our goal is to return to year over year net revenue growth. We have already delivered an improved web and app experience in the growth standard, a health standard customers can see and trust.

In the fourth quarter, we plan to launch our AI powered shopping assistant in a further enhanced auto ship experience, building on the infrastructure launch through the end of the third quarter. We are continuing to broaden selection through drop ship, driving targeted reengagement with customers who have lapsed. And with a stronger platform in place, reinvesting in customer acquisition where the return is supported. We see continued opportunity to optimize our cost structure by leveraging internal AI capabilities, and we are building Grove into a durable profitable business with human health at the center. These are the foundations we are building on as we work to return Grove to revenue growth in 2027. That ends my prepared remarks.

Operator: Thank you. We will now be conducting a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press *1. Depending on your equipment, it may be necessary to pick up the handset before pressing the star keys. Our first question comes from the line of Susan Anderson with Canaccord Genuity. Please proceed with your question.

Susan Anderson: Hi, good evening. Thanks for taking my questions. Was wondering if maybe you can give some color, I guess, looking out to next year, how you are thinking about the sales growth? Should we expect continued sequential growth in sales to continue? And then I guess, you have any thoughts around when you think you will get back to year over year growth? Thanks.

Jeff Yurcisin: Thank you, Susan. Yes, like we always knew that sequential growth was the first step. And that is what we are delivering this year. I would say when we look forward into 2027, we are really planning for year over year growth. We are not at a point where we will lay out quarter by quarter what that looks like. But we see the business truly turning. We think that we have delivered a new customer experience, and we are really shifting our priorities towards human health, and we are seeing the right type of return on that. So across the board, I would just say that we are planning on 2027 being a return to year over year growth.

Susan Anderson: Okay. Great. And then maybe if you could just talk about how you are thinking about marketing expense in the fourth quarter and into next year. I guess should we think about it increasing as we kind of move forward? or kind of staying the same? And then, I guess, just on the tariff refunds, I think you said there was $1 million or $2 million in there. I guess, is there more to come? Or was that all of it? Thanks.

Jeff Yurcisin: Thank you, Susan. Let me address the tariff first. It was $1.2 million It all arrived in Q3, and we are not expecting any additional refunds. The first question was more tied towards the drivers of revenue growth next year. Is that right? Oh, no. Marketing spend. Apologies. So this is exactly. You are hitting on the way we think about our business, which is we obviously need to increase marketing spend to drive the right type of growth. We always will increase when it makes the right type of payback sense. At times, we pulled back over the last year.

And when we pulled back, that has a lingering impact on total active customers, but we are proud of the type of 90-day active customers that we are seeing in our business. And we are still focused on investing where we are seeing the right returns. What is notable is that a year ago, we thought almost all of that was in customers that we were introducing our brand to. And now we are seeing some returns on going after customers who have been inactive for over a year or 2 years with us, but understand the brand. And we are seeing some returns and going back and addressing and targeting them.

And we also see an opportunity to accelerate the Amazon business, which we intentionally, for years, been positioned as a second channel to growth, and now we are willing to meet prime customers where they may be, which is on the Amazon platform. So I think when you think about the total marketing spend as a percentage of revenue, we would hope that increases in 2027. We also see it going to inactive and reactivating customers and some on other platforms like Amazon.

Susan Anderson: Okay. Great. And then maybe last 1 for me, just Yeah. Maybe if you could give a little bit of color on, I guess, the breakout by category now in sales, I guess, with all the different categories such as wellness and being that you have added to your website. I guess I am just kind of curious, what percent of sales do those new categories make up versus the core categories? Thanks.

Jeff Yurcisin: Yeah. I do not think we have specific kind of percentages to kind of share at this moment. But what I would say is what Dropship has enabled is the ability to translate the trust that we have earned from customers into more reasons to shop and more relevant assortment to them. And this makes particular sense when it comes to larger items or items like water filters or air filters, are great examples that we have seen thus far. Or even like yoga mats. We are finding an easy ability to extend that assortment.

What you are going to see is we think of human health not just being vitamins, minerals, and supplements, which, of course, are a double digit percent of all of our shipments have those. But we see it as helping customers find the healthy things for their home, and that can include things like bedding, and it could even include mattresses. And, of course, water filters and vitamins and supplements and all of the cleaning supplies that we are known for. But I think what you will see in the coming years is a continued focus on the human health element and making sure that customers. We enable them to have the healthiest home for the people they love. Okay.

Great. Thanks so much. Good luck with the rest of the year.

Operator: Thank you, Susan. Thank you. And we have reached the end of the question and answer session. I will now turn the call back over to Jeff Yurcisin for closing remarks.

Jeff Yurcisin: Thank you, operator. I want to thank everyone for joining the call. I hope you have a great day. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's conference and you may disconnect your lines at this time. And we thank you for your participation.

#3079. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates went up today, but they're still in a much better place than this time last month.

Mortgage rates are higher today, but only by a little. And they're still hovering below 7%, which is much better than what we saw around this time last month.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked up to 6.98% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is two basis points higher than Friday and five basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Mortgage rates have more room to rise, as a stronger-than-expected jobs report reinforced expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at a different inflation measure, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn strong: The October jobs report, released Friday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Considering Friday’s jobs data, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing, and market sentiment could shift over the next month. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as intended and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates might remain around 7%.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.48% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

#3077. If the Tech Stock Sell-Off Turns Into a Bear Market, History Says This Investing Strategy Has Never Failed

The Nasdaq Composite is 11% off its recent high.

Tech stocks were routed last week after a blue wave in the midterm elections. There was plenty already bubbling beneath the surface, and a new government that could be hostile to tech growth set off alarm bells. Since peaking about a month ago, the S&P 500 is down almost 4%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.74%) is down nearly 9%.

The tech sell-off could be a brief dip that rebounds to new highs, or it could turn into a bear market. In other words, no one knows what will happen next. While that's always the case, the underlying political and economic factors affecting the market are intensifying, increasing the likelihood of volatility and a market correction.

Investors who've never experienced this can feel fear, and even investors who have been there before can feel anxiety watching their holdings plummet. If you're not sure what to do right now, this one investing strategy has never failed.

First, a definition. Technically, the market turns bear when it's 20% off its recent high. When it happens, the worst thing you can do if stocks start to fall is sell. That turns paper losses into real losses, whereas if you hold on, the odds are that your stocks will rebound and go higher.

The last bear market was in 2022, and it lasted for most of the year. The Nasdaq lost 35% of its value in total by the time it bottomed out. Since then, it's up 150%.

What you need to do in a bear market is hold on to your stocks and wait it out. This is even more important when the market is volatile and could spring back up at any moment. It could rise again next week, but if you've sold, you won't get your money back.

Consider that history is on your side. In the 12 months following midterm elections going back to 1950, the S&P 500 has posted a gain every time, with an average gain of 15%.

Taking that a step further (back), since the end of World War II, the S&P 500 has delivered a gain 74.7% of the time. It lost value in consecutive years only twice (and once three years in a row), but it also posted gains of at least four consecutive years five times.

Holding on through the difficult years has led to fabulous wealth. And this holds whether investors have found the optimal time to invest or not.

For example, the investment company Charles Schwab studied five theoretical investors who had $2,000 to invest annually over 20 years. One had perfect timing; one invested on the first day of each trading year; another invested on the first of each month; one had exceptionally bad timing and invested only at market peaks; and the fifth shunned the stock market in favor of Treasury bills.

The investor who timed everything right had the best return with $186,000. But interestingly, the second and third investors did almost as well, coming away with $171,000 and $167,000. And the one with awful timing still walked away with $151,000.

The only investor who suffered was the one who skipped the market altogether; the Treasury bills generated only $47,000 over 20 years.

So, you don't need to time the market to benefit from its compounding over many years. If you invest consistently and tune out the noise about market ups and downs, your money can compound over time and grow into a solid nest egg.

One parting word: you can still make moves now to protect your portfolio during the rough years. If you're still loaded up on hot tech stocks, you may want to move some of your funds into dividend stocks and value stocks that can perform well under pressure. And if you might need some of your cash in the near future, it could make sense to sell a portion of your stocks before a bear market.

#3074. Amaero (AMRO) Q2 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Titanium output restarts as argon costs fall and defense demand builds.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Amaero Inc. (AMRO -13.63%) reported third quarter results that reflected a transition from facility build-out to commercial production scaling. Management stated that the company is currently focused on the simultaneous demand from several United States defense programs, including hypersonic weapon development and nuclear submarine construction. The company reported the successful restart of its titanium production lines following a safety review and the commissioning of specialized throughput equipment. Management indicated that the strategic focus remains on reshoring critical supply chains for high-value metal powders and near-net-shape components.

Operator: Please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Shannon Devine, Investor Relations. Thank you. You may begin.

Shannon Devine: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining Amaero's third quarter 2026 earnings call. I am Shannon Devine. Joining me today are Hank Holland, Amaero's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, and Brett Paduch, Amaero's Chief Financial Officer. Earlier this afternoon, Amaero issued its earnings release and posted its earnings presentation, both of which are available on the investor relations section of the company's website. Before we begin, please note that today's discussion will contain forward-looking statements regarding Amaero's business, financial performance, outlook, and future operating plans. Actual results may differ materially from those discussed today. Please refer to Amaero's earnings materials and SEC filings for a discussion of factors that could cause actual results to differ.

Any forward-looking statements that are made on this call speak only as of the date of this call, and Amaero disclaims any obligation to update any forward-looking statements, except as required by law. Certain non-GAAP financial measures will also be discussed. Information regarding Amaero's non-GAAP financial measures, including reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures, can be found in Amaero's earnings release and supplemental materials available on Amaero's investor relations website. With that, I will now turn the call over to Hank.

Hank Holland: Thank you, Shannon. Welcome. Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us. Good morning to those joining from Australia. Welcome to Amaero's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call, and the inaugural earnings call as a Nasdaq-listed company. Our first earnings call as a Nasdaq-listed company also marks our first results reported in U.S. dollars under U.S. GAAP, so comparative figures may differ from those we previously reported on the ASX, where our CDIs continue to be quoted under the symbol 3DA. To our new shareholders, welcome, and thank you for your confidence. To our longstanding shareholders, thank you for your support over the past four and a half years.

Because many of you are new to Amaero, I want to begin with the bigger picture, the opportunity in front of us, why we believe that Amaero has a differentiated market position, and why we believe the company is at an inflection point. Then I will highlight the financial results in the third quarter and revenue guidance for the fourth quarter. Then Brett will take you through the financials in more detail. Amaero sits at the intersection of three enduring themes, rebuilding the U.S. defense industrial base, reshoring and scaling sovereign manufacturing, and the adoption of additive and advanced manufacturing. For the first time in decades, aerospace and defense are simultaneously experiencing peak demand.

The Columbia and Virginia-class submarine programs, the advent of hypersonic weapons, the replacement of the Minuteman ICBM with Sentinel, and the build-out of missile defense are driving generational investment. At the same time, the war in Ukraine exposed how thin our domestic capacity is in large castings and forgings, among the most constrained links in the defense supply chain. I want to emphasize all these themes are structural, not cyclical. The United States allowed its defense industrial base to atrophy over three decades. Rebuilding it and bringing critical supply chains home is both a national security imperative and sound economic policy. Amaero's corporate strategy has been driven by a demand pull that is a direct result of these thematic forces.

Within that backdrop, Amaero addresses two specific bottlenecks. The first in high-value spherical metal powders. Powder is the consumable of metal 3D printing, the ink cartridge to the printer. So as the installed base of metal 3D printers expands, powder demand expands with it. It is a pick-and-shovel business. Titanium alloy powders serve defense, aerospace, medical, and consumer applications. Refractory alloy powders, such as niobium C103, serve high-temperature applications in high-growth verticals that include the defense, space, and nuclear energy sectors. The second is PM-HIP, or powder metallurgy hot isostatic pressing, a mature technology that was developed over seven decades ago and has the benefit of military specifications and mature datasets.

Amaero's technical team has done much of the pioneering work over the past two decades for producing large, complex, near-net-shape parts as an alternative to constrained castings and forgings. We estimate the U.S. addressable market across our three product lines at approximately $737 million in 2026, growing to approximately $1.5 billion by 2030. That is large enough to build a significant business, yet specialized enough to attract limited competition, which supports a specialty margin structure. As the largest shareholder, that combination is the thesis that led to my investment into Amaero, and it continues to guide our forward-leaning strategy.

Amaero has commissioned the largest U.S. domestic production capacity for titanium and refractory alloy spherical powders, co-located with PM-HIP manufacturing in AS9100D-certified facility near Chattanooga, Tennessee. The competitive landscape is narrow. In titanium powder, our two primary competitors operate in Canada. We have no primary competitor in the United States. In refractory powders, we have one primary competitor. In PM-HIP, others make simple parts, but our proprietary know-how and experience with complex near-net-shape components is highly differentiated. Our advantage rests on three things that are difficult to replicate. First, technology and know-how. We operate EIGA Premium atomizers, a crucible-free process that the Air Force Research Laboratory has called the industry standard for reactive and refractory materials.

Equipment alone does not make commercially viable powder. Our technical team, anchored by Eric Bono, our Chief Technology Officer, has made modifications to the equipment and optimized the process parameters to deliver roughly twice the usable yield while consuming about half the argon gas of conventional atomizers. That matters because yield determines how much feedstock and labor go into every kilogram of sellable powder. Our two largest variable costs, and argon is a significant input of its own right. Our argon recycling system targets a further reduction in argon cost of at least 77%. Second, qualifications. The highest barrier to new entries and to production contracts.

Our C103 has been qualified to a manned space flight standard, and we've closely collaborated with the U.S. Navy, BPMI, and the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program for development, first articles, and qualification of critical submarine components. Third, customer relationships built on demand pull. Shortly after we moved to Tennessee, we committed to dedicating EIGA Premium atomizer to refractory alloys, including niobium, tungsten, tantalum, and molybdenum. This was a direct response to the long lead times from a sole supplier that was slowing down the development of hypersonic programs. Months later, we began close collaboration with leading stakeholders in Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, developed PM-HIP as a substitute for long lead time forgings.

Following a roundtable convened at our facility last December, the Navy's Maritime Industrial Base Program Office issued a formal letter of support validating our PM-HIP manufacturing as a viable and technically ready alternative casting and forgings. In July, we received our first low-rate initial production contract with BPMI. On the commercial side, we've structured long-term agreements with leaders in high-growth verticals, several naming Amaero as exclusive supplier. In July, we were awarded a $4.5 million Department of War contract to develop alternative refractory alloy powders that reduce cost and reliance on foreign raw materials. As other companies are beginning multi-year capital programs to address these bottlenecks, we have largely completed ours. Amaero is now shifting from build-out to scaling production.

Through September 30th, we had invested $52.2 million in plant and equipment. We operate three EIGA Premium atomizers with approximately 680 metric tons of annual capacity, 480 metric tons of titanium, and 200 metric tons refractory. Our fourth atomizer, expected in June 2027, takes total capacity to 920 metric tons. In August, we commissioned a custom-designed titanium sieving system that, together with our third atomizer, doubled our titanium throughput capacity. In our first full year of commercial production, the 12 months ended June 30th, we generated $12.5 million in revenue. Trailing 12-month revenue through September 30th was $13.5 million, up 191%, and our backlog as of September 30th of $13.4 million is roughly equal to that.

Because our fixed production costs are largely in place, we expect revenue growth to drive operating leverage. I also want to directly address safety. Following safety incidents earlier this year, we committed to lean in. We paused titanium production and completed a comprehensive process, system, and facility safety review with Jensen Hughes, a leader in safety, dust hazard, and risk-based engineering. We engaged Jensen Hughes to identify risk mitigation strategies that were utilized by larger-scale industrial operations with dust hazards, such as the sugar industry, paper mills, and grain operations. We implemented resulting improvements, and titanium production resumed in late July after approximately a six-week pause. No order cancellations and no employee attrition.

As for Q3 highlights and outlook, turning to the quarter. Third quarter revenue grew 35% to $4.1 million, landing near the top of the previously disclosed range, and nine-month revenue grew 170% to $11.5 million. We ended the period with a backlog of $13.4 million, an increase of 180% from September 2025, and approximately 100% of trailing 12-month revenue. Operating cash use for the quarter fell $1 million year-over-year to $6.3 million. Commercially, the Department of War award and our first BPMI contract advanced both of our production lines in defense, refractory powders and PM-HIP. Operationally, we restarted titanium production and doubled titanium throughput capacity with commissioning an expanded custom-designed fabricated sieving system.

In the capital markets, we began trading on Nasdaq on October 15, receiving aggregate net IPO proceeds of $17.0 million, and amended our EXIM Bank credit agreement to release $2.1 million of restricted cash and move the liquidity covenant test to 2028. As of October 31, we had $19.3 million of cash and cash equivalents after October operating cash use and capital expenditures. Today, we are issuing our first formal guidance as a U.S. listed company. We expect Q4 2026 revenue of $4.5 million-$5.0 million, which would result in a quarterly increase of 121%-146% year-over-year. Combined with our results to date, that would result in full year 2026 revenue of $16.0 million-$16.5 million, up 154%-162%.

Our priorities are clear, convert backlog into revenue, expand the breadth and depth of our commercial partnerships, and bring argon recycling and our fourth atomizer online in the first half of 2027. With that, I will turn it over to our CFO, Brett, to provide more detail on our financial results.

Brett Paduch: Thank you, Hank, and good afternoon. I will start by tying our actual financial results back to our previously disclosed ranges and to provide more detail to our financial performance. Revenue of $4.11 million was near the top end of $3.96 million-$4.12 million range. Cash of $4.96 million and backlog of $13.44 million landed within the range. Net loss attributable to stockholders of $9.06 million, operating cash use of $6.34 million, and Adjusted EBITDA of $-7.11 million all came in modestly favorable to the range. Turning to revenue. Q3 revenue rose 35% to $4.1 million, with growth in both product lines.

Metal powders contributed $3.2 million, up 19%, reflecting the continued ramp of our atomization capacity and the expansion of new and existing customer relationships. PM-HIP contributed $0.9 million, up 146%, including the first revenue attributable to our LRIP contract with BPMI. Looking beyond any single quarter, nine-month revenue through Q3 grew 170% to $11.5 million from $4.3 million, and trailing 12-month revenue grew 191% to $13.5 million from $4.7 million. Backlog as of September 30th of $13.4 million is up 34% from $10 million at June 30th, up 96% from $6.9 million at year-end 2025, and up 180% from $4.8 million a year ago.

It includes $4.4 million attributable to the Department of War development contract, and it spans both powder and PM-HIP. Turning to the income statement. Cost of revenue in Q3 was $8.5 million compared with $3.1 million in Q3 2025, resulting in a gross loss for Q3 2026 of $4.4 million. I want to be clear about what drove that. The increase reflects the continued scale-up of our Tennessee operations together with titanium production in the quarter running below installed capacity, first because of the restart in late July, and then because optimizing the new sieving system reduced throughput and yields.

As a result, our portion of production labor and fixed production costs were not absorbed into inventory and were expensed in the period, and lower yields increased the cost of titanium powder sold. Our fixed production costs consisted principally of plant salaried labor and overhead, depreciation on manufacturing equipment and leasehold improvements, and the lease on our Tennessee facility. With the equipment and the plant operating and technical teams for both product lines largely in place, we do not expect those costs to increase in proportion to revenue. That is why we expect revenue growth to drive continued operating leverage and gross margin improvement. SG&A in Q3 was $4.3 million, up $0.5 million compared to the prior year period.

The increase reflects $0.6 million of non-ordinary course redomiciliation and IPO-related costs, primarily legal, tax, and audit fees, together with higher corporate legal and audit fees, partially offset by $0.5 million decrease in stock-based compensation. Q3 R&D was $0.1 million. Loss from operations was $8.8 million, and net loss attributable to stockholders was $9.1 million, or $0.38 per share, compared to $4.1 million, or $0.20 per share, in the prior year period. Adjusted EBITDA in Q3, which excludes stock-based compensation of $0.3 million and $0.6 million of redomiciliation and IPO-related costs, was negative $7.1 million compared with negative $3.1 million in Q3 2025.

For the nine months ending September 30th, 2026, revenue grew 170% from the prior year period to $11.5 million, and Adjusted EBITDA was $-15.6 million versus $-10.7 million in the prior year period. Let me close with four takeaways. First, quarterly revenue grew 35% year-over-year. Second, forward visibility has improved. Backlog at quarter end was 2.8x its level a year earlier, and our guidance implies full-year revenue growth of 154%-162%. Third, with our fixed production cost base largely in place and titanium throughput capacity doubled, we expect higher titanium output to drive operating leverage and gross margin improvement.

Fourth, our next capacity additions, argon recycling in the first quarter of 2027 and our fourth EIGA atomizer in June 2027, remain on schedule, funded in part by our IPO proceeds. I'll turn it back to Hank.

Hank Holland: Thank you, Brett. Let me close where I began, the themes behind our business, rebuilding the defense industrial base, reshoring sovereign manufacturing, and the adoption of additive manufacturing. These are enduring, and Amaero is positioned at their intersection. Our foundational build-out is complete. Our capacity is commissioned and AS9100D certified. The qualifications, the highest barrier in this industry, are well advanced. PM-HIP has moved into production for the submarine industrial base, and our Department of War program is advancing. Revenue is ramping against a backlog equal to a full year of trailing revenue. Our job now is execution. Continue to scale production, convert backlog into revenue, bring argon recycling, our fourth atomizer, online the first half of 2027.

We believe this is how we build durable value for shareholders and make a durable contribution to U.S. national security. Thank you for your time today. Brett and I are happy to take your questions.

Operator: Thank you. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. Our first question is from Peter Arment with Baird. Please proceed.

Peter Arment: Yeah. Good afternoon, Hank and Brett. Nice results. Hey, Hank, good to see titanium process restarted. Could you maybe talk about just how you're seeing the process, have things stabilized, and then is the new sieving system fully optimized? How we should be thinking about any remaining bottlenecks there?

Hank Holland: Yeah, absolutely. Thank you very much, Peter. As you've seen firsthand, the sieving system that we installed, we believe to be the largest system of its type in the world outside of China for reactive metals. The sieving is the bottleneck process of powder production. As you stated, we restarted titanium production the end of July, and that has gone quite well. We had already commissioned the third atomizer, the second dedicated titanium in June. Then in the month of August is when we commissioned the sieving system. I would say that by the time we got into early to mid-September, most of the parameter optimization was dialed in.

We're continuing to make small tweaks, and I would expect that through the very end of this year, we'll be making small tweaks. I would say from a yield standpoint, the yield was below optimal for last quarter, and I would expect this quarter, over the course of the quarter, we will begin to approach where we would expect it to be longer term.

Peter Arment: Got it. That's helpful. Brett, a quick one on, I know you're not guiding to gross margins or anything for Q4, but just given that maybe some of these startup or restart costs maybe are a little bit behind you, should we expect to see some of that leverage begin to show up here in Q4?

Brett Paduch: Yeah, I would say the fixed cost in our cost of goods sold is significantly scaled at this point. That includes both the rent, depreciation, it includes our technical and operating teams. So, as our revenue grows into Q4 and beyond, we would not expect a commensurate rise in those fixed production costs, which is where we would start seeing that operating leverage lead to improvement in our gross margin moving forward.

Hank Holland: Peter, the one thing that I would add, what Brett said, which is exactly right, the other thing is there tends to be about a six-week lag of inventory. The inventory cost that will come into Q4 of this, the current quarter that we are in, there will be a number of weeks of that inventory from last quarter that will be impacted by some of the same issues from yields and so forth. I would expect to see an improvement in gross margin, but we really will not begin to see the favorable trend as we would expect until we get into the next calendar year because of that modest lag.

Peter Arment: Okay. Just a quick one, just regarding your backlog. Is there anything that is unfunded as we are still in a continuing resolution in the U.S. for FY 2027, or do you have all the funding you need for what is in backlog?

Hank Holland: Yeah, I will take that briefly. All of the backlog as reported is contracted firm orders, all of which is expected to be recognized prior to June 30th, with the exception of there are two payments on the Department of War contract that I believe total about $700,000. Most of that backlog will be recognized before June 30th, all of which are firm commitments and all of which funding is in place. I will tell you that obviously none of us know exactly what will happen with the FY 2027 defense appropriation budget, particularly given the midterm elections, when that might be approved.

I would not see it having an impact on us so long as we eventually got the FY 2027 budget approved, i.e., even if it was in February or March of next year. We have got a significant pipeline of opportunities that have already received funding at our tier one supplier level. I would not expect any CR in the short term to impact what we see in calendar year 2027 or first half of calendar year 2027 revenues.

Peter Arment: Appreciate all the details, guys. I'll jump back in the queue. Thanks, Hank.

Operator: Our next question is from Jaeson Schmidt with Lake Street Capital Markets. Please proceed.

Jaeson Schmidt: Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my questions, and congrats on the solid results. Sticking with backlog, I know you mentioned it spans both businesses. Just curious, if outside the DoW contract, are there any sort of larger, chunkier awards within that, or is it pretty broad-based across the diverse customer base?

Hank Holland: Yeah, I'll take that to start. The DoW award, as we've announced, was about $4.5 million, and so that is a chunk of that $13.4 million backlog. Beyond that, we do have long-term agreements in place, as in 12-month purchase orders. Keep in mind, Jaeson, that prior to the redomiciliation, our fiscal year ended June 30th, and so many of those 12-month POs had been structured from a July to June basis. So by the time we get through the end of December, we will have burnt off half of that 12-month PO. We'll obviously begin to restructure those on a going-forward basis, more so on a calendar year basis.

I think the other interesting thing, as you know, we announced back in July, I believe it was, the contract with BPMI. It was our first LRIP, or low-rate production contract. It was not a particularly large contract, about $350,000. However, it was a very important contract in that it was our first production. It was the seventh contract we had with BPMI, albeit the first one that we announced. And what we would now expect to see is that opens the door to a series of production contracts to follow. They're not yet showing up in backlog. They're showing up essentially in our pipeline.

But I would expect to see some relatively chunky orders that will follow in the PM-HIP business over time. The rest of it, again, I would say would be ordinary course of business, either spot orders or relatively short-term orders that we have in coupled with the Department of War contract.

Jaeson Schmidt: Got you. That's really helpful. And, Hank, my next question was going to be on BPMI and when we could see some production contracts. Any sense on the timeline there?

Hank Holland: Yeah, we're not in a position to say much more. A, we haven't given any guidance on that, and B, Jaeson, as you can appreciate, a lot of times the approval of these contracts take on kind of a life of their own, and we're always very, very mindful to be conservative with any guidance that we give. We do think that the announcement of the BPMI contract was quite consequential and does now position us for a series of contracts to follow. That's probably all we can say at this point, though.

Jaeson Schmidt: Okay. Makes sense. Thanks a lot, guys.

Operator: Our next question is from Doug Smith with Curran & Company. Please proceed.

Doug Smith: Hi, Hank. Hi, Brett. Congrats on the first U.S. quarterly report. I thought I'd ask about the backlog as well, and I've seen some news flow regarding hypersonic programs moving forward. Are you seeing some C103 signals start to come through related to [Castheon]? Also, what's the inbound sort of look like on the titanium, and how do we see that growing as we go forward?

Hank Holland: Yeah, so beginning with C103, this is one of the areas, as you well know, Doug, and that you've followed the company for quite some time, the FY 2025 CR and the subsequent government shutdown had a real impact on Amaero in delaying the revenue. Some of the C103 programs, I think about certain strategic missile programs, for example, were significantly impacted, and we're only now seeing some of those programs down select from what was probably as much as a two-year delay. Yes, we are seeing an uptick in C103 demand from defense applications. We're also seeing it on the space side.

As you know, in the case of niobium C103, first used in the Apollo lunar landing vehicle in 1969, it's really become the go-to high-temperature alloy. Where we have mission-critical applications, and whether that's particularly sensitive defense applications and/or space, it does seem to be the go-to alloy. I will tell you, part of what's exciting about our Department of War contract, though, is, as you well know, Doug, that one of the challenges with niobium C103, it's comprised 10% of hafnium, and hafnium prices are up about 700% the last several years.

The Department of War is anxious to find alternatives in the refractory high-temperature alloy space that do not include hafnium, and that's really where our program, the DoW, is focused. Yes, we are seeing uptick in demand for C103, but importantly, we're also seeing uptick in demand in alternative refractories as well.

Doug Smith: Okay, fantastic. Thanks for that, Hank. That is all for me.

Operator: We have reached the end of our question and answer session. This will conclude today's conference. You may disconnect your lines at this time, and thank you for your participation.
