#3073. Best Hotels in Chase’s The Edit in 2026

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site or when you click to or take an action on their website. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Chase's hotel and resort program, The Edit, gives some cardholders the chance to book stays at spectacular hotels.

Many premium credit cards have their own travel portals where you can earn and redeem your points. They also have a curated list of hotels with which they partner to offer elevated benefits to their cardholders who book directly through their program.

The Edit is Chase’s program, and similar to the Fine Hotels & Resorts program from American Express, travelers need to book a prepaid reservation directly through a Chase Travel channel and pay with their Chase card to receive the benefits.

What benefits do you receive when you book through the program? Well, they can be substantial.

At nearly 1,400 hotels and resorts, The Edit customers will enjoy:

If the hotel is an all-inclusive property, guests would instead receive a $200 property credit to use for experiences like spa treatments. While stays at hotels in The Edit Boutique Collection do include the other perks, those stays are not eligible for a room upgrade or early check-in/late checkout considerations.

The tradeoff of using The Edit program is that it does not necessarily always have the lowest rate. Sometimes you can find a lower rate directly with the hotel or another website. But, when you consider the list of benefits above, any differential in price can more than outweigh the extra cost.

While it belongs to Chase, The Edit is not open to all Chase cardholders. It is a dedicated perk for primary cardholders and authorized users of the Chase Sapphire Reserve® and J.P. Morgan Reserve cards, as well as primary Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ cardholders.

Even better is that these eligible Chase cards come with a total of $500 in credits that can be used at The Edit hotels each year. They are divided into two $250 credits that each must be used for at least a two-night stay. And when paying for the rest of your stay through The Edit, cardholders earn 8x Chase Ultimate Rewards® points per dollar spent. In addition, hotel stays booked through The Edit and labeled as “Loyalty Plus” are eligible to also earn points with any associated hotel loyalty program.

These are some of our favorite hotels in the program where you can take advantage of your annual $500 credits as well as earn significant Chase points for a prepaid stay.

This oasis in the desert enjoys distant views of the Atlas Mountains from its various pools and riad-like accommodation buildings. It also has a full-service spa, kids club and access to Al Maaden Golf course. Its Moroccan restaurant is worth a visit and offers cuisine from all of Morocco and the North African region (with many ingredients coming from the chef’s onsite garden). Guests can add a stash of World of Hyatt points to their account after a stay here, but be sure to look to see if it is “eligible” in the search results (as shown below).

Guests can arrive at this luxury resort by its own fleet of two sea planes that serve the three properties in the Four Seasons portfolio. (Two of the properties are in The Edit, the third is a private island: Four Seasons Maldives Kuda Huraa, Four Seasons Resort Maldives at Landaa Giraavaru and Four Seasons Maldives Private Island at Voavah, respectively.)

Overwater villas with their own pools and hammocks dangling over the sea, beach bungalows with private access pools and excellent dining (from Asian to Lebanese) are hallmarks of the resort. Its newest element is the AyurMa wellness program at the spa with onsite practitioners who guide guests on personalized, multiday journeys covering everything from nutrition to physical therapy.

This resort is designed around 64 pool suites and villas with access to a beautiful beachfront, swimming pools and a jungle spa. Its island location lies within the Gulf of Thailand near Koh Samui, and its beach is well-known for its famous Full Moon parties. Other activities, besides relaxing, include Muay Thai boxing, scuba diving, snorkeling, kayaking, stand-up paddle boarding and yoga sessions.

Anantara is part of Minor Hotels that are associated with the Discovery program, which means travelers can earn Discovery Dollars, even when booking via The Edit.

Along the Southbank Promenade, this luxury hotel has great views of the Melbourne skyline and is within walking distance of the city’s great shopping, museums and dining options. When you enter the lobby, the first thing you notice is the grand Waterford crystal chandelier, one of the largest in the Southern Hemisphere.

This is also one of the city’s biggest hotels, and it is highly regarded as a top hotel in town. Be sure to request one of the rooms with a balcony or terrace to take in the views.

Known by many as Dublin’s grande dame, this Autograph Collection member is fresh off the heels of a top-to-bottom renovation that renewed its interiors, but didn’t change its historic spirit. While renovation work will linger into 2027, the refreshed rooms are worth experiencing.

The hotel is where the drafting of the Irish Constitution took place, but today it serves as a hub for visiting elite and locals to mix and mingle. When booking through The Edit, members can earn Marriott Bonvoy points in addition to Chase Ultimate Rewards®.

This beachfront hotel is a favorite destination for European travelers who want a Dalmatian coastline view while also being in close proximity to the historic center of town. There are multiple pools, a beach club and spa for onsite entertainment. Radisson Rewards members would also be able to earn points for their stay.

Radisson is growing its portfolio of high-end hotels, resorts and luxury properties, which makes the loyalty program one not to overlook for Americans who may not be as familiar with it.

This city-center hotel is ideal for business travelers, but also attracts attention for its rooftop bar and restaurant. Chase cardholders using The Edit should think beyond just booking a vacation stay through the program because business trips can also yield significant Ultimate Rewards points bonuses. Just remember you need to book through The Edit with a prepaid, eligible rate.

In a historic bank building, the hotel’s Bauhaus-inspired design with colorful art make this more than just a standard business property. And like Kimpton properties worldwide, guests here can take advantage of morning coffee and refreshments in the lobby, an evening happy hour, free bikes and yoga mats to use, and of course the secret password. Mention that password (which changes seasonally) at reception to be eligible for a prize that could include drink vouchers or room upgrades among other things.

This family-friendly resort features the largest and first waterpark on the island (with three waterslides and a lazy river) as well as some of its finest dining venues, including the only high-end steakhouse on the island. Golfers can enjoy the island’s only 18-hole golf course here, too.

Because it's an independent resort, booking through The Edit is a great way to still earn points for your stay since it does not have a loyalty program of its own.

Celebrating 100 years, the hotel has unveiled renovations across the hotel, which sits in midtown Manhattan, and they will continue for the next year. Guests who book a Club rate or have the annual lounge benefit they can select as a Milestone Reward can visit the lobby-level club lounge here.

The building was built as part of the Grand Central Terminal design plan and now belongs to the Historic Hotels of America group. Guests who book through The Edit will receive IHG One Rewards for their stay and any eligible elite status perks.

The “Pink Palace of the Pacific” will celebrate its 100th anniversary in 2027 and is a famous hotel along one of Hawaii’s most famous beaches. This is one of many Marriott Bonvoy family hotels in Honolulu, and it is surrounded by lush gardens and has stunning ocean views. Guests can walk to nearby shopping, take the onsite history tour or snap photos with Diamond Head in the background. Guests can earn Marriott Bonvoy points for their stay, and elite status members can take advantage of any eligible perks.

This all-inclusive, family hotel is a great option for those looking for great dining, sunshine and oceanfront accommodations. Parents can enjoy the spa while kids are having fun in the kids club. Other activities include movie nights outside, painting classes, beach barbecues and lawn games. The resort is part of the Preferred Hotels & Resorts program, and earning Ultimate Rewards points for booking a stay through The Edit is a nice bonus.

Prepare for a new experience at one of the Chilean capital’s most posh hotels, and you can book your entire stay through The Edit. As a result, you would receive the perks of the program as well as Marriott Bonvoy points at the only Ritz-Carlton in South America.

Big changes at the hotel include new menus that refocus the restaurant cuisine on modern takes of Chilean recipes. The chef partners with a local farmer for produce, but goes one step further in being able to have first dibs on the best produce and herbs available each season. On the top floor, guests can enjoy a panoramic indoor swimming pool beneath a glass atrium, panoramic rooftop terrace and spa offering traditional Andean healing treatments.

Booking a hotel via The Edit leads to instant benefits like free breakfast, property credits, and early check-in and late checkout. While the rates may not always be the lowest you’ll find online, the perks that come with The Edit may more than outweigh any cost differential.

The Edit’s curated collection of hotels and resorts covers a broad range of high-end properties, and the program is only open to select Chase credit cardholders. When making a prepaid, eligible reservation through The Edit, the cardholder also receives 8x Ultimate Rewards points on top of the onsite perks that make this a great offer. Even better, if the property participates in its own loyalty program, Chase has worked out that members can double dip and earn Chase Ultimate Rewards® and the relevant hotel points and potential elite status perks, too (as long as it is labeled as “eligible” in the search function).

Don’t forget about the $500 in built-in credits that come with your card, which renew each year and only further the value with Chase’s The Edit program.

#3072. Hornbeck Offshore (HOS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

First full quarter after the Helix merger shows a $1.9 billion backlog.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Hornbeck Offshore Services, Inc. (HOS -2.97%) reported its first financial results following the Sept. 1 completion of its combination with Helix, establishing a diversified platform across marine transportation, subsea services, and well intervention. Management indicated the transaction enables the company to participate across the full offshore project life cycle, from development through decommissioning. The combined entity is pursuing an integrated services strategy, aiming to capture higher margins by bundling vessel, robotics, and engineering capabilities. Management issued full-year 2027 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $500 million to $550 million, supported by a $1.9 billion contracted backlog and the expected delivery of two high-specification newbuild vessels starting in late 2027.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Hornbeck Offshore Services Third Quarter Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Today's call is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to introduce Potter Adams, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. Please go ahead, sir.

Robert Adams: Thanks, operator, and good morning, everyone. We appreciate you joining us for Hornbeck Offshore's conference call to review our third quarter 2026 results and recent developments. We also welcome participants listening to the call over the web. Joining me on the call today is Todd Hornbeck, President and Chief Executive Officer of Hornbeck Offshore. Please note that information reported on this call speaks only as of today, November 5, 2026, and therefore, you are advised that time-sensitive information may no longer be accurate as of the time of any replay listening or transcript reading.

During today's conference call, Todd and I will make certain projections about future financial performance, liquidity, operations and events that are not statements of historical fact and thus constitute forward-looking statements. These forward-looking statements are subject to risks, uncertainties and other factors that may cause such future matters, including the company's actual future performance to be materially different from that which is projected today. You can locate additional information about factors that could cause the company's results to materially differ from those projected in the forward-looking statements in Hornbeck's SEC filings and in yesterday's press release under the Investors section of the company's website, which is www.hornbeckoffshore.com or through the SEC website at www.sec.gov.

The earnings call also contains references to adjusted EBITDA and adjusted free cash flow, which are non-GAAP financial measures. A reconciliation of these financial measures is provided in the press release issued by the company yesterday afternoon. And finally, please note that the company uses its website as a means of disclosing material and other public information and for complying with disclosure obligations under SEC's Regulation FD. Such disclosures will be included on the company's website under the heading Investors. Accordingly, investors should monitor that portion of the company's website in addition to following the company's press releases, SEC filings, public conference calls and website. Now I'll turn the call over to Todd. Todd?

Todd Hornbeck: Thanks, Potter, and good morning, everyone. We thank you for joining us. This is an important quarter for Hornbeck as it marks our first earnings call following the completion of our combination with Helix on September 1. The transaction brought together 2 organizations with complementary assets, capabilities, talent and customer relationships. More details around the transaction can be found in the slides posted to our website. Potter will share some additional details later in his remarks. When we announced the combination in late April, we said we saw an opportunity to create a premier integrated offshore service company providing innovative marine and subsea solutions across deepwater oilfield, defense and renewable industries. This thesis has not changed.

What has changed is that we're now successfully executing it. Before we get to the results, I'd like to spend a moment discussing 3 key questions that we believe are most important to our shareholders. First, what exactly is the combined Hornbeck Offshore. Second, how does bringing these 2 businesses together create significant value. And third, what should investors expect from us as we continue to integrate the businesses and allocate capital. Let me start with the first question. What is Hornbeck Offshore Services today? The combined Hornbeck is a diversified deepwater offshore services business operating across 3 distinct segments: Marine Transportation & Specialty, Subsea Services and Well Intervention. We're not simply a larger offshore vessel company.

We now have a global reach, especially into additional premier energy basins around the world and participate across a considerably broader portion of the offshore life cycle with an emphasis on traditional and renewable energy and diversity through defense support and emerging technologies. Through our Marine Transportation & Specialty segment, we own and operate supply vessels, flotels and other assets to support drilling, development, military and other specialty activities. In our Subsea Services segment, we own and operate subsea vessels and robotics to provide inspection, repair and maintenance, engineering, construction and specialized project services. And through our Well Intervention segment, we help customers maintain, restore and extend production from existing traditional offshore infrastructure and ultimately provide decommissioning services.

This full life cycle exposure complete with innovative technologies that we deploy is a key part of our investment thesis. Offshore projects create demand for vessels, robotics and Subsea Services. Producing assets require ongoing inspection, repair, maintenance and intervention. And as oil fields mature, customers increasingly need well intervention and ultimately decommissioning services. In addition, our Well Intervention fleet should benefit from higher levels of production enhancement demand and the forecast increases in utilization and day rates for deepwater rigs. With this in mind, I also want to provide an update on our progress towards exiting the activities that are noncore to what I just outlined.

Prior to closing the merger, Helix divested of its shallow water decommissioning business, and we intend to wind down the oil and gas interest, including Thunder Hawk and Droshky that were previously acquired by Helix. We also expect to reduce our reliance on in-chartered vessels over time. We've already replaced one in chartered vessel. Because several existing commitments are long term, that transition will take some time, but the direction is clear. Given the focused portfolio we now operate, our job is to translate this full life cycle platform into higher utilization, stronger margins, greater free cash flow and improved returns on invested capital. Turning now to value creation. We see 4 primary ways that Hornbeck can deliver outsized returns.

First, our diversified platform gives us greater visibility across our customers' offshore programs. That allows us to identify more opportunities, compete for a greater scope of work and deploy a range of integrated assets and services across more projects and geographies. Second, it creates opportunities to improve asset utilization. A MPSV is more valuable when marketed as part of a broader solution, incorporating ROVs, engineering, subsea tooling and/or intervention capabilities. Likewise, our Subsea and Intervention business benefit from access to owned marine assets while creating opportunities for pull-through work for our high-specification OSV fleet. We have positioned the company and its assets into specific markets where we can drive integrated services.

Third, by assembling more capabilities within the same organization, we will retain a greater portion of the revenue, margin and cash flow associated with the projects. And fourth, our scale allows us to eliminate redundant costs and create efficiencies across procurement, maintenance, operations and the supply chain. In terms of what investors should expect from us as we continue to integrate the business and allocate capital, there are a few key points I'd like to highlight. One of the most important opportunities created by the combination is our integrated services. Complex offshore projects frequently require multiple service contractors with different operating schedules and commercial agreements.

The timing and scope of each of those vendors needs to be harmonized and each additional interface creates complexity and increases project risk. By bringing marine assets, ROVs, trenchers, engineering capabilities and intervention systems together under one roof, we can simplify and optimize those interfaces and coordinate a broader scope of work around our customers' requirements. For our customers, this means simpler contracting, more coordinated scheduling and clear accountability for execution. For Hornbeck, it means a greater share of our customer spending, better asset utilization and less economic leakage to third-party providers. We are already seeing the evidence that our customers value this model. This week, we announced service agreements with Shell covering operations in the U.S. Gulf of America.

The contemplated scope brings together assets from all 3 of our operating segments, including a riser-based well intervention vessel, and intervention riser system, ROVs, project management and engineering as well as a high-specification MPSV with ROVs and technical services and a Jones Act-compliant OSV to support these operations. Operations under those agreements are scheduled to commence in 2027 for a 5-year duration for the well intervention vessel and OSV. Importantly, this marks the first 5-year agreement for a Q vessel in over a decade. This is even a broader illustration of the opportunity we saw in combining these 2 companies.

Just like our North Sea award announced in September, these Shell agreements confirm that Hornbeck's unique offering and ability to bundle services is differentiating and positions us for sustainable growth and value creation. We also believe the combined businesses will create additional opportunities to grow our defense support business. We currently have several vessels chartered to the U.S. government performing a variety of work scopes. Most recently, we successfully completed a proof of concept to demonstrate the ability to quickly retrofit autonomous capabilities into a commercial supply vessel that had been previously modified for defense support work scope.

It has been reported that this HOS vessel is the largest vessel retrofitted with autonomy across the entire Department of Defense commercial fleet. Within the full spectrum of our market exposure, we currently see attractive opportunities in both Subsea Services and Well Intervention. In Subsea, one area of particular interest is deep and ultra-deepwater inspection, repair and maintenance. The offshore industry has accumulated a large installed base of subsea infrastructure, and that infrastructure continues to age. At the same time, EPIC or major subsea contractors have accumulated record levels of contracting backlog that will create demand as that backlog moves into execution over the next several years.

Operators need to inspect, repair and maintain these assets, extend their economic lives and support ongoing production. This creates recurring demand for vessels with large subsea cranes, ROVs and specialized technical capabilities, which is where we come in. Our recent organic investment in 8 additional world-class ROV systems is intended to position more of our MPSV fleet to address this opportunity by combining the vessel and subsea capability as these new assets deliver throughout 2027. We also believe Well Intervention gives us exposure to a growing part of the offshore life cycle. As the global offshore infrastructure continues to mature, operators are increasingly focused on maximizing recovery from existing subsea infrastructure they already own.

In many cases, intervention can restore or enhance production without requiring the capital and lead time associated with the new greenfield exploratory development. In addition, attractive commodity prices should drive production enhancement demand and forecasted increases in utilization and rates for deepwater rigs to support offshore drilling campaigns, which should benefit our well intervention fleet. That makes well intervention an important strategic complement to our marine and subsea businesses and gives Hornbeck additional exposure to production and decommissioning customer spending as offshore fields continue to mature. Defense and renewables remain another attractive long-term opportunity. Hornbeck spent the last 25 years developing the U.S.-flagged marine platform, customer relationships and operating capabilities required to serve the defense market.

This, in combination with Helix's subsea robotics, engineering and technical capabilities allows the combined company to now serve a broader range of missions. Our stacked fleet includes 23 Jones Act vessels and 1 Mexican flagged vessel that uniquely afford us the ability to rapidly and efficiently respond to incremental defense requirements. Those vessels can potentially be returned to service more quickly and with less capital than a new build. We will only reactivate capacity when the commercial arrangement appropriately compensates us for the required investment and execution risk. We're also well equipped to support offshore renewable energy projects.

We see indicators that our renewable customers in the North Sea have a growing backlog of projects requiring trenching and ROV services in that region, which is exactly what we're designed to do. I'd also like to touch a little bit on our organic growth strategy, which will remain focused on investments that increase the earnings capability of assets we already own or have under construction. As I mentioned, as a part of our strategy to grow our Subsea Services business, we will be acquiring 8 world-class ROV systems for approximately $56.4 million. Deliveries are expected to begin in the second quarter of 2027 and continue throughout the year with 4 systems designated for our 400 class ultra-deepwater newbuilds.

We also expect the first newbuild MPSV to become commercially available late in the third quarter of 2027 and the second in the second quarter of 2028. These highly capable assets designed for demanding subsea work were contemplated from the outset as vessels capable of supporting more technical complex services, including intervention and defense work. As a combined company, our commercial opportunity for these vessels is much broader because now we can market them alongside our robotics, engineering and subsea intervention capabilities. In closing, we believe the long-term deepwater offshore opportunity is especially attractive. But we also know that an attractive market by itself does not guarantee attractive shareholder returns. Performance and execution do.

Our responsibility is to operate safely, maintain asset reliability, price risk appropriately, integrate the business thoughtfully and allocate capital when prospective returns justify the investment. If we execute consistently against those priorities, we believe we can build a company capable of creating value not simply at the top of an offshore cycle, but throughout the cycle. I want to thank all of our offshore and shore-based employees for their continued focus during a period of substantial organizational change. Our team has been working tirelessly to ensure the successful integration of these 2 companies, and I want to recognize their efforts and dedication.

On that note, one thing I want to highlight is that we prioritize share ownership in the new company for our entire shoreside support team, not just the executives. We aim to foster a culture of ownership that is closely aligned with our investors, which we believe makes us unique among our public peers. With that, I'll turn over the call to Potter to take you through the numbers in more detail. Potter?

Robert Adams: Thanks, Todd. Before reviewing our third quarter results, there are 2 important points about this transitional quarter. First, because legacy Hornbeck is the accounting acquirer, our third quarter results include 3 months of legacy Hornbeck, but only 1 month of legacy Helix. Accordingly, the quarter should not be viewed as a run rate quarter for the combined company. Second, the quarter includes $79 million of merger and integration costs and $41 million of accelerated stock-based compensation expense associated with the transaction. With this in mind, our fourth quarter results will be the first to include 3 full months of operations from all 3 segments and will provide a better baseline for sequential comparisons going forward.

Please note, though, that the fourth quarter will reflect normal seasonality, planned dry dock and maintenance activity, project timing, mobilizations and integration costs. Following the merger, we have 326 million total basic shares. Additional details are included in the earnings release and our forthcoming 10-Q. We posted some slides to accompany the earnings release to our website yesterday. In those materials, you will find more information about the merger and certain consolidated and segment financial data, which we have adjusted to reflect results of the combined companies for the third quarter and certain historical periods for illustrative purposes.

With that context, rather than discussing the as-reported results and reviewing variances, which are included in the press release we issued yesterday, I'll walk through the third quarter results on an as-adjusted basis, which reflect the full quarter contribution of both legacy companies. I'll focus on the key financial data provided in the slides and the underlying operating drivers we believe will be most useful in evaluating our performance going forward. Against that backdrop, I'll now provide a recap of our consolidated results. Third quarter revenue was $503 million. Adjusted EBITDA was $155 million or 31% of revenue. Adjusted free cash flow was $99 million, resulting in a free cash flow conversion of 64%.

As we move beyond this transitional quarter, free cash flow conversion will be an important measure of our ability to translate adjusted earnings into capital available for committed investment, balance sheet management and other return-based opportunities. Before returning to the segment results, I wanted to emphasize that these are new reporting segments for the combined company and the historical results of legacy Hornbeck and legacy Helix do not match directly to the new structure. The assets, operations and related results of legacy Hornbeck and legacy Helix have been reassigned among the Marine Transportation, Subsea Services and Well Intervention segments.

Across the 3 segments, we believe the most useful operating statistics for modeling the business moving forward are the number of active vessels, average day rates, utilization and operating expense per vessel day. Together, these measures provide the clearest view of available earnings capacity, pricing, asset productivity and the cost required to generate that revenue. Project and geographic mix will also affect quarterly results, particularly in Subsea Services and Well Intervention. But these core statistics should provide investors with a consistent starting point for evaluating segment margins and cash generation over time. We have included more information, including the vessels that make up each segment in the slides posted to our website yesterday.

Our Marine Transportation and Specialty segment includes the OSVs, flotels and specialty vessels from the legacy Hornbeck fleet. Since this segment only includes legacy Hornbeck vessels, its results reflect a full quarter of operations. Total revenue was $153 million and adjusted EBITDA was $68 million with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 44%. We operated an average of 38.5 active vessels during the third quarter. Average day rates were approximately $52,000, active utilization was 77% and the resulting effective day rate for the active fleet was approximately $39,900. Subsea Services generated $106 million of revenue and $34 million of adjusted EBITDA, resulting in an adjusted EBITDA margin of 33% for the third quarter.

The active fleet was 12.3 vessels and included the full quarter contribution from 7 legacy Hornbeck vessels and 5 legacy Helix vessels and a partial quarter contribution from 1 vessel. Average day rates were $101,000, utilization was 78% and effective day rates were roughly $78,500. Well Intervention generated $237 million of revenue, $76 million of adjusted EBITDA and an adjusted EBITDA margin of 32%. The average fleet count was 8 for the quarter, inclusive of in-chartered vessels. Utilization was 91% with an average day rate of $349,000 and an effective day rate of $316,000. Please note that the sum of the segments does not reflect the additional results from the unallocated and other segments. Shifting to backlog.

As of September 30th, contracted revenue backlog was approximately $1.9 billion, including approximately $333 million expected during the remainder of 2026, $793 million during 2027 and $741 million thereafter. Our total backlog is comprised of $668 million, $431 million and $760 million for the Marine Transportation, Subsea Services and Well Intervention segments, respectively. While backlog provides meaningful visibility, ultimate realization will depend on project timing, vessel availability and execution. Let me now turn to synergies. At announcement of the merger, we identified at least $75 million of anticipated annual revenue and cost synergies to be realized within the first 3 years after closing, consisting of $45 million of revenue synergies and $30 million of cost synergies.

We have implemented actions representing approximately $20 million of expected annualized cost savings and expect to achieve our targeted cost synergies by the end of the first full year of combined operations. We are also targeting approximately $15 million of revenue synergies within the first year. The recently announced services agreements with Shell demonstrate the commercial opportunities created by the combined platform and the company's ability to provide a broader suite of offshore services to its customers. Beginning with fourth quarter reporting, our goal is to provide clearer visibility into these actions and their effect on margins and free cash flow. Ultimately, the combination should be judged by measurable improvements in earnings, cash conversion and returns.

I will now review some of our key balance sheet and liquidity-related items for the third quarter as well as our capital allocation priorities. We ended the quarter with approximately $472 million of cash, net of $1.6 million of restricted cash. That balance reflects roughly $230 million of payments for deal-related costs, including around $90 million for professional fees and integration, approximately $17 million for the brand licensing agreement and $58 million related to compensation due to the merger triggering a change in control for both legacy companies. We also used approximately $63 million of cash for withholding taxes related to net share settlements due to the vesting of stock previously issued under each legacy company's long-term incentive plan.

Importantly, we funded those obligations with cash rather than using shares, thereby avoiding additional dilution to our shareholders. Total debt had a face value of just over $730 million, and we had no borrowings under our $125 million revolving credit facility. Including revolver capacity, total liquidity was approximately $597 million. This financial flexibility of a healthy cash balance, low financial leverage and ample liquidity is important, and we will remain highly disciplined. Looking ahead, our capital allocation priorities remain straightforward: Maintain safe and reliable operations, fund required maintenance and recertification and complete committed investments that enhance the earnings capability of assets we already own.

Other reactivations, conversions, acquisitions, debt reduction and potential returns of capital will be evaluated based on their potential to create accretive shareholder value. Our 2 U.S.-flagged, Jones Act 400 class MPSVs remain on track for physical shipyard delivery during 2027. We expect approximately $74 million of remaining cash outlays related to the outfitting engineering and post-delivery enhancements, excluding capitalized interest. We expect the first vessel to enter commercial service late in the third quarter of 2027 and the second in 2Q 2028. Separately, we expect the majority of the remaining spending under our approximately $56 million ROV newbuild program to occur in 2027. Turning to the market.

We continue to view the long-term deepwater outlook as constructive, although near-term conditions vary by geography and service line. Activity in the Gulf of America remains measured while we continue to see attractive opportunities across several international markets, including Brazil, the North Sea and Europe. Importantly, the combined company's broader geographic and service line exposure means our investment thesis no longer depends on the activity level of any one single basin. With that context, I'll now spend a few more minutes on our guidance. Based on current backlog, customer commitments and operating plans, we expect adjusted EBITDA of $90 million to $100 million for the fourth quarter of 2026 and $500 million to $550 million for full year 2027.

The fourth quarter range reflects the first full quarter of combined operations, including normal seasonal and operational variability. It should not be annualized from September or viewed as a straight-line progression from the third quarter. Utilization for the fourth quarter is expected to be negatively impacted by 223 days of downtime associated with regulatory dry dockings comprised of 114, 75 and 34 days for the Marine Transportation, Subsea Services and Well Intervention segments, respectively. This compares to 50 days in total for the third quarter of 2026. There are several important assumptions underlying our outlook that I want to make clear about our 2027 guidance.

First, we assume no material earnings contribution from the noncore assets and activities that Todd discussed earlier. Second, 2027 will be a comparatively heavy regulatory dry dock year with scheduled downtime weighted towards the first half. We currently expect 407 days of regulatory dry dock downtime during the first quarter alone, including 148 days in Marine Transportation, 89 days in Subsea Services and 170 days in Well Intervention. When operationally feasible, we intentionally schedule this work during seasonally lower activity periods. Third, the outlook includes the $20 million of cost synergies already implemented and therefore, does not assume realization of the full synergy opportunity.

Fourth, as I just discussed, we assume contribution from the first HOS 400 class MPSV newbuild beginning late in the third quarter 2027. Finally, our guidance assumes U.S. Gulf of America deepwater drilling activity remains consistent with current levels. We are not relying on a material increase in GoA rig activity to achieve the outlook. To the extent customer activity improves from current levels, that could provide additional opportunities, but our base case does not require it. Our 2027 guidance incorporates current expectations for backlog conversion, vessel availability, project timing, geographic and service line mix and normal seasonal variability. We will provide a more detailed 2027 guidance framework when we report our fourth quarter results in February.

Looking ahead, our objective over the coming quarters is to establish a clear combined company baseline and demonstrate measurable progress in our results across margins, free cash flow conversion and synergy realization. These measures connect the strategic case Todd described earlier to the financial outcomes we are accountable for delivering. With that, I'll turn the call back to the operator to entertain questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question we will hear from Keith Beckmann with Pickering Energy Partners.

Todd Hornbeck: Yes. Look, it's going great. We just -- it's been 60 days since we announced the merger. The teams are working great. And I think it's a big win to justify why we put these companies together within 60 days, signing a major contract for the company with a Q vessel, a supply vessel and an MPSV and a bundling contract. So I think that's a testament of why we put the companies together. We're getting a tremendous amount of response from our customer base since we announced about these types of opportunities that we can offer today that each individual company could not do on their own before.

So we can actually take the entire life of field, use our supply vessels, our MPSVs, robotics, engineering across all of our engineering disciplines, do stimulation work, intervention work and then at the end, the decommissioning and take up all the jewelry and everything on the seaport at a one-stop shop. That's a very unique combination of heavy assets, tooling assets and engineering capability that I think differentiates us from all the other service companies and really puts Hornbeck in a different league of company. We're not just an asset owning company anymore.

We're actually an execution company and integration company as well. So very excited about that. And within 60 days, signing a major contract like that is pretty remarkable.

Keith Beckmann: Awesome. That's very helpful. And then, my second question just kind of revolves around thinking about the Gulf longer term as well. And then -- but maybe how are you guys thinking about that region longer term and a potential return to activity and particularly next year as well on the support vessel side, I mean, what is some of the offsetting factors? Is that some potential defense work? Just maybe how you're thinking about that longer term in the Gulf here.

Todd Hornbeck: Well, the Gulf has been relatively flat on rig count for the last 3 years, but we've expanded our margins and utilization during that time and putting the company together even makes it a more robust company. We're not just a Gulf of Mexico player, even though I believe in long-term basin play, it's a world-class basin for hydrocarbons. I think that will continue in the future. But we operate all over the world. We're a global player now. So -- and with our defense and our alternative opportunities, we can move these assets around very efficiently. And also, we don't really need the rig count to do the bundling and do the life of field services.

And what you've seen also is major announcements with tree installation and development in the Gulf of Mexico that is a big portion of our business with the robotics and the MPSVs and the well intervention and stimulation assets. So I think that combination today, we can still utilize all the PSVs and everything on other projects than just turning a bit. Operator: And next, we'll move to Don Crist with Johnson Rice.

They understood what we were doing. And the influx of us being able to put work packages together to do life of field services and bundling has been more robust than anything else that we've seen.

While we do have a lot of opportunities in the company because of the global reach now, we can do a proper alternative analysis on what's the best -- how we maximize revenue and manage risk because we can weigh all these opportunities against each other for the company. And also what's driving is what you know is our military business, our defense work is really starting to pick up. And you can see just read the papers every day and you know why. So pretty excited about just not only geographic reach, but all of the inbound that we're getting across the globe of looking at projects that we probably never -- individually, we probably wouldn't see if the companies were separated today because of the work packages and the engineering and the back office things that we can do that we couldn't do as each company independent.

Donald Crist: Appreciate that. And one question on the comments on your scripted remarks. I think you said that you wanted to exit charter vessels. Were you referring to the Siem vessels down in Brazil? Or are those vessels that they have not had?

Todd Hornbeck: Well, we look at everything. Everything is on the table. In-chartered vessels, as you know, carry a liability, long-term contracts, and we're a heavy asset-owning company with the soft skills of the engineering and the tooling. So it's better for us to own our own equipment and manage our destiny a little bit better than relying on third parties. Number one, not just to capture the cash flow and the returns, but also when you get to a tight market, if something was to happen to a third-party vessel for any reason at all, it could be pretty difficult to replace. So controlling the destiny of where we're going in the capital return and really lowering the risk.

And look, when you have too many in-chartered vessels, in my mind, it's also a credit issue as well with the rating agencies and others. So we're also looking for the lowest cost of capital for the company over the time period. And we believe that is owning our own equipment and servicing our clients 100%.

Donald Crist: Okay. And just one more final one for me, if I could slip it in. On the M&A front, obviously, you have a really good balance sheet here, which you may have to refinance the debt and put it together here shortly. But after that, are there some attractive targets that may be in a region that you're not operating in today, whether it be Brazil or West Africa or somewhere else that look attractive today?

Todd Hornbeck: There's a tremendous amount of opportunities across the globe to look at. And with our company today, the integration that we've done with the 2 companies, it opens up more opportunities. But as a public company, as investors, natural to ask about our growth plans. The way we think about it is our financial strength provides us significant flexibility to evaluate a wide range of accretive growth opportunities. But always, we're going to focus on increasing shareholder value. So it's got to pass the smell test with us. But I can tell you that there are opportunities around. Operator: And moving on, we'll hear from James West with Melius Research.

James West: Todd, the Shell transaction or the Shell contract, sorry, is really, really impressive. And I know that Hornbeck has a long legacy relationship with Shell. And look, we will -- we expect to expand on that relationship. This is just the first phase, but we are getting inbounds from other major oil companies to do the exact same thing. So whether it's a bundling or whether it's life of field services, all of that is coming into focus as a one-stop shop, very easy to contract with us because we own all the equipment.

We can build a lot of efficiencies in with our customers because they're not chartering from 4 or 5 different asset owning companies and trying to marry up the different agreements, the insurances, the time they have to put them on and off. James West: And then maybe a quick follow-up for me, maybe unrelated, but on the military business, I know you can't go into a lot of detail here, but it's become a big part of the company. Is there room to grow that further? I mean it's a great kind of consistent cash flow business that underpins your interest expense and things like that. Todd Hornbeck: Yes. The way we think about it in the future is that, look, we've got 23 vessels that are able to go quickly to the military at a very low cost. And it's like almost an internal acquisition. It's organic growth, but they've been well maintained. They were the deepwater vessels of the last up cycle. And they are very adaptable to the projects that we're looking at with the military and what we know they need in the future. And as we reported, we've done -- the technology that we're developing with several others on autonomy and AI is really moving that forward.

So yes, there's not just an opportunity just to expand our defense services, but also not just to fees or debt or anything, but actually a profitable -- big profitable segment of the company with a tremendous amount of upside growth there. Look, we're doing a lot with technology. Hornbeck Offshore has always been a technology company first. And what we've done is we developed whether it was back in the day when we were developing the very first DP1 continuous duty rating DP systems or Dynamic Positioning Systems or DP2 or all of the other technology we've brought over the years to the market.

We take that technology and then we just wrap it in a steel hull with different components to do a service. So really, what drives the force of the company and the growth a lot of times is our technology that we're developing right now that we can use on our existing fleet and then eventually ships of the future could be a decade out or for whatever it may be with the military, it may be in alternatives. It may be new ventures in ultra-deepwater complex areas to operate.

So we're pretty excited about the field of view, not just in the oil and gas business, but all the other deepwater regions of the world that have different applications that are coming to the forefront because of technology, and that's where we're at the pointy end of the stick.

Operator: Next from Greg Lewis with BTIG.

Gregory Lewis: Just following up on James' question around the Shell contract. So this is just the first phase, but this is -- you're on it, on that it is -- it's got minimums with growth opportunities as well. But the minimums are very, very substantial.

Gregory Lewis: And then, Potter, just as we think about the guidance, the $500 million to the $550 million, I don't know what else you -- like as we think about the swing factors in that, just thinking about marine transportation, is that largely the driver between the high end and the low end? Is it mid- high 70s? Is that kind of a fair way to start thinking about '27?

Robert Adams: Yes. I mean we outlined kind of those key assumptions in the prepared remarks, Greg. One of the key things is the heavy dry dock year, and we gave you those numbers in the slide deck and on our guidance slide to show what the impact on utilization should be for those dry dock days. But really, I mean, I think when we think about upside, yes, Marine Transportation, we kind of outlined the Gulf of America, should activity pick up there. We see upside from that basin. But also, as Todd provided, there is a growing Well Intervention market. And with rig utilization tightening and day rates increasing there, that only benefits our assets in that segment.

And then as we build out the IRM business in Subsea, we think that there's additional opportunities there. So as we said, we're constructive on the overall macro. But in the Gulf of America, we're not reliant on increased activity, but that could produce upside to our guidance if that does come to fruition.

Todd Hornbeck: Greg, I would also add to that is that we have a tremendous amount of operating leverage in the business. And not just from -- on every segment, we see growth opportunities, whether the rigs are going back to drilling rigs are doing more exploratory development drilling or the military business with more contracts coming there or even alternatives. But what we've created here is new demand for the company by being able to bundle and do life of field services that didn't exist for each company before. So even without demand drivers increasing, if it stayed flat, we are creating more demand for our equipment by the nature of how we're redoing the business model and the business plan.

We're no longer dependent on just a drilling rig going to work or something that happened with the commodity price going up. We can stay in the environment here and still have a tremendous amount of operating leverage. So with that type of exposure and the strengths of the company that we're putting together, we can really full life cycle exposure that we didn't have before. We've got innovative technologies that we're bringing to create demand as well for our business. The market diversity geographically opening up a tremendous amount of markets. That's opened up demand for the company without changing any of the demand profile out there.

It's opened up demand for us because of putting the companies together, the expanded geographic footprint. But I do believe the share price doesn't fully reflect the value of HOS today. So I think it's a good time to buy. I got to just put that in there.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn the floor back to Todd Hornbeck for closing remarks.

Apparel grew 38% at constant currency, and management's plan to triple that category over three years is a goal worth tracking.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, On Holding (ONON -7.54%) announced that quarterly net sales grew 17.8% at constant currency (excluding foreign exchange rate fluctuations) to CHF 931.4 million. The footwear maker expanded gross margins by protecting full-price selling despite promotional pressure across the broader apparel market. Three takeaways from management's comments illustrate how the business is positioning for long-term compound growth.

The Cloudsurfer 3 performance running shoe represents the first launch of On Holding's new sensation-based franchise architecture and SURREAL superfoam technology. Run specialty retail partners are seeing rapid product turnover without relying on price markdowns.

Direct-to-consumer (DTC) sales, which include transactions through company stores and e-commerce platforms, expanded faster than wholesale while deepening engagement with younger shoppers. Management maintained strict full-price discipline across channels to expand underlying profit margins.

Apparel revenue expanded rapidly as On Holding introduced dedicated women's training collections and high-productivity store layouts. Accelerating store apparel productivity supports management's plan to triple category sales over three years.

Full-year net sales are tracking toward low 20s percentage growth at constant currency, and momentum is building across global retail markets as new innovation cycles land.

Proprietary foam technology and direct retail channels provide structural competitive advantages while management maintains pricing discipline and controlled international expansion.

#3070. Kraft Heinz Yields 6.6% and Coca-Cola Yields 2.3%. Here's Why Only 1 of These Dividend Stocks Is a Buy This November.

One stock offers a massive 6.6% yield, while the other pays a modest 2.3%. Here's why the smaller dividend is actually the better buy for serious income investors right now.

Some yields make an investor's eyebrows go up before the brain catches up. Kraft Heinz (KHC -0.74%) at 6.6% is one of them. Coca-Cola's (KO +0.92%) 2.3% yield barely registers beside it.

That's what makes this pairing fun, because the quiet number is the one I'd actually want to own.

A yield that large is the wedge of cheese in the mousetrap: attractive precisely because something went wrong with the price.

Kraft Heinz shares sit at $24.24 on Nov. 10, down 35.3% over five years and 70.2% over ten. The $1.60 annual dividend didn't get fatter in the last five years. The stock fell, driving the yield higher without any help from payout boosts.

The latest quarter didn't help. Net sales fell 2% to $6.1 billion, adjusted operating income dropped 15.2%, and adjusted EPS slid from $0.61 to $0.53. Philadelphia cream cheese is losing sales volume as shoppers drift toward cottage cheese and other protein-forward options, and the company's own pricing moves have backfired in the category. Addressing cost inflation on the Q3 earnings call, CEO Steven Cahillane called it "disappointing, but it's real," and management expects it to run slightly above 5% in 2027. That forecast looks like a warning shot on Kraft Heinz's margins.

There are bright spots, to be fair. Emerging markets grew 15.6% organically, and a ramen version of Kraft Dinner in Canada sold three months of inventory in one week. That's a real winner. But the broader North American market, which is the largest part of Kraft Heinz's business, saw organic sales fall by 3.2%. Solid international revenue growth didn't help much, accounting for only $6.4 billion of last year's $24.9 billion total. Good news from the smallest part of the company can't carry the bigger chunk.

The dividend isn't in imminent danger. Free cash flow was $2.4 billion in the first nine months of 2026, about 120% of adjusted net income, against $1.4 billion of dividend payouts. Third-quarter free cash flow of $702 million covered the $474 million dividend about 1.5 times. The worry is direction.

Adjusted EPS guidance ranged from $2.07 to $2.13, so the $1.60 eats about 76% of the midpoint. Adjusted operating income is headed for a roughly 17% drop. A flat payout against shrinking profit is how a cushion thins out, and one more year of inflation outrunning the company's price increases could scuttle this turnaround.

Coca-Cola, meanwhile, posted 7% organic revenue growth in the third quarter. Pair that with 5% unit case volume growth, and comparable EPS up 11% to $0.91. If the Coca-Cola company is an engine, India is the piston that never misfires: all 10 of Coke's top brands there grew by double-digit percentages, and Sprite alone rose nearly 20%.

"We expanded our Sprite & Spicy platform into the QSR channel in India with meal combo activations, social media content, and influencer collaborations," CEO Henrique Braun explained on Coke's latest earnings call.

Now the company is applying the lessons learned in India to other potential growth markets, including single-serve drinks in South Africa.

The dividend looks sturdy next to that well-oiled cash machine. The estimated $2.20 annual payout is 67.1% of earnings, and it has grown about 5% a year over both three and five years. Free cash flow was $11.4 billion through nine months, compared with roughly $6.8 billion in dividends, and full-year free cash flow is guided to at least $13 billion. Net debt is 1.3 times EBITDA, below the 2 to 2.5 times target range, which leaves room to breathe.

The stock isn't cheap. I see a P/E of 28.6 and a price-to-free-cash-flow ratio of 29.2, and the shares are up 39% year to date, setting all-time highs on a weekly basis recently.

The average analyst target of $99.05 implies just 2.2% upside. Refranchising the African bottler is expected to cost 8 points of 2027 revenue and 2 points of EPS, and an IRS dispute is still waiting on a court decision.

New money buys a 2.3% yield. That doesn't look terribly generous at first glance.

I'd rather own the 2.3% that grows than the 6.6% that is waiting to be rescued. Kraft Heinz might well pull off its turnaround, and management plans to provide more details on 2027 at an investor meeting this month. But until the numbers say so, Kraft Heinz's big yield is a warning sign, not a gift.

#3069. The Homebuying Advice Service Members Need (but Don’t Always Get)

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

VA mortgage borrowers are quietly navigating a knowledge gap. Here’s how to close it.

If your understanding of a VA home loan starts and ends with “it’s for the military,” you’re not alone. For many eligible veterans and service members, the intricate workings (and benefits) of this U.S. government-backed mortgage are obscured behind lackluster guidance.

While there are classes and resources available, the military is broadly wary of steering members in a specific direction, says Alex Rodino, a real estate agent and U.S. Army veteran who served 10 years as an infantry officer and military advisor. “A lot of the course material is just very generic,” he says.

And that’s not a surprise. Considering the sheer size and scope of the military, providing personalized advice on VA loans to all its members would be no easy task.

That leaves real estate agents and lenders as the last line of defense, which is where a big part of the knowledge gap exists. Rodino purchased his first home in 2020 with a VA loan and says he didn’t like how ignorant he felt during the process.

“The reason I actually got my real estate license to begin with was because of that experience I had,” Rodino says. “Looking back on it, I had a lot of questions that didn't really get answered.”

But how can VA borrowers navigate this knowledge gap without having to become mortgage experts in their spare time? Here are some of the most important things to know when considering a VA loan, according to the financial experts and borrowers who have lived it.

“My mortgage broker said, hey, you might qualify for this, look it up,” says Elizabeth Valente, a real estate investor and former U.S. Army officer who bought her first home using a VA loan in 2021. When it came to the application process, she felt crucial information wasn’t readily available to her or fully explained.

In hindsight, Valente says, working with an agent or lender who had detailed VA loan experience would have been beneficial. Not only would it help untangle the specific paperwork and appraisal requirements, but that expertise offers an important layer of support for military borrowers.

“For some processes in the military, it's very hand-holding,” Valente says. “I'll tell you what to wear, what to bring, when to be there.” But that’s not always true when transitioning back to civilian life, and parsing specifics of a loan process can be challenging. “I don't think a typical Realtor would understand what that person's going through,” Valente says.

Finding professionals with the right expertise involves asking questions — and lots of them.

“If I'm the smartest person in the room, we have an issue,” Valente says. “Don't be afraid to tell someone if something doesn't make sense or if you don't understand the numbers.”

Before agreeing to work with a lender or mortgage broker, ask how their process works, what companies they work with, and how familiar they are with VA loans. Treat the initial conversation like an interview — you’re hiring them, not the other way around.

Knowing where to find your Certificate of Eligibility (COE) and how much you might be eligible to borrow is the responsibility of the person applying, Valente says. “All that information — it is available in the [VA] website but you really have to dig for it.”

And this information isn’t recreational reading — your COE lists your "basic entitlement," which is a crucial figure in VA lending. If you have full basic entitlement, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) generally guarantees 25% of the loan, which in most cases lets you put 0% down.

Why? With a quarter of the loan guaranteed by the VA, the lender is more protected and thus more willing to forgo a down payment.

So how do you know if you have full basic entitlement? Look for the figure $36,000 on your COE. This dollar amount represents full entitlement. Technically, basic entitlement is for loans up to $144,000, but then your bonus entitlement kicks in and you can go higher. The VA doesn’t set loan limits when you have full entitlement — though your lender will still decide how much you can borrow based on your income, debts, credit and the home’s appraised value.

Let’s say you want to buy a home in Fayetteville, North Carolina, and you need a $200,000 loan. In order to put no money down, your entitlement needs to cover at least 25% of the loan amount — in this example, that’s $50,000. After you purchase the home, your COE will show your basic entitlement as $0 and the entitlement charged to a previous loan as $50,000.

“Serving in the military is a unique investing opportunity that most people don't get,” Rodino says. “I wish someone had told me to buy a house when I got to my first duty station.”

If he’d known it was possible or understood how, Rodino says he would have been able to buy in 2017, move in 2020, rent out his first home and then repeat the process. “I'd have three by now and the first one would probably be paid off.”

This particular plan is partly based on the unique schedule of many military members. “Generally, you're moving anywhere from two to four to six years,” Rodino says. Owning multiple properties also leverages two big (and often misunderstood) perks of the VA loan: It’s possible to have more than one active loan at the same time, and after one year, you may be able to convert your primary residence to a rental.

Let’s go back to Fayetteville, North Carolina. After two years, you decide to rent out the home because you’re moving to Bell County, Texas. The home you want to buy in Bell County is $300,000, and in order to make no down payment, you need the VA to guarantee 25% of the loan ($75,000).

Because you no longer have full basic entitlement — remember, you already have an active VA loan elsewhere — your entitlement is capped at 25% of the conforming loan limit in the county where you plan to buy, minus what’s already being used on your first loan ($50,000 in our Fayetteville example).

Now for the math: The current conforming loan limit in Bell County is $832,750. Multiply this figure by 25% and subtract the $50,000 already in use: You have $158,187.50 of entitlement available to you — plenty to guarantee the $75,000 needed on the new loan.

If all of this sounds overwhelming, you’re not wrong. There are resources out there to help you figure all of this out, Rodino says. “The problem is, they're not always practical or they're not always apparent.”

The VA has a website that can walk you through entitlement calculations, but you should also ask your lender, broker or agent. If you’re working with experienced folks, they’ll be able to explain these details and help you get the most out of the VA’s guarantees.

The key takeaway is this: While each VA loan must initially be for a primary residence, borrowers can leverage their entitlement to build an investment portfolio without needing to cough up large down payments.

But these examples don’t consider all of the factors that go into approvals. Like most mortgages, your income, debts and assets dictate your eligibility. And although the VA doesn’t impose credit score minimums, most lenders do — NerdWallet's analysis shows 620 is a common floor.

It’s also important to note that a VA loan’s 0% down isn’t free. VA loans carry a funding fee based on how much you’re putting down and whether it’s your first or subsequent use (certain disabled veterans are exempt). You can pay this up front at closing or roll it into the loan amount; again, your team of professionals should be able to walk you through your options.

“I think there's the assumption that this is what we do: We get our VA home loan and we go buy a home,” says Julie Soares, financial readiness director for the Wounded Warrior Project. When we’re given access to a benefit that offers discounts and perks, it can be hard not to take advantage of it. But this is why financial awareness is critical.

There are a lot of conversations happening right now around homeownership and whether it’s the right choice, especially as affordability remains challenging. So if you haven’t heard it recently, here’s a reminder: Buying property is not the only way to build wealth or create financial security.

“The financial readiness program at Wounded Warrior Project is really leaning into getting further upstream in those conversations,” Soares says. Having a clear understanding of your benefits before you need to use them allows you to make more informed choices.

While it's helpful to understand your entitlement and what you may be eligible to borrow, you don't have to know every little detail about mortgages, or navigate the process alone. Sometimes, the most important thing to know about VA loans is where to turn for help.

If you are unsure of your eligibility or want more information about home loans, you can call the VA's home loans hotline at 877-827-3702.

“Please reach out to Wounded Warrior Project, reach out to the VA, reach out to any service organization,” Soares says. “Not one organization is gonna be able to fix or solve all of these problems. We have to do this as a group.”

#3068. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

#3067. Groupon: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Groupon's push to rebuild buyer trust and its LivingSocial relaunch for AI agents hinge on whether repeat purchases can offset the near-term billings cost.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 10, 2026, Groupon (GRPN -23.05%) announced Q3 revenue of $125 million, a 2% year-over-year increase. Long-term investors must track how management rebuilds marketplace quality while shifting operations toward artificial intelligence. Three things management said stand out.

Management is purging low-quality merchants and offering easier refunds to build long-term buyer trust. Refunding unhappy customers reduced billings growth by nearly two percentage points, but leadership expects higher repeat purchases over time.

Leadership is restructuring internal workflows using FoundryAI, the company's proprietary artificial intelligence (AI) platform. Automating customer service interactions cuts operating overhead and lets smaller software engineering teams develop features faster.

Consumers are increasingly relying on autonomous digital assistants to search for and reserve local activities. Management relaunched LivingSocial as a testbed for agentic commerce, allowing AI agents to book deals directly for users.

Automation and efficiency gains reshape internal workflows as the platform leans into technology. The business builds leverage through direct software connections into partner booking systems and automated customer support.

Management prioritizes inventory expansion in local services while demanding disciplined marketing returns. Leadership expects expanded experience inventory and automated operations to build long-term value.

Burn-center rollout advances as international sales timing slips into 2027.

Spectral AI, Inc. (MDAI +0.65%) reported a strategic transition from a research-focused organization to a commercial enterprise during the third quarter.
